Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 20, verses 1–3:

On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿Ta Ha. We did not send down the Qur'an to you to make you distressed. Only as a reminder for one who fears.﴾

Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn Jarir said: The people of interpretation differed concerning the interpretation of His words ﴿Ta Ha﴾. Some of them said: its meaning is "O man."

Mention of those who said this:

Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Abu Tumaylah related to us, from al-Hasan ibn Waqid, from Yazid al-Nahwi, from Ikrimah, from Ibn Abbas: "Ta Ha" – in Nabataean – means "O man."

Muhammad ibn Sa'd related to me, saying: my father related to me, saying: my paternal uncle related to me, saying: my father related to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿Ta Ha. We did not send down the Qur'an to you to make you distressed﴾: his people said, "This man has become wretched through his Lord," so Allah, mentioned and exalted, sent down ﴿Ta Ha﴾, meaning: "O man," ﴿We did not send down the Qur'an to you to make you distressed﴾.

Al-Qasim related to us, saying: al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: Abd Allah ibn Muslim, or Ya'la ibn Muslim, informed me, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, that he said: "Ta Ha" means "O man" in Syriac.

Ibn Jurayj said: Zam'ah ibn Salih informed me, from Salamah ibn Wahram, from Ikrimah, from Ibn Abbas, the same. Ibn Jurayj said: Mujahid also said that.

Imran ibn Musa al-Qazzaz related to us, saying: Abd al-Warith ibn Sa'id related to us, saying: Amarah related to us, from Ikrimah, regarding His words ﴿Ta Ha﴾, he said: "O man"; he spoke to him in Nabataean.

Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Yahya ibn Wadih related to us, saying: Abd Allah related to us, from Ikrimah, regarding His words ﴿Ta Ha﴾, he said: "In Nabataean: O human being."

Muhammad ibn Bashshar related to us, saying: Abu Asim related to us, from Qurrah ibn Khalid, from al-Dahhak, regarding His words ﴿Ta Ha﴾, he said: "O man" in Nabataean.

Muhammad ibn Bashshar related to us, saying: Abd al-Rahman related to us, saying: Sufyan related to us, from Husayn, from Ikrimah, regarding His words ﴿Ta Ha﴾, he said: "O man."

Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah, regarding His words ﴿Ta Ha﴾, he said: "O man," and it is in Syriac.

Al-Hasan related to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah and al-Hasan, regarding His words ﴿Ta Ha﴾, they both said: "O man."

I was told on the authority of al-Husayn, who said: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: Ubayd, meaning Ibn Sulayman, informed us, saying: I heard al-Dahhak say regarding His words ﴿Ta Ha﴾: "O man."

Others said: it is one of the names of Allah, and an oath that Allah swore by.

Mention of those who said this:

Ali related to us, saying: Abd Allah related to us, saying: Mu'awiyah related to me, from Ali, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿Ta Ha﴾, he said: "It is an oath that Allah swore by, and it is one of the names of Allah."

Others said: it is the letters of the alphabet (huruf hija').

Others said: it is disconnected letters (huruf muqatta'ah), each letter of which indicates a meaning, and they differed about this just as they differed concerning Alif Lam Mim.

We have mentioned this in its proper places and explained it with its evidences.

The view that is closer to correctness in my opinion among these views is the view of the one who said: its meaning is "O man," because it is a word known among the tribe of 'Akk, as has reached me, and its meaning among them is "O man." Someone recited to Mutammim ibn Nuwayrah:

"I called out 'Ta Ha' in the battle, but he did not answer, so I feared for him that he would be a fugitive."

[The verse is by Mutammim ibn Nuwayrah as the author said. In Lisan al-'Arab (under "tahtaha"): al-Layth, in explaining "Ta Ha," said it is definitively Ethiopian for "O man." He said: whoever reads "Ta Ha" reads two letters. It has reached us that when Moses heard the speech of the Lord, mighty and majestic, fear seized him until he stood on the tips of his toes out of fear, so Allah, mighty and majestic, said: "Ta Ha," meaning: be at peace. Al-Farra': "Ta Ha" is a letter of the alphabet. He said: it came in the tafsir that "Ta Ha" means "O man," "O human being." He said: Qays related from Asim, from Zirr, who said: a man recited to Ibn Mas'ud "Ta Ha," and Abd Allah said to him: "Ta Ha" with two kasras. The man said: Was it not only commanded that he should set his foot down? Abd Allah said to him: "Thus did the Messenger of Allah ﷺ recite it to me." Al-Farra' said: some reciters would separate it as "Ta. Ha." Al-Azhari related from Abu Hatim, who said: "Ta Ha" is the opening of a surah; then the speech resumed, addressing the Prophet ﷺ, saying: ﴿We did not send down the Qur'an to you to make you distressed.﴾ Qatadah said: "Ta Ha" in Syriac means "O man." Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Ikrimah said: it is in Nabataean, "O man," and this was related from Ibn Abbas. End quote from Lisan.]

Another said:

"Indeed foolishness is 'Ta Ha' among your character traits; may Allah not bless the accursed people."

[This verse is like the previous one, indicating that the meaning of "Ta Ha" in Arabic speech is "O man"; I have not identified the poet of this verse.]

Since this is known among them as we have mentioned, it is obligatory that its interpretation be directed to what is known among them of its meaning, especially when this agrees with the interpretation of the people of knowledge among the Companions and the Successors.

So the interpretation of the speech, then, is: "O man, We did not send down the Qur'an to you to make you distressed," meaning: We did not send it down to you so that We burden you with deeds beyond your capacity. It was mentioned that this was said to him because of the hardship, toil and sleeplessness he endured in standing at night in prayer.

Mention of those who said this:

Muhammad ibn Amr related to me, saying: Abu Asim related to us, saying: Isa related to us; and al-Harith related to me, saying: al-Hasan related to us, saying: Warqa' related to us, all from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding ﴿We did not send down the Qur'an to you to make you distressed﴾, he said: it is like His saying ﴿So recite what is easy of it﴾; they used to hang ropes on their chests during the prayer.

Al-Qasim related to us, saying: al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, regarding ﴿We did not send down the Qur'an to you to make you distressed﴾, he said: in prayer, like His saying ﴿So recite what is easy of it﴾; they used to hang ropes on their chests in prayer.

Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah, regarding ﴿We did not send down the Qur'an to you to make you distressed﴾: "By Allah, Allah did not make it a cause of wretchedness, but made it a mercy, a light, and a guide to Paradise."

And His words ﴿Only as a reminder for one who fears﴾.

He, mentioned and exalted, says: We did not send down this Qur'an to you except as a reminder for one who fears the punishment of Allah, so that he guards himself by performing the obligations of his Lord and avoiding His prohibitions.

As:

Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah, regarding His words ﴿Only as a reminder for one who fears﴾: Allah sent down His books and sent His messengers as a mercy by which Allah had mercy on His servants, so that the one who remembers may remember, and a man may benefit from what he hears of the Book of Allah, which is a reminder to him, in which Allah sent down what is lawful and unlawful, and He said ﴿A revelation from He who created the earth and the high heavens﴾.

Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His words ﴿Only as a reminder for one who fears﴾: "What We sent down to you is a reminder for one who fears."

So the meaning of the speech is: "O man, We did not send down this Qur'an to you so that you would be distressed by it; We did not send it down except as a reminder for one who fears."

The people of Arabic grammar differed concerning the grammatical case of "tadhkirah" (reminder). Some grammarians of Basra said: it is in apposition (badal) to His words ﴿to make you distressed﴾, so that it means: "We did not send down the Qur'an to you except as a reminder." Some grammarians of Kufa said: it is in the accusative on the basis of His words "We did not send it down except as a reminder." Some of them denied the statement of the one who says it is in apposition to ﴿to make you distressed﴾, saying: that is not permissible, because ﴿to make you distressed﴾ is in the negated context, while ﴿except as a reminder﴾ is in the affirmed context; rather it is a repetition. Some said: the meaning of the speech is: "We did not send down the Qur'an to you except as a reminder for one who fears, not to make you distressed."

Some said: the meaning of the speech is: "We did not send down the Qur'an to you except as a reminder for one who fears, not to make you distressed."

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 20, verse 4–5:

The interpretation of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿A revelation from He who created the earth and the high heavens (4). The Most Merciful, who is established upon the Throne (5)﴾

His saying, may He be exalted and remembered, to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ): this Qur'an is a revelation from the Lord who created the earth and the high heavens. Al-ʿUlā (the high) is the plural of ʿulyā.

The grammarians of Arabic differed over the reason for the accusative case of His saying ﴿tanzīlan﴾ (a revelation). Some of the grammarians of Basra said: it is put in the accusative by the sense of "Allah revealed a revelation." Others, who rejected this, said: this is from two utterances, but the meaning is: "It is a revelation," then the word "huwa" (it) was dropped and it was joined to the speech before it, so it came out of it and was not part of its wording.

Abu Jaʿfar (al-Tabari) said: Both opinions are, in my view, not wrong.

* *

As for His saying ﴿The Most Merciful, who is established upon the Throne﴾:

His saying, may He be exalted and remembered: the Most Merciful is raised up over His Throne and exalted.

I have already explained the meaning of "istiwāʾ" (establishment/settling) with its evidences earlier, and mentioned the disagreement of those who differ concerning it, so that is sufficient and there is no need to repeat it in this place. As for the nominative case of "al-Raḥmān," there are two possibilities. One is that it is in apposition to the meaning of His saying "tanzīlan," so the sense of the speech becomes: He sent it down from the One who created the earth and the heavens; it was sent down by the Most Merciful who is established upon the Throne. The other is that it is governed by His saying ﴿established upon the Throne﴾, because in His saying "istawā" there is a pronoun referring back to "al-Raḥmān."

The interpreters of the Qur'an have said something similar to what we have said regarding this.

Those who said this:

- Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying ﴿and whatever is beneath the soil﴾: al-thara is every moist thing.

- I was told by al-Husayn ibn al-Faraj, who said: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: 'Ubayd informed us, saying: I heard al-Dahhak say regarding His saying ﴿and whatever is beneath the soil﴾: what is dug out of the earth while still moist. He only meant by that: what is beneath the seven earths.

Similarly:

- Muhammad ibn Ibrahim al-Sulaymi, known as Ibn Sadran [[In al-Khulasah by al-Khazraji: Muhammad ibn Ibrahim ibn Sadran, with a dammah on the first unpointed letter, al-Azdi, with a ya' after the lam that is kasrah.]], narrated to me, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Rifa'ah narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn Ka'b regarding ﴿and whatever is beneath the soil﴾: he said: al-thara is seven earths.

* *

The interpretation of His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿And if you speak aloud, then indeed He knows the secret and that which is more hidden (akhfa). Allah – there is no deity except Him. To Him belong the most beautiful names﴾ (7–8)

He, may He be exalted and remembered, says: And if you, O Muhammad, speak aloud or keep it quiet, it is the same to your Lord, to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. ﴿Indeed He knows the secret﴾ means: nothing is hidden from Him of what you conceal within yourself, which you have not displayed with your limbs nor uttered with your tongue, and have not spoken, and akhfa.

Then the interpreters differed regarding the meaning of His saying ﴿akhfa﴾. Some of them said: its meaning is: "more hidden than the secret." He said: What is more hidden than the secret is what a person speaks to himself about and does not act upon.

Those who said this:

- Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Hakkam narrated to us, from 'Amr, from 'Ata', from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿He knows the secret and akhfa﴾: he said: the secret is what you have done, and akhfa is what Allah has cast into your heart of what you have not done.

- Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to me, saying: my paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿He knows the secret and akhfa﴾: by akhfa he means what he has not done while he is the one who will do it.

- 'Ali narrated to me, saying: 'Abd Allah narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiyah narrated to me, from 'Ali, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿He knows the secret and akhfa﴾: he said: the secret is what the son of Adam conceals in himself, and akhfa is what the son of Adam conceals of what he is going to do before he does it. Allah knows that, and His knowledge of what has passed of that and what remains is one knowledge, and all creatures before Him are in that like a single soul. This is His saying: ﴿Your creation and your resurrection are not but as a single soul﴾.

- al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, saying: Ibn Jurayj said: Sa'id ibn Jubayr narrated, from Ibn 'Abbas: the secret is what a person conceals in himself; and akhfa is what a person does not know of what will occur.

- Zakariyya ibn Yahya ibn Abi Za'idah and Muhammad ibn 'Amr narrated to me, both saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, from 'Isa; and al-Harith narrated to me, saying: al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Warqa' narrated to us, all from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding the saying of Allah ﴿He knows the secret and akhfa﴾: he said: akhfa is the whispering (waswasah). Ibn 'Amr and al-Harith added in their two narrations: and the secret is the deed that they conceal from people.

- al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, regarding ﴿akhfa﴾: he said: the whispering.

- Hannad narrated to us, saying: Abu al-Ahwas narrated to us, from Simak, from 'Ikrimah, regarding His saying ﴿He knows the secret and akhfa﴾: he said: akhfa is the talk of your own self.

- Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn ibn al-Hasan al-Ashqar narrated to us, saying: Abu Kudaynah narrated to us, from 'Ata', from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿He knows the secret and akhfa﴾: he said: the secret is what is in your self today, and akhfa is what will be in tomorrow and the day after tomorrow, which none knows but Allah.

Others said: rather, its meaning is: "and more hidden than the secret is what a person has not spoken to himself about."

Those who said this:

- al-Fadl ibn al-Sabbah narrated to us, saying: Ibn Fudayl narrated to us, from 'Ata', from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, regarding His saying ﴿He knows the secret and akhfa﴾: he said: the secret is what you have concealed in yourself, and more hidden than that is what you have not spoken to yourself about.

- Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding ﴿And if you speak aloud, then indeed He knows the secret and akhfa﴾: he said: We used to narrate that the secret is what you speak to yourself about, and that what is more hidden than the secret is what will occur of what you have not spoken to yourself about.

- Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Sulayman ibn Harb narrated to us, saying: Abu Hilal narrated to us, saying: Qatadah narrated to us, regarding His saying ﴿He knows the secret and akhfa﴾: he said: He knows what you have concealed in yourself, and akhfa is what has not yet occurred.

- al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying ﴿He knows the secret and akhfa﴾: he said: more hidden than the secret is what you have spoken to yourself about, and also what you have not spoken to yourself about of what will occur.

- I was told by al-Husayn ibn al-Faraj, who said: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: 'Ubayd narrated to us, saying: I heard al-Dahhak say regarding His saying ﴿He knows the secret and akhfa﴾: as for the secret, it is what you have concealed in yourself; and as for what is more hidden than the secret, it is what you have not done while you are doing it. Allah knows all of that.

Others said: rather, the meaning of that is: He knows the secrets of the servants, and He keeps His own secret hidden, so He has revealed it to no one.

Those who said this:

- Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His saying ﴿He knows the secret and akhfa﴾: he said: He knows the secrets of the servants, and He keeps His own secret hidden, so it is not known.

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: It seems that those who directed the meaning toward the secret being what a person tells another privately, and that akhfa means what he tells himself, directed the interpretation of akhfa to the hidden (al-khafi). Some of them said: af'al may be placed in the position of the active participle (fa'il), and they cited for their saying the verse of a poet:

Men wish that I would die, and if I die, that is a path, and I am not the only one on it (bi-awhad).

[[This verse occurs in a set of five verses that al-Walid ibn 'Abd al-Malik wrote when he fell ill, having learned that his brother Sulayman had wished for his death because of the covenant he had regarding succession; al-Walid rebuked him in his letter, and these verses were in it. Its opening is: "Men wish... etc." Al-Mas'udi mentioned it in (Muruj al-Dhahab, Dar al-Raja' edition, 3: 103), and the evidence is in the word bi-awhad, which means bi-wahid.]]

The correct view on this matter is the saying of those who said: its meaning is: He knows the secret and what is more hidden than the secret, because that is the apparent sense of the speech. If the meaning were what Ibn Zayd interpreted, the sentence would be: "and He hid His secret," because akhfa would then be a transitive verb taking a direct object, since it would mean "fa'al" as Ibn Zayd interpreted; and the separate mention of akhfa from its object, and what it governs, would be clear evidence, if it meant fa'al, that it means af'al. The meaning of the speech is: "indeed He knows the secret and what is more hidden than it." When that is its meaning, the correct statement about the meaning of "more hidden than the secret" is that it is what Allah knows of what is concealed from the servants, and which they do not know, of what is occurring and what has not yet occurred. For what has appeared and occurred is no longer a secret; and what has not occurred and is not occurring is nothing; and what has not occurred yet is going to occur is more hidden than the secret, because none knows it except Allah, and then whomever He informs of it among His servants.

As for His saying, may He be exalted and remembered: ﴿Allah – there is no deity except Him﴾, it means: the worshipped one, to whom alone worship is fitting. He says: So worship Him alone, O people, rather than whatever else is worshipped, of gods and idols. ﴿To Him belong the most beautiful names﴾: He, may His praise be great, says: to your worshipped one, O people, belong the most beautiful names. He said "al-husna" in the singular, and it is an attribute of "al-asma'" (the names), and He did not say "al-ahasin" (the beautiful ones), because "asma'" takes this form, so one says: "hadhihi asma'" (these are names) and "hadhihi" in a single word. From this is the saying of al-A'sha:

"And he will recompense me for it, if I prevail with it, with a Lord who is Forgiving, and fair, pure women."

[[In Lisan al-'Arab (root 'q-b): it is said: a'aqabahu Allah bi-ihsan wa khayran (Allah recompensed him with goodness and good). Al-'uqba is its name, which is like a substitute. Ista'aqaba minhu khayran aw sharran means he took it in exchange: he recompensed him with good, i.e., replaced it and changed it for him. The evidence in the verse is that the poet described "al-bid" (fair ones), the plural of bayda', with the word "dhat", which is singular, and did not make the attribute agree with the described in number. The author's explanation is that the word "al-bid" is a plural, but it is pointed to with "hadhihi" and "hadhihi", which originally point to the singular; since it is permissible to point to the plural with "hadhihi", it is permissible to describe "al-bid" with "dhat", which is for the singular. This is like the Qur'anic statement "lahu al-asma' al-husna", where "asma'" is plural and "al-husna" is its attribute and is singular.]]

So he used the singular "dhat", which is an attribute of "al-bid", because it takes "hadhihi", as He said: ﴿gardens of delight (hada'iq dhata bahjah)﴾. From it is His saying, may His praise be great: ﴿other needs (ma'arib ukhra)﴾, so He used the singular "ukhra", which is an attribute of "ma'arib". "Ma'arib" is a plural, and its singular is "ma'raba". He did not say "ukhar", for the reason we have described; and had it been said "ukhar", it would have been correct.

From it is His saying, may His praise be great: ﴿other needs (ma'arib ukhra)﴾, so He used the singular "ukhra", which is an attribute of "ma'arib". "Ma'arib" is a plural, and its singular is "ma'raba". He did not say "ukhar", for the reason we have described; and had it been said "ukhar", it would have been correct.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 20, verse 6–8:

The interpretation of His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth and whatever is between them and whatever is beneath the soil (al-thara)﴾ (6)

He, may He be exalted and remembered, says: To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens, whatever is on the earth, and whatever is between them, and whatever is beneath the soil, as His dominion, and He is the one who governs all of that and directs all of it. By al-thara he means the moisture.

It is said of moist, wet earth: thara (moisture) with the final vowel shortened (thara manquus). From it is derived: "tharat al-ard yatharа" (the earth became moist), thara manquus, and al-thara is a verbal noun.

The interpreters of the Qur'an have said something similar to what we have said regarding this.

Those who said this:

- Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying ﴿and whatever is beneath the soil﴾: al-thara is every moist thing.

- I was told by al-Husayn ibn al-Faraj, who said: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: 'Ubayd informed us, saying: I heard al-Dahhak say regarding His saying ﴿and whatever is beneath the soil﴾: what is dug out of the earth while still moist. He only meant by that: what is beneath the seven earths.

Similarly:

- Muhammad ibn Ibrahim al-Sulaymi, known as Ibn Sadran [[In al-Khulasah by al-Khazraji: Muhammad ibn Ibrahim ibn Sadran, with a dammah on the first unpointed letter, al-Azdi, with a ya' after the lam that is kasrah.]], narrated to me, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Rifa'ah narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn Ka'b regarding ﴿and whatever is beneath the soil﴾: he said: al-thara is seven earths.

* *

The interpretation of His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿And if you speak aloud, then indeed He knows the secret and that which is more hidden (akhfa). Allah – there is no deity except Him. To Him belong the most beautiful names﴾ (7–8)

He, may He be exalted and remembered, says: And if you, O Muhammad, speak aloud or keep it quiet, it is the same to your Lord, to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. ﴿Indeed He knows the secret﴾ means: nothing is hidden from Him of what you conceal within yourself, which you have not displayed with your limbs nor uttered with your tongue, and have not spoken, and akhfa.

Then the interpreters differed regarding the meaning of His saying ﴿akhfa﴾. Some of them said: its meaning is: "more hidden than the secret." He said: What is more hidden than the secret is what a person speaks to himself about and does not act upon.

Those who said this:

- Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Hakkam narrated to us, from 'Amr, from 'Ata', from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿He knows the secret and akhfa﴾: he said: the secret is what you have done, and akhfa is what Allah has cast into your heart of what you have not done.

- Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to me, saying: my paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿He knows the secret and akhfa﴾: by akhfa he means what he has not done while he is the one who will do it.

- 'Ali narrated to me, saying: 'Abd Allah narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiyah narrated to me, from 'Ali, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿He knows the secret and akhfa﴾: he said: the secret is what the son of Adam conceals in himself, and akhfa is what the son of Adam conceals of what he is going to do before he does it. Allah knows that, and His knowledge of what has passed of that and what remains is one knowledge, and all creatures before Him are in that like a single soul. This is His saying: ﴿Your creation and your resurrection are not but as a single soul﴾.

- al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, saying: Ibn Jurayj said: Sa'id ibn Jubayr narrated, from Ibn 'Abbas: the secret is what a person conceals in himself; and akhfa is what a person does not know of what will occur.

- Zakariyya ibn Yahya ibn Abi Za'idah and Muhammad ibn 'Amr narrated to me, both saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, from 'Isa; and al-Harith narrated to me, saying: al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Warqa' narrated to us, all from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding the saying of Allah ﴿He knows the secret and akhfa﴾: he said: akhfa is the whispering (waswasah). Ibn 'Amr and al-Harith added in their two narrations: and the secret is the deed that they conceal from people.

- al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, regarding ﴿akhfa﴾: he said: the whispering.

- Hannad narrated to us, saying: Abu al-Ahwas narrated to us, from Simak, from 'Ikrimah, regarding His saying ﴿He knows the secret and akhfa﴾: he said: akhfa is the talk of your own self.

- Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn ibn al-Hasan al-Ashqar narrated to us, saying: Abu Kudaynah narrated to us, from 'Ata', from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿He knows the secret and akhfa﴾: he said: the secret is what is in your self today, and akhfa is what will be in tomorrow and the day after tomorrow, which none knows but Allah.

Others said: rather, its meaning is: "and more hidden than the secret is what a person has not spoken to himself about."

Those who said this:

- al-Fadl ibn al-Sabbah narrated to us, saying: Ibn Fudayl narrated to us, from 'Ata', from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, regarding His saying ﴿He knows the secret and akhfa﴾: he said: the secret is what you have concealed in yourself, and more hidden than that is what you have not spoken to yourself about.

- Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding ﴿And if you speak aloud, then indeed He knows the secret and akhfa﴾: he said: We used to narrate that the secret is what you speak to yourself about, and that what is more hidden than the secret is what will occur of what you have not spoken to yourself about.

- Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Sulayman ibn Harb narrated to us, saying: Abu Hilal narrated to us, saying: Qatadah narrated to us, regarding His saying ﴿He knows the secret and akhfa﴾: he said: He knows what you have concealed in yourself, and akhfa is what has not yet occurred.

- al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying ﴿He knows the secret and akhfa﴾: he said: more hidden than the secret is what you have spoken to yourself about, and also what you have not spoken to yourself about of what will occur.

- I was told by al-Husayn ibn al-Faraj, who said: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: 'Ubayd narrated to us, saying: I heard al-Dahhak say regarding His saying ﴿He knows the secret and akhfa﴾: as for the secret, it is what you have concealed in yourself; and as for what is more hidden than the secret, it is what you have not done while you are doing it. Allah knows all of that.

Others said: rather, the meaning of that is: He knows the secrets of the servants, and He keeps His own secret hidden, so He has revealed it to no one.

Those who said this:

- Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His saying ﴿He knows the secret and akhfa﴾: he said: He knows the secrets of the servants, and He keeps His own secret hidden, so it is not known.

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: It seems that those who directed the meaning toward the secret being what a person tells another privately, and that akhfa means what he tells himself, directed the interpretation of akhfa to the hidden (al-khafi). Some of them said: af'al may be placed in the position of the active participle (fa'il), and they cited for their saying the verse of a poet:

Men wish that I would die, and if I die, that is a path, and I am not the only one on it (bi-awhad).

[[This verse occurs in a set of five verses that al-Walid ibn 'Abd al-Malik wrote when he fell ill, having learned that his brother Sulayman had wished for his death because of the covenant he had regarding succession; al-Walid rebuked him in his letter, and these verses were in it. Its opening is: "Men wish... etc." Al-Mas'udi mentioned it in (Muruj al-Dhahab, Dar al-Raja' edition, 3: 103), and the evidence is in the word bi-awhad, which means bi-wahid.]]

The correct view on this matter is the saying of those who said: its meaning is: He knows the secret and what is more hidden than the secret, because that is the apparent sense of the speech. If the meaning were what Ibn Zayd interpreted, the sentence would be: "and He hid His secret," because akhfa would then be a transitive verb taking a direct object, since it would mean "fa'al" as Ibn Zayd interpreted; and the separate mention of akhfa from its object, and what it governs, would be clear evidence, if it meant fa'al, that it means af'al. The meaning of the speech is: "indeed He knows the secret and what is more hidden than it." When that is its meaning, the correct statement about the meaning of "more hidden than the secret" is that it is what Allah knows of what is concealed from the servants, and which they do not know, of what is occurring and what has not yet occurred. For what has appeared and occurred is no longer a secret; and what has not occurred and is not occurring is nothing; and what has not occurred yet is going to occur is more hidden than the secret, because none knows it except Allah, and then whomever He informs of it among His servants.

As for His saying, may He be exalted and remembered: ﴿Allah – there is no deity except Him﴾, it means: the worshipped one, to whom alone worship is fitting. He says: So worship Him alone, O people, rather than whatever else is worshipped, of gods and idols. ﴿To Him belong the most beautiful names﴾: He, may His praise be great, says: to your worshipped one, O people, belong the most beautiful names. He said "al-husna" in the singular, and it is an attribute of "al-asma'" (the names), and He did not say "al-ahasin" (the beautiful ones), because "asma'" takes this form, so one says: "hadhihi asma'" (these are names) and "hadhihi" in a single word. From this is the saying of al-A'sha:

"And he will recompense me for it, if I prevail with it, with a Lord who is Forgiving, and fair, pure women."

[[In Lisan al-'Arab (root 'q-b): it is said: a'aqabahu Allah bi-ihsan wa khayran (Allah recompensed him with goodness and good). Al-'uqba is its name, which is like a substitute. Ista'aqaba minhu khayran aw sharran means he took it in exchange: he recompensed him with good, i.e., replaced it and changed it for him. The evidence in the verse is that the poet described "al-bid" (fair ones), the plural of bayda', with the word "dhat", which is singular, and did not make the attribute agree with the described in number. The author's explanation is that the word "al-bid" is a plural, but it is pointed to with "hadhihi" and "hadhihi", which originally point to the singular; since it is permissible to point to the plural with "hadhihi", it is permissible to describe "al-bid" with "dhat", which is for the singular. This is like the Qur'anic statement "lahu al-asma' al-husna", where "asma'" is plural and "al-husna" is its attribute and is singular.]]

So he used the singular "dhat", which is an attribute of "al-bid", because it takes "hadhihi", as He said: ﴿gardens of delight (hada'iq dhata bahjah)﴾. From it is His saying, may His praise be great: ﴿other needs (ma'arib ukhra)﴾, so He used the singular "ukhra", which is an attribute of "ma'arib". "Ma'arib" is a plural, and its singular is "ma'raba". He did not say "ukhar", for the reason we have described; and had it been said "ukhar", it would have been correct.

**Commentary on the interpretation of His words, the Exalted:** ﴿And has there reached you the story of Musa? (9) When he saw a fire and said to his family, "Wait, indeed I have perceived a fire; perhaps I will bring you from it a burning brand, or find at the fire some guidance." (10)﴾

The Exalted says to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), consoling him for the hardship he suffers from the polytheists of his people, and informing him of the outcome of his affair and theirs, that He will make him victorious over them and will weaken the plots of the disbelievers. He urges him to be earnest in his affair and patient in worship, and to take as an example what befell his brother Musa, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, from his enemy, then from his own people, and from the Children of Israel, and the trial and hardship he endured, as a small child, then as a youth growing up, then as a full-grown man. ﴿And has there reached you﴾, O Muhammad, ﴿the story of Musa﴾, son of Imran, ﴿when he saw a fire﴾. It is mentioned that this was in winter, at night, and that Musa had lost his way. So when he saw the light of the fire, ﴿he said to his family﴾ what he said.

**Mention of those who said this:**

⁕ Musa ibn Harun narrated to us, saying: Amr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, from Abu Malik and from Abu Salih, from Ibn Abbas, who said: When Musa had fulfilled the term, he set out with his family and lost the way. Abdullah ibn Abbas said: It was in winter, and a fire appeared to them. When he saw it, he thought it was a fire, but it was from the light of Allah. ﴿He said to his family, "Wait, indeed I have perceived a fire."﴾

⁕ Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salama narrated to us, from Ibn Ishaq, from Wahb ibn Munabbih al-Yamani, who said: When Musa had fulfilled the term, he went out with his sheep, with his firestarter (zand) and his staff in his hand, with which he herded his sheep by day. When evening came, he struck his firestarter to make a fire, and he and his family and his sheep would spend the night by it. In the morning he would set out with his family and sheep, leaning on his staff. But on the night when Allah willed to honour Musa, and to begin with him His prophethood and His speech, he lost the way, so that he did not know where to head. He took out his firestarter to strike a fire for his family, so they could spend the night by it until morning and he would know the direction of his path. But the firestarter failed to produce any fire for him, and he struck it until he was exhausted. Then [[The context requires: "until when he was exhausted, there appeared..." etc., or: "so there appeared, then there appeared again."]] the fire appeared, and he saw it. ﴿He said to his family, "Wait, indeed I have perceived a fire; perhaps I will bring you from it a burning brand, or find at the fire some guidance."﴾ By His words ﴿I have perceived a fire﴾ is meant: I found it. Among the proverbs of the Arabs: "after the sighting of companionship (iniyas)," and it is also said: "after the rising of companionship." It is derived from the word *uns* (intimacy/companionship).

* *

As for His words ﴿perhaps I will bring you from it a burning brand﴾:

He means: perhaps I will come to you from the fire I have perceived with a flame.

The *qabas* is fire at the tip of a stick or reed. One says to his companion, "Give me fire (aqbisni naran)," and he gives it to him at the tip of a stick or reed. Musa, by his words to his family, ﴿perhaps I will bring you from it a burning brand﴾, meant: perhaps I will bring you that, so that you may warm yourselves by it.

As related:

⁕ Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salama narrated to us, from Ibn Ishaq, from Wahb ibn Munabbih, concerning ﴿perhaps I will bring you from it a burning brand﴾, he said: a burning brand by which you may warm yourselves.

* *

As for His words ﴿or find at the fire some guidance﴾:

A sign that indicates the path which we had lost, either from a guide who directs us to it, or from a clarification and knowledge by which we may discern it and recognise it.

Those who engage in ta'wil (interpretation of the Qur'an) have said what is similar to what we have said.

**Mention of those who said this:**

⁕ Ali narrated to me, saying: Abdullah narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiya narrated to us, from Ali, from Ibn Abbas, concerning His words ﴿or find at the fire some guidance﴾, he said: meaning, someone who shows the way.

⁕ Muhammad ibn Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu Asim narrated to us, saying: Isa narrated to us. And al-Harith narrated to me, saying: al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Waraqa narrated to us, all of them from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, concerning the saying of Allah ﴿or find at the fire some guidance﴾, he said: a guide who would direct him to the way.

⁕ al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, the same.

⁕ Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatada concerning His words ﴿or find at the fire some guidance﴾: that is, guides who would show him the way.

⁕ Ahmad ibn al-Miqdam narrated to me, saying: al-Mu'tamir narrated to us, saying: I heard my father narrate, from Qatada, from a companion of his, from a report of Ibn Abbas, that he claimed it was Ayla. ﴿or find at the fire some guidance﴾. My father said: And Qatada claimed that it showed the way.

⁕ al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatada, concerning His words ﴿or find at the fire some guidance﴾, he said: someone who would guide me to the way.

⁕ Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salama narrated to us, from Ibn Ishaq, from Wahb ibn Munabbih, concerning ﴿or find at the fire some guidance﴾, he said: guidance by knowledge of the path we had lost, by a description from a report.

⁕ Yunus narrated to me, saying: Sufyan informed us, from Abu Sa'id, from Ikrima, who said: Ibn Abbas said: ﴿perhaps I will bring you from it a burning brand or find at the fire some guidance﴾. He said: They had lost their way, so he said: perhaps I will find someone who will guide me to the way, or I will bring you a burning brand, so that you may warm yourselves.

On the interpretation of His words, "So when he came to it, he was called: 'O Moses! (11) Indeed I am your Lord, so take off your sandals; indeed you are in the sacred valley, Tuwa. (12)'"

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: When Moses came to the fire, his Lord called to him, "O Moses! Indeed I am your Lord, so take off your sandals."

As related:

Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salamah narrated to us, from Ibn Ishaq, from Wahb ibn Munabbih, who said: Moses set out towards it, meaning towards the fire, and behold, it was in a tree of ʿawlaq (a thorny plant). Some of the People of the Book say it was in a ʿawsajah (a thorn bush). When he drew near, it withdrew from him. When he saw its withdrawing, he turned back from it, and he sensed fear within himself because of it. When he wanted to return, it drew near to him, and then he was addressed from the tree. When he heard the voice, he became at ease, and God, blessed and exalted, said: "O Moses! Indeed I am your Lord, so take off your sandals; indeed you are in the sacred valley, Tuwa." So he took them off and cast them aside.

The scholars differed concerning the reason why God commanded Moses to take off his sandals. Some of them said: He commanded him to do so because they were made of the skin of a dead donkey, and He disliked that he should tread the sacred valley with them, and He wanted him to receive the blessing of the valley.

Mention of those who said this:

Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Rahman narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from ʿAsim, from Abu Qilabah, from Kaʿb, that he saw them taking off their sandals. [He recited] "So take off your sandals; indeed you are in the sacred valley, Tuwa," and said: They were of the skin of a dead donkey, so God wanted the sanctity to touch him.

Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Yahya ibn Wadih narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, from Yazid, from ʿIkrimah, regarding His words "So take off your sandals," he said: They were of the skin of a dead donkey.

Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Saʿid narrated to us, from Qatadah, who said: We were told that his sandals were of donkey skin, so he took them off and then came to him.

al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Maʿmar informed us, from Qatadah, regarding His words "So take off your sandals," he said: They were of donkey skin, so it was said to him: Take them off.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 20, verses 13–14:

The interpretation of His words, the Exalted: ﴿And I have chosen you, so listen to what is revealed (13). Indeed, I am Allah; there is no deity except Me, so worship Me and establish prayer for My remembrance (14).﴾

The reciters differed regarding the recitation of this. The majority of reciters who recited "wa-anna" with a shaddah on the nun, and "anna" with a fatha on the alif, read it as a response to "Nuddiya: Ya Musa" (It was called out: O Musa), as if the meaning of the speech according to them is: "It was called out: O Musa, indeed I am your Lord, and I have chosen you." This is the reading by which the majority of the reciters of Kufa recited. As for the majority of the reciters of Medina and Basra and some of the people of Kufa, they recited: ﴿wa-ana akhtartuka﴾ with a light nun, in the form of a statement from Allah about Himself that He had chosen him.

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: The correct view on this matter, in my opinion, is to say: both are recitations, and each of them has been recited by the reciters of the people of knowledge of the Qur'an, with their two meanings in agreement. Whichever of them the reciter recites, he is correct in it. The meaning of the speech is: "It was called out: that We have chosen you, so We have selected you for Our message to those to whom We send you." ﴿So listen to what is revealed﴾ means: listen to Our revelation which We reveal to you, retain it, and act upon it.

﴿Indeed, I am Allah﴾ means, the Exalted in remembrance says: indeed I am the one worthy of worship, to whom alone worship is due. ﴿There is no deity except Me﴾, so do not worship other than Me, for there is no one who is worthy or fit to be worshipped besides Me. ﴿So worship Me﴾ means: devote worship sincerely to Me alone, apart from everything that is worshipped besides Me. ﴿And establish prayer for My remembrance﴾.

The people of interpretation differed regarding the meaning of this. Some of them said: the meaning of that is: establish prayer for Me, for when you establish it, you remember Me.

Mention of those who said that:

Muhammad ibn 'Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu 'Asim told us, saying: 'Isa told us; and al-Harith narrated to me, saying: al-Hasan told us, saying: Warqa' told us, all from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His words ﴿And establish prayer for My remembrance﴾, he said: when he prays, he remembers his Lord.

Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn told us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, regarding His words ﴿And establish prayer for My remembrance﴾, he said: when the servant remembers his Lord.

Others said: rather, the meaning of that is: establish prayer when you remember it.

Mention of those who said that:

Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Abu 'Asim told us, saying: Sufyan told us, from Mughira, from Ibrahim, regarding His words ﴿And establish prayer for My remembrance﴾, he said: he prays it when he remembers it.

Ahmad ibn 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Wahb narrated to me, saying: my uncle 'Abd Allah ibn Wahb narrated to me, saying: Yunus and Malik ibn Shihab narrated to me, saying: Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab informed me, from Abu Hurayrah, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever forgets a prayer, let him pray it when he remembers it, for Allah says: ﴿And establish prayer for My remembrance﴾." And al-Zuhri used to recite it: ﴿li-dhikra﴾ (for its remembrance) in the manner of fa'ala (as in "fa-'ala" form).

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: The more correct of the two interpretations is the interpretation of the one who said: its meaning is: establish prayer so that you remember Me in it, because that is the more apparent of its two meanings. Had its meaning been "when you remember it," the wording would have been: "establish prayer for its remembrance." In His words ﴿for My remembrance﴾ there is clear evidence for the soundness of what Mujahid said in its interpretation. Even if the recitation mentioned from al-Zuhri were a widely transmitted recitation among the regional readings, the interpretation of the one who interpreted it as "establish prayer when you remember it" would be sound, since al-Zuhri directed his recitation ﴿li-dhikra﴾ with an alif rather than as an annexation (idafah) to "its remembrance" (dhikraha), because the ha' and the alif were dropped, though both are intended in the speech, in order to harmonize it with the other verse-endings, since they were with alif and fatha. If someone were to say, regarding this recitation of al-Zuhri that we mentioned from him, that al-Zuhri by opening it intended to make the annexation an alif in order to harmonize it with the verse-endings before and after it, since by his reading he differed from the one who read it with annexation, and said: this is like the saying of the poet:

"I wander about, then return / to ... ami (my mother) and my cup of naqi' (milk) quenches me" [the line is among the witnesses of al-Farra' in Ma'ani al-Qur'an; he said: the Arabs say "bayta" and "amma," meaning "by my father and my mother," and similarly "ya waylata a'jaztu"; and if you wish you may make it ya of annexation, and if you wish, ya of lamentation. The naqi' is pure milk that has been cooled.]

He means: "to my mother," and like the Arab saying: "Ya aba wa-amma," meaning: "O my father and my mother," he would have something to say in that.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 20, verses 13–14:

The interpretation of His words, the Exalted: ﴿And I have chosen you, so listen to what is revealed (13). Indeed, I am Allah; there is no deity except Me, so worship Me and establish prayer for My remembrance (14).﴾

The reciters differed regarding the recitation of this. The majority of reciters who recited "wa-anna" with a shaddah on the nun, and "anna" with a fatha on the alif, read it as a response to "Nuddiya: Ya Musa" (It was called out: O Musa), as if the meaning of the speech according to them is: "It was called out: O Musa, indeed I am your Lord, and I have chosen you." This is the reading by which the majority of the reciters of Kufa recited. As for the majority of the reciters of Medina and Basra and some of the people of Kufa, they recited: ﴿wa-ana akhtartuka﴾ with a light nun, in the form of a statement from Allah about Himself that He had chosen him.

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: The correct view on this matter, in my opinion, is to say: both are recitations, and each of them has been recited by the reciters of the people of knowledge of the Qur'an, with their two meanings in agreement. Whichever of them the reciter recites, he is correct in it. The meaning of the speech is: "It was called out: that We have chosen you, so We have selected you for Our message to those to whom We send you." ﴿So listen to what is revealed﴾ means: listen to Our revelation which We reveal to you, retain it, and act upon it.

﴿Indeed, I am Allah﴾ means, the Exalted in remembrance says: indeed I am the one worthy of worship, to whom alone worship is due. ﴿There is no deity except Me﴾, so do not worship other than Me, for there is no one who is worthy or fit to be worshipped besides Me. ﴿So worship Me﴾ means: devote worship sincerely to Me alone, apart from everything that is worshipped besides Me. ﴿And establish prayer for My remembrance﴾.

The people of interpretation differed regarding the meaning of this. Some of them said: the meaning of that is: establish prayer for Me, for when you establish it, you remember Me.

Others said: rather, the meaning of that is: establish prayer when you remember it.
