Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 20, verse 15–16 (part 1 of 2):

The explanation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the Hour is coming; I almost conceal it, so that every soul may be recompensed for what it strives for. (15) So do not let one who does not believe in it and follows his desire divert you from it, lest you perish.﴾ (16)

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: Indeed, the Hour in which Allah will raise the creatures from their graves to the place of standing on the Day of Resurrection is coming. ﴿I almost conceal it﴾. As for the reading of the alif in akhfīhā with a damma, it is the reading of all the readers of the cities of Islam, meaning: I almost conceal it from myself, so that no one may be informed of it. This is also the interpretation of most of the people of knowledge.

Mention of those who said this:

- Ali narrated to me, he said: ʿAbd Allah narrated to us, he said: Muʿawiya narrated to me, from ʿAli, from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His saying ﴿I almost conceal it﴾: he says, "I do not make it manifest to anyone other than Myself."
- Muhammad ibn Saʿd narrated to me, he said: My father narrated to me, he said: My paternal uncle narrated to me, he said: My father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His saying ﴿Indeed, the Hour is coming; I almost conceal it﴾: he said, "It will not come to you except suddenly."
- Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, he said: Abu Ahmad narrated to us, he said: Sufyan narrated to us, from Layth, from Mujahid, ﴿Indeed, the Hour is coming; I almost conceal it﴾: he said, "from myself."
- Muhammad ibn ʿAmr narrated to us, he said: Abu ʿAsim narrated to us, he said: ʿIsa narrated to us; and al-Harith narrated to me, he said: al-Hasan narrated to us, he said: Warqa narrated to us, all from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding the saying of Allah ﴿I almost conceal it﴾: he said, "from myself."
- al-Qasim narrated to us, he said: al-Husayn narrated to us, he said: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, the same.
- Ibn Humayd narrated to us, he said: Jarir narrated to us, from ʿAta ibn al-Sa'ib, from Saʿid ibn Jubayr, from Ibn ʿAbbas, ﴿I almost conceal it﴾: he said, "from myself."
- ʿAbd al-Aʿla ibn Wasil narrated to me, he said: Muhammad ibn ʿUbayd al-Tanafisi narrated to us, he said: Ismaʿil ibn Abi Khalid narrated to us, from Abu Salih, regarding His saying ﴿I almost conceal it﴾: he said, "He conceals it from Himself."
- Bishr narrated to us, he said: Yazid narrated to us, he said: Saʿid narrated to us, from Qatada, regarding His saying ﴿I almost conceal it﴾, and in some readings it is: "I conceal it from myself." By my life, He concealed it from the nearest angels and from the sent prophets.
- al-Hasan narrated to us, he said: ʿAbd al-Razzaq informed us, he said: Maʿmar informed us, from Qatada, he said: In some letters (readings): ﴿Indeed, the Hour is coming; I almost conceal it from myself﴾.

Others said: Rather, it is: ﴿Akādu akhfīhā﴾ with a fatha on the alif of akhfīhā, meaning: I make it manifest.

Mention of those who said this:

- Ibn Humayd narrated to us, he said: Yahya ibn Wadih narrated to us, he said: Muhammad ibn Sahl narrated to us, he said: A man asked me in the mosque about this verse of poetry:

*"Dāba shahrayni thumma shahran damīkā ... bi-Ariīkayni yakhfiyāni ghamīrā"* [Footnote: The line is by Kaʿb (al-Lisan, al-Taj, d-m-k). They said: one says "aqamtu ʿindahu shahran damīkan," meaning a complete month. Kaʿb said: "Dāba shahrayni thumma shahran damīkā." He did not mention the second hemistich. In Muʿjam ma staʿjam by al-Bakri (p. 144), Abu ʿUbayda said: Ariik is in the lands of Dhubyan. He said: there are two Ariks: Ariik al-Aswad and Ariik al-Abyad, and al-Ariik is a small mountain. "Yakhfiyan": with a fatha on the yāʾ, meaning they come out. And al-Ghamir has many meanings, among them in Taj al-ʿArus: al-Ghamir, like Amir: the grain of the bahmi grass that falls from its spike when it dries, or a green plant that has been covered by dryness... etc.]

I said: "They make it manifest." Then Warqa ibn Iyas, who was behind me, said: Saʿid ibn Jubayr recited to me ﴿akādu akhfīhā﴾ with a fatha on the alif. It has also been related from Saʿid ibn Jubayr that he agreed with the view of the others who said its meaning is: I almost conceal it from myself.

Mention of the narration from him to that effect: Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, he said: ʿAbd al-Rahman narrated to us, he said: Sufyan narrated to us, from ʿAta and Mansur, from Mujahid, both said: ﴿Indeed, the Hour is coming; I almost conceal it﴾, they both said: "from myself."

- ʿUbayd ibn Ismaʿil al-Hibbari narrated to me, he said: Ibn Fudayl narrated to us, from ʿAta ibn al-Sa'ib, from Saʿid ibn Jubayr, ﴿I almost conceal it﴾: he said, "from myself."

Abu Jaʿfar (al-Tabari) said: The view most appropriate to the interpretation of the verse is the view of those who said its meaning is: "I almost conceal it from myself," because the interpretation of the people of interpretation came with this. As for what was related from Saʿid ibn Jubayr regarding reading it with a fatha on the alif, it is a reading I do not consider permissible to recite with, because it opposes the reading of the proof (the established reading), which it is not permissible to oppose, as it came to us through widespread transmission.

If someone says: Why did you direct the interpretation of His saying ﴿I almost conceal it﴾ with a damma on the alif toward the meaning "I almost conceal it from myself," rather than directing it toward the meaning "I almost make it manifest"? You know that ikhfa in the speech of the Arabs has two meanings: one is manifestation, and the other is concealment, and that manifestation in this place is closer to the meaning of the statement, since concealing it from oneself would almost have an impossible meaning for the listeners, for it is impossible that anyone conceals from himself something he knows, while Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, has nothing hidden from Him. Answer: The matter is contrary to what you supposed. We directed the meaning of ﴿akhfīhā﴾ with a damma on the alif toward the meaning "I conceal it from myself," because the known meaning of ikhfa in the speech of the Arabs is concealment. It is said: "I have concealed the thing" when I have covered it. And those who directed its meaning toward manifestation relied on a line of verse by Imru' al-Qays ibn ʿAbis al-Kindi.

- It was narrated to me from Maʿmar ibn al-Muthanna that he said: Abu al-Khattab recited it to me, from his people in his town:

*"Fa-in tudfinū al-dāʾa lā nukhfihi ... wa-in tabʿathū al-ḥarba lā naqʿud"* [Footnote: The line is by Imru' al-Qays ibn ʿAbis al-Kindi. The author of al-Lisan (kh-f-a) cited it as evidence that his saying "lā nukhfihi," with a fatha on the nūn, means "we do not make it manifest." Likewise, the verse "akādu akhfīhā" means "I make it manifest," as al-Lihyani related from al-Kisai, from Muhammad ibn Sahl, from Saʿid ibn Jubayr. The author of al-Lisan said: It is said "khafaytu al-shayʾ akhfīhi" means I made the thing manifest and extracted it; it is said "khafiya al-matar al-fa'ār" when it brings them out of their burrows, i.e., their holes. Imru' al-Qays described a horse: "khafāhunna min anfāqihinna ka-annamā ... khafāhunna waddqu min ʿashiyyin mujallabi." And "khafaytu al-shayʾ akhfīhi" means I concealed it; it is one of the words with two opposite meanings (adad). "Akhfaytu al-shayʾ" means I covered and concealed it. The narrator's version of the verse is as in Maʿani al-Quran by al-Farra. In al-Lisan (kh-f-a): "Fa-in taktumū al-sirra lā nukhfihi."]

with a damma on the nūn of "lā nukhfihi," meaning "we do not make it manifest." Their reliance in directing the concealment in this place toward manifestation was on what they mentioned from hearing this line, with the damma on the nūn of "nukhfihi," as I have described. But a trustworthy man narrated to me from al-Farra:

*"Fa-in tadfinū al-dāʾa lā nakhfihi"*

with a fatha on the nūn of "nakhfihi," from "khafaytuhu akhfīhi," and this is more correct, because it is the known usage of the Arabs.

Since this is so, and the fatha on the alif of "akhfīhā" is not permissible in our view for the reason we have mentioned, the other possibility is established and confirmed, namely that the meaning is: "I almost conceal it from myself."

As for the correct basis of this view, it is that Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, addressed the Arabs in the Qur'an according to what they know of their speech and what their discourse among themselves proceeds by. Since it was known in their speech that one of them, when he wishes to emphasize his report about concealing something he is keeping secret, says: "I nearly concealed this matter from myself because of how intensely I keep it secret; and if I could conceal it from myself, I would conceal it," He addressed them according to what their usage in this has been in their speech among themselves and what they know in their manner of speaking. Other views have been stated on this besides what we have said. We chose this view over the others because it agrees with the views of the people of knowledge among the Companions and the Successors, since we do not permit ourselves to oppose them in what has been widely transmitted from them and has come down from them in a manner that removes excuse. As for those who said other than our view, from among those who spoke on it by deriving meanings from the speech of the Arabs without attributing it to an imam among the Companions or the Successors, and in a way that allows the speech to bear other than its well-known sense, they differed among themselves about its meaning. Some of them said: its meaning may be: "I want to conceal it," and said: this is known in the language, and it is mentioned that it is related from the Arabs that they say: "Those are my companions upon whom I almost descend (akādu anzilu)," meaning: I only descend upon them. And it is related: "akādu abraḥu manzilī," meaning: I do not leave my dwelling. He argued with a line of verse recited by one of the poets:

*"Kādat wa-kidtu wa-tilka khayru irādatin ... law ʿāda min ʿahdi al-ṣabābati mā maḍā"* [Footnote: The line is in al-Lisan (k-y-d). It says: "Fulan yakīdu amran mā adrī mā huwa," when he seeks it, schemes for it, and strives for it. He said: "Balaghū al-amr alladhī kādū": meaning they sought or intended. Abu Bakr recited, for kāda in the meaning of arāda, the line of al-Afwah: "Fa-in tajmaʿ awtādun wa-aʿmidatun ... wa-sākinu balaghū al-amra alladhī kādū," meaning: that which they intended. And he recited: "Kādat wa-kidtu..." He said: its meaning is "mā arādat" (she did not intend). And the verse "lam yakad yarāhā" may bear this sense, since what he saw in the darknesses made him despair of looking at his hand and of seeing it. The line is evidence that kāda means arāda, which the author cited at the words "akādu akhfīhā."]

He said: He means by "kādat": "arādat" (she intended). He said: then the meaning is "I intend to conceal it, so that every soul may be recompensed for what it strives for." He said: Similar to this is the saying of Zayd al-Khayl:

*"Sarīʿun ilā al-hayjāʾi shākin silāḥuhu ... famā an takādu qirnuhu yatanaffasu"* [Footnote: The line is by Zayd al-Khayl as the author said. The author of al-Lisan (k-y-d) cited it as evidence that kāda may come as a connecting particle in speech. He said: kāda may be a connecting (or redundant) element in speech, as al-Akhfash, Qutrub, and Abu Hatim permitted, and Qutrub argued with the poet's saying: "Sarīʿ... etc." Its meaning: "his opponent does not breathe." But Abu Jaʿfar al-Tabari made it similar to the preceding witness, while Qutrub's explanation of this witness is clearer and better, and the particle before "yakād" is redundant or a negation reinforcing the negation before it.]

He said: It is as if he said: "fa-mā yatanaffasu qirnuhu," otherwise the meaning would be weakened. He said: Dhu al-Rummah also said:

*"Idhā ghayyara al-nanʾu al-muḥibbīna lam yakad ... rasīsu al-hawā min ḥubbi Mayyata yabraḥu"* [Footnote: This line is from the famous rhyming ode of Dhu al-Rummah (Diwan, Cambridge edition 1919, p. 78). Its commentator said: al-nanʾ is distance; rasīs al-hawā is its touch, and what remains hidden of it or its beginning. It is said: "lam yajid rasīs al-ḥummā" (he did not feel the trace of fever). The author cited the line to show that the meaning is: "lam yabraḥ" (he did not leave), or "lam yurid yabraḥ" (he did not intend to leave). On this, "yakād" is redundant in the speech. A different version of the line occurs in al-Lisan (r-s-s), which supports what the author held, that the meaning is with "yakād" redundant: "Idhā ghayyara al-nanʾu al-muḥibbīna lam yakad ... rasīsu al-hawā min ḥubbi Mayyata yabraḥu." This is the version to which the poet shifted when Ibn Shubrumah, judge of Basra, corrected him on hearing him recite the ode in al-Mirbad. But the verifiers said that Dhu al-Rummah's first version was better than the second. Al-Allama al-Muhaqqiq Radi Allah al-Dili al-Astarabadi, Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, clarified the correctness of the first version: that the meaning of "lam yakad" is "lam yaqrab" (he did not approach), and that negating the approach of a thing is more forceful than negating the thing; so the meaning of the line is: when distance changed the hearts of the lovers, the distance of Mayya from me does not take away what I feel of her firm and enduring love, nor does it approach taking it away. (See al-Radi's commentary on Ibn al-Hajib's Kafiya, Astana edition 2:306, on verbs of approximation.) al-Radi refuted the claim of some grammarians that "the negation of kāda is affirmation and its affirmation is negation," and this is a precious statement showing his intelligence and precision of understanding.]

He said: The meaning is not "lam yakad yabraḥ," i.e., he went far with ease and left with difficulty; rather the meaning is "lam yabraḥ" or "lam yurid yabraḥ," otherwise the meaning would be weakened. He said: Likewise is the saying of Abu al-Najm:

*"Wa-in atāka naʿiyyun fa-ndubanna abā ... qad kāda yaḍṭliʿu al-aʿdāʾa wal-khuṭaba"* [Footnote: The line is by Abu al-Najm as the author said. The witness is in "kāda yaḍṭliʿu." The author holds that its meaning is: "qad iḍṭalaʿa al-aʿdāʾ" (the enemies have risen to it), since otherwise it would not be praise if he meant "kāda" and did not intend "yafʿalu." In the commentary on the line, the verb "kāda" is a connecting (redundant) element, like the two witnesses before it in his view. "Yaḍṭliʿu al-aʿdāʾ": i.e., he rises up with them and with the sermons; he dropped the bāʾ, so the verb reached its object directly, which had been in the genitive with bāʾ before its removal. It is said "iḍṭalaʿa bi-ḥamlihi," meaning he was strong enough to bear it and rose to it. It derives from ḍalāʿa, meaning strength. In al-Lisan (ḍ-l-ʿ): "iḍṭalaʿa al-ḥimla," meaning his ribs bore it. Ibn al-Sikkit said: it is said "huwa muḍṭaliʿun bi-ḥamlihi," meaning he is strong enough to carry it; it is a derived form (mufta'al) from ḍalāʿa. The naʿī is the messenger who reports the death of one who has died.]

He said: The meaning would be: "qad iḍṭalaʿa al-aʿdāʾ" (the enemies have risen), otherwise it would not be praise if he meant "kāda" and did not intend "yafʿalu."

Others said: Rather, the meaning is: "Indeed, the Hour is coming, akādu," and the report ends at His saying "akād," because its meaning is: "I almost bring it." Then he begins: "But I conceal it so that every soul may be recompensed for what it strives for." He said: This is parallel to the saying of Ibn Dabi:

*"Hamamtu wa-lam af'al wa-kidtu wa-layt anī ... tarakta ʿalā ʿUthmāna tabkī aqāribuhu"* [Footnote: The line is by Dabi' ibn al-Harith al-Barjumi, whom Caliph ʿUthman imprisoned because he was a licentious man who satirized some people, so ʿUthman wanted to discipline him. When he was summoned to be disciplined, he tied a knife to his leg intending to kill ʿUthman with it, but he was caught, beaten, and returned to prison until he died there. The line is from an ode of his recited by Abu al-ʿAbbas al-Mubarrad (see Raghbat al-Amil, with the commentary of al-Marsafi on the Kamil, 4:91): "Fa-la tatbaʿīnī in halaktu malāmatan ... fa-laysa bi-ʿārin qatlu man lā uqātiluhu / Hamamtu wa-lam af'al wa-kidtu wa-layt anī ... tarakta ʿalā ʿUthmāna tabkī ḥalāʾiluhu." The witness is in "kidtu," meaning I almost did what I intended, namely killing ʿUthman. It is parallel to the Qur'anic "inna al-sāʿata ātiyatun akādu": some held its meaning is "akādu an ātī bihā" (I almost bring it), then began: "wa-lakinnī ukhfīhā li-tujzā kullu nafsin bi-mā tasʿā." The line is by Dabi', not by his son as the author said.]

So he said "kidtu," and its meaning is "kidtu af'alu" (I almost did).

Others said: The meaning of "ukhfīhā" is "uzhirhā" (I make it manifest). They said: concealment and secrecy may be directed by the Arabs toward the meaning of manifestation, and some cited for their saying the line of al-Farazdaq:

*"Falammā ra'ā al-Ḥajjāja jarrada sayfahu ... asarra al-Ḥarūrī alladhī kāna aḍmarā"* [Footnote: I did not find this line in the Diwan of al-Farazdaq; it is among the witnesses of Abu ʿUbayda (al-Lisan, s-r-r). He said: "asrartu al-shayʾ" means I concealed it, and "asrartuhu" means I announced it; and from manifestation is His saying: "wa-asarrū al-nadāma lammā raʾaw al-ʿadhāb" (and they concealed the regret when they saw the punishment), meaning they made it manifest. He recited al-Farazdaq: "Falammā ra'ā al-Ḥajjāja..." The line. Shamir said: I did not find this line for al-Farazdaq, and no one but Abu ʿUbayda said that in "wa-asarrū al-nadāma" it means "uẓhirūhā." He said: I have not heard that from anyone else. Al-Azhari said: the lexicographers strongly denied Abu ʿUbayda. It was said: "asarrū al-nadāma" means: the leaders among the polytheists concealed the regret before their followers whom they misled, and they concealed it; so al-Zajjaj said, and this is the view of the exegetes. "Al-Ḥarūrī" is the Kharijite, a nisba to Harurā', which was their first gathering when they renounced Amir al-Mu'minin ʿAli and made manifest arbitration: "lā ḥukma illā lillāh." They were called the Muhakkima, the Harūriyya, and the Khawarij.]

He said: By his saying "asarra" he meant "aẓhara" (made manifest). He said: It may also be that the meaning of His saying "wa-asarrū al-nadāma" is "wa-aẓharūhā," because they said: "Yā laytanā nuraddu wa-lā nukadhdhiba bi-āyāti rabbinā" (Would that we were returned, and that we did not deny the signs of our Lord).

All these whose views we have related said: it is permissible that the saying of the one who said "the meaning is: I almost conceal it from myself" means: "I conceal it from my side and from my presence." All these views we have mentioned from those we have mentioned are interpretations by them that direct the speech to other than its well-known meaning, and it is not permissible to direct the meanings of Allah's speech to other than the predominant aspects known to those addressed by it. In that, together with their disagreement with the interpretation of the people of knowledge, there is a just witness against the error of what they went to.

* *

As for His saying ﴿so that every soul may be recompensed for what it strives for﴾

Al-Tabari, Jami' al-Bayan, on surah 20, verses 15–16 (part 2 of 2):

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: Indeed, the Hour is coming, so that every soul may be recompensed: that is, so that every soul which its Lord has tested through worship in this world may be rewarded for what it strives at, that is, for what it does of good and evil, of obedience and disobedience. As for His words, ﴿So let not one who does not believe in it turn you away from it﴾, He, may His remembrance be exalted, means: so let not one who does not believe in it, O Musa, turn you away from preparing for the Hour. By "one who does not believe in it" is meant one who does not acknowledge the rising of the Hour, does not affirm the resurrection after death, does not hope for reward, and does not fear punishment.

* *

As for His words, ﴿and follows his desire﴾, that is: follows the desire of his own self and opposes the command and prohibition of God, ﴿and so you will perish﴾, that is: you will be ruined if you are turned away from preparing for the Hour and from belief in it, and from the belief that God will raise the creation for its rising from their graves after their annihilation, by the turning away of one who disbelieves in it.

Some of them claimed that the pronoun (al-ha' wa'l-alif, "the ha and the alif") in His words, ﴿So let not one who does not believe in it turn you away from it﴾, refers back to belief (al-iman), saying: "It is said 'from it' (anha), while it refers back to belief, just as ﴿Indeed your Lord, after it [i.e., after that deed], is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ is said, referring to the deed." But there has been no mention of belief in this passage, so that this pronoun should be taken as referring to it. Rather, the mention has been of the Hour, so it is more appropriate that the pronoun refers to it.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 20, verse 15–16 (part 1 of 2):

The explanation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the Hour is coming; I almost conceal it, so that every soul may be recompensed for what it strives for. (15) So do not let one who does not believe in it and follows his desire divert you from it, lest you perish.﴾ (16)

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: Indeed, the Hour in which Allah will raise the creatures from their graves to the place of standing on the Day of Resurrection is coming. ﴿I almost conceal it﴾. As for the reading of the alif in akhfīhā with a damma, it is the reading of all the readers of the cities of Islam, meaning: I almost conceal it from myself, so that no one may be informed of it. This is also the interpretation of most of the people of knowledge.

Mention of those who said this:

- Ali narrated to me, he said: ʿAbd Allah narrated to us, he said: Muʿawiya narrated to me, from ʿAli, from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His saying ﴿I almost conceal it﴾: he says, "I do not make it manifest to anyone other than Myself."
- Muhammad ibn Saʿd narrated to me, he said: My father narrated to me, he said: My paternal uncle narrated to me, he said: My father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His saying ﴿Indeed, the Hour is coming; I almost conceal it﴾: he said, "It will not come to you except suddenly."
- Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, he said: Abu Ahmad narrated to us, he said: Sufyan narrated to us, from Layth, from Mujahid, ﴿Indeed, the Hour is coming; I almost conceal it﴾: he said, "from myself."
- Muhammad ibn ʿAmr narrated to us, he said: Abu ʿAsim narrated to us, he said: ʿIsa narrated to us; and al-Harith narrated to me, he said: al-Hasan narrated to us, he said: Warqa narrated to us, all from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding the saying of Allah ﴿I almost conceal it﴾: he said, "from myself."
- al-Qasim narrated to us, he said: al-Husayn narrated to us, he said: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, the same.
- Ibn Humayd narrated to us, he said: Jarir narrated to us, from ʿAta ibn al-Sa'ib, from Saʿid ibn Jubayr, from Ibn ʿAbbas, ﴿I almost conceal it﴾: he said, "from myself."
- ʿAbd al-Aʿla ibn Wasil narrated to me, he said: Muhammad ibn ʿUbayd al-Tanafisi narrated to us, he said: Ismaʿil ibn Abi Khalid narrated to us, from Abu Salih, regarding His saying ﴿I almost conceal it﴾: he said, "He conceals it from Himself."
- Bishr narrated to us, he said: Yazid narrated to us, he said: Saʿid narrated to us, from Qatada, regarding His saying ﴿I almost conceal it﴾, and in some readings it is: "I conceal it from myself." By my life, He concealed it from the nearest angels and from the sent prophets.
- al-Hasan narrated to us, he said: ʿAbd al-Razzaq informed us, he said: Maʿmar informed us, from Qatada, he said: In some letters (readings): ﴿Indeed, the Hour is coming; I almost conceal it from myself﴾.

Others said: Rather, it is: ﴿Akādu akhfīhā﴾ with a fatha on the alif of akhfīhā, meaning: I make it manifest.

Mention of those who said this:

- Ibn Humayd narrated to us, he said: Yahya ibn Wadih narrated to us, he said: Muhammad ibn Sahl narrated to us, he said: A man asked me in the mosque about this verse of poetry:

*"Dāba shahrayni thumma shahran damīkā ... bi-Ariīkayni yakhfiyāni ghamīrā"* [Footnote: The line is by Kaʿb (al-Lisan, al-Taj, d-m-k). They said: one says "aqamtu ʿindahu shahran damīkan," meaning a complete month. Kaʿb said: "Dāba shahrayni thumma shahran damīkā." He did not mention the second hemistich. In Muʿjam ma staʿjam by al-Bakri (p. 144), Abu ʿUbayda said: Ariik is in the lands of Dhubyan. He said: there are two Ariks: Ariik al-Aswad and Ariik al-Abyad, and al-Ariik is a small mountain. "Yakhfiyan": with a fatha on the yāʾ, meaning they come out. And al-Ghamir has many meanings, among them in Taj al-ʿArus: al-Ghamir, like Amir: the grain of the bahmi grass that falls from its spike when it dries, or a green plant that has been covered by dryness... etc.]

I said: "They make it manifest." Then Warqa ibn Iyas, who was behind me, said: Saʿid ibn Jubayr recited to me ﴿akādu akhfīhā﴾ with a fatha on the alif. It has also been related from Saʿid ibn Jubayr that he agreed with the view of the others who said its meaning is: I almost conceal it from myself.

Mention of the narration from him to that effect: Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, he said: ʿAbd al-Rahman narrated to us, he said: Sufyan narrated to us, from ʿAta and Mansur, from Mujahid, both said: ﴿Indeed, the Hour is coming; I almost conceal it﴾, they both said: "from myself."

- ʿUbayd ibn Ismaʿil al-Hibbari narrated to me, he said: Ibn Fudayl narrated to us, from ʿAta ibn al-Sa'ib, from Saʿid ibn Jubayr, ﴿I almost conceal it﴾: he said, "from myself."

Abu Jaʿfar (al-Tabari) said: The view most appropriate to the interpretation of the verse is the view of those who said its meaning is: "I almost conceal it from myself," because the interpretation of the people of interpretation came with this. As for what was related from Saʿid ibn Jubayr regarding reading it with a fatha on the alif, it is a reading I do not consider permissible to recite with, because it opposes the reading of the proof (the established reading), which it is not permissible to oppose, as it came to us through widespread transmission.

If someone says: Why did you direct the interpretation of His saying ﴿I almost conceal it﴾ with a damma on the alif toward the meaning "I almost conceal it from myself," rather than directing it toward the meaning "I almost make it manifest"? You know that ikhfa in the speech of the Arabs has two meanings: one is manifestation, and the other is concealment, and that manifestation in this place is closer to the meaning of the statement, since concealing it from oneself would almost have an impossible meaning for the listeners, for it is impossible that anyone conceals from himself something he knows, while Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, has nothing hidden from Him. Answer: The matter is contrary to what you supposed. We directed the meaning of ﴿akhfīhā﴾ with a damma on the alif toward the meaning "I conceal it from myself," because the known meaning of ikhfa in the speech of the Arabs is concealment. It is said: "I have concealed the thing" when I have covered it. And those who directed its meaning toward manifestation relied on a line of verse by Imru' al-Qays ibn ʿAbis al-Kindi.

- It was narrated to me from Maʿmar ibn al-Muthanna that he said: Abu al-Khattab recited it to me, from his people in his town:

*"Fa-in tudfinū al-dāʾa lā nukhfihi ... wa-in tabʿathū al-ḥarba lā naqʿud"* [Footnote: The line is by Imru' al-Qays ibn ʿAbis al-Kindi. The author of al-Lisan (kh-f-a) cited it as evidence that his saying "lā nukhfihi," with a fatha on the nūn, means "we do not make it manifest." Likewise, the verse "akādu akhfīhā" means "I make it manifest," as al-Lihyani related from al-Kisai, from Muhammad ibn Sahl, from Saʿid ibn Jubayr. The author of al-Lisan said: It is said "khafaytu al-shayʾ akhfīhi" means I made the thing manifest and extracted it; it is said "khafiya al-matar al-fa'ār" when it brings them out of their burrows, i.e., their holes. Imru' al-Qays described a horse: "khafāhunna min anfāqihinna ka-annamā ... khafāhunna waddqu min ʿashiyyin mujallabi." And "khafaytu al-shayʾ akhfīhi" means I concealed it; it is one of the words with two opposite meanings (adad). "Akhfaytu al-shayʾ" means I covered and concealed it. The narrator's version of the verse is as in Maʿani al-Quran by al-Farra. In al-Lisan (kh-f-a): "Fa-in taktumū al-sirra lā nukhfihi."]

with a damma on the nūn of "lā nukhfihi," meaning "we do not make it manifest." Their reliance in directing the concealment in this place toward manifestation was on what they mentioned from hearing this line, with the damma on the nūn of "nukhfihi," as I have described. But a trustworthy man narrated to me from al-Farra:

*"Fa-in tadfinū al-dāʾa lā nakhfihi"*

with a fatha on the nūn of "nakhfihi," from "khafaytuhu akhfīhi," and this is more correct, because it is the known usage of the Arabs.

Since this is so, and the fatha on the alif of "akhfīhā" is not permissible in our view for the reason we have mentioned, the other possibility is established and confirmed, namely that the meaning is: "I almost conceal it from myself."

As for the correct basis of this view, it is that Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, addressed the Arabs in the Qur'an according to what they know of their speech and what their discourse among themselves proceeds by. Since it was known in their speech that one of them, when he wishes to emphasize his report about concealing something he is keeping secret, says: "I nearly concealed this matter from myself because of how intensely I keep it secret; and if I could conceal it from myself, I would conceal it," He addressed them according to what their usage in this has been in their speech among themselves and what they know in their manner of speaking. Other views have been stated on this besides what we have said. We chose this view over the others because it agrees with the views of the people of knowledge among the Companions and the Successors, since we do not permit ourselves to oppose them in what has been widely transmitted from them and has come down from them in a manner that removes excuse. As for those who said other than our view, from among those who spoke on it by deriving meanings from the speech of the Arabs without attributing it to an imam among the Companions or the Successors, and in a way that allows the speech to bear other than its well-known sense, they differed among themselves about its meaning. Some of them said: its meaning may be: "I want to conceal it," and said: this is known in the language, and it is mentioned that it is related from the Arabs that they say: "Those are my companions upon whom I almost descend (akādu anzilu)," meaning: I only descend upon them. And it is related: "akādu abraḥu manzilī," meaning: I do not leave my dwelling. He argued with a line of verse recited by one of the poets:

*"Kādat wa-kidtu wa-tilka khayru irādatin ... law ʿāda min ʿahdi al-ṣabābati mā maḍā"* [Footnote: The line is in al-Lisan (k-y-d). It says: "Fulan yakīdu amran mā adrī mā huwa," when he seeks it, schemes for it, and strives for it. He said: "Balaghū al-amr alladhī kādū": meaning they sought or intended. Abu Bakr recited, for kāda in the meaning of arāda, the line of al-Afwah: "Fa-in tajmaʿ awtādun wa-aʿmidatun ... wa-sākinu balaghū al-amra alladhī kādū," meaning: that which they intended. And he recited: "Kādat wa-kidtu..." He said: its meaning is "mā arādat" (she did not intend). And the verse "lam yakad yarāhā" may bear this sense, since what he saw in the darknesses made him despair of looking at his hand and of seeing it. The line is evidence that kāda means arāda, which the author cited at the words "akādu akhfīhā."]

He said: He means by "kādat": "arādat" (she intended). He said: then the meaning is "I intend to conceal it, so that every soul may be recompensed for what it strives for." He said: Similar to this is the saying of Zayd al-Khayl:

*"Sarīʿun ilā al-hayjāʾi shākin silāḥuhu ... famā an takādu qirnuhu yatanaffasu"* [Footnote: The line is by Zayd al-Khayl as the author said. The author of al-Lisan (k-y-d) cited it as evidence that kāda may come as a connecting particle in speech. He said: kāda may be a connecting (or redundant) element in speech, as al-Akhfash, Qutrub, and Abu Hatim permitted, and Qutrub argued with the poet's saying: "Sarīʿ... etc." Its meaning: "his opponent does not breathe." But Abu Jaʿfar al-Tabari made it similar to the preceding witness, while Qutrub's explanation of this witness is clearer and better, and the particle before "yakād" is redundant or a negation reinforcing the negation before it.]

He said: It is as if he said: "fa-mā yatanaffasu qirnuhu," otherwise the meaning would be weakened. He said: Dhu al-Rummah also said:

*"Idhā ghayyara al-nanʾu al-muḥibbīna lam yakad ... rasīsu al-hawā min ḥubbi Mayyata yabraḥu"* [Footnote: This line is from the famous rhyming ode of Dhu al-Rummah (Diwan, Cambridge edition 1919, p. 78). Its commentator said: al-nanʾ is distance; rasīs al-hawā is its touch, and what remains hidden of it or its beginning. It is said: "lam yajid rasīs al-ḥummā" (he did not feel the trace of fever). The author cited the line to show that the meaning is: "lam yabraḥ" (he did not leave), or "lam yurid yabraḥ" (he did not intend to leave). On this, "yakād" is redundant in the speech. A different version of the line occurs in al-Lisan (r-s-s), which supports what the author held, that the meaning is with "yakād" redundant: "Idhā ghayyara al-nanʾu al-muḥibbīna lam yakad ... rasīsu al-hawā min ḥubbi Mayyata yabraḥu." This is the version to which the poet shifted when Ibn Shubrumah, judge of Basra, corrected him on hearing him recite the ode in al-Mirbad. But the verifiers said that Dhu al-Rummah's first version was better than the second. Al-Allama al-Muhaqqiq Radi Allah al-Dili al-Astarabadi, Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, clarified the correctness of the first version: that the meaning of "lam yakad" is "lam yaqrab" (he did not approach), and that negating the approach of a thing is more forceful than negating the thing; so the meaning of the line is: when distance changed the hearts of the lovers, the distance of Mayya from me does not take away what I feel of her firm and enduring love, nor does it approach taking it away. (See al-Radi's commentary on Ibn al-Hajib's Kafiya, Astana edition 2:306, on verbs of approximation.) al-Radi refuted the claim of some grammarians that "the negation of kāda is affirmation and its affirmation is negation," and this is a precious statement showing his intelligence and precision of understanding.]

He said: The meaning is not "lam yakad yabraḥ," i.e., he went far with ease and left with difficulty; rather the meaning is "lam yabraḥ" or "lam yurid yabraḥ," otherwise the meaning would be weakened. He said: Likewise is the saying of Abu al-Najm:

*"Wa-in atāka naʿiyyun fa-ndubanna abā ... qad kāda yaḍṭliʿu al-aʿdāʾa wal-khuṭaba"* [Footnote: The line is by Abu al-Najm as the author said. The witness is in "kāda yaḍṭliʿu." The author holds that its meaning is: "qad iḍṭalaʿa al-aʿdāʾ" (the enemies have risen to it), since otherwise it would not be praise if he meant "kāda" and did not intend "yafʿalu." In the commentary on the line, the verb "kāda" is a connecting (redundant) element, like the two witnesses before it in his view. "Yaḍṭliʿu al-aʿdāʾ": i.e., he rises up with them and with the sermons; he dropped the bāʾ, so the verb reached its object directly, which had been in the genitive with bāʾ before its removal. It is said "iḍṭalaʿa bi-ḥamlihi," meaning he was strong enough to bear it and rose to it. It derives from ḍalāʿa, meaning strength. In al-Lisan (ḍ-l-ʿ): "iḍṭalaʿa al-ḥimla," meaning his ribs bore it. Ibn al-Sikkit said: it is said "huwa muḍṭaliʿun bi-ḥamlihi," meaning he is strong enough to carry it; it is a derived form (mufta'al) from ḍalāʿa. The naʿī is the messenger who reports the death of one who has died.]

He said: The meaning would be: "qad iḍṭalaʿa al-aʿdāʾ" (the enemies have risen), otherwise it would not be praise if he meant "kāda" and did not intend "yafʿalu."

Others said: Rather, the meaning is: "Indeed, the Hour is coming, akādu," and the report ends at His saying "akād," because its meaning is: "I almost bring it." Then he begins: "But I conceal it so that every soul may be recompensed for what it strives for." He said: This is parallel to the saying of Ibn Dabi:

*"Hamamtu wa-lam af'al wa-kidtu wa-layt anī ... tarakta ʿalā ʿUthmāna tabkī aqāribuhu"* [Footnote: The line is by Dabi' ibn al-Harith al-Barjumi, whom Caliph ʿUthman imprisoned because he was a licentious man who satirized some people, so ʿUthman wanted to discipline him. When he was summoned to be disciplined, he tied a knife to his leg intending to kill ʿUthman with it, but he was caught, beaten, and returned to prison until he died there. The line is from an ode of his recited by Abu al-ʿAbbas al-Mubarrad (see Raghbat al-Amil, with the commentary of al-Marsafi on the Kamil, 4:91): "Fa-la tatbaʿīnī in halaktu malāmatan ... fa-laysa bi-ʿārin qatlu man lā uqātiluhu / Hamamtu wa-lam af'al wa-kidtu wa-layt anī ... tarakta ʿalā ʿUthmāna tabkī ḥalāʾiluhu." The witness is in "kidtu," meaning I almost did what I intended, namely killing ʿUthman. It is parallel to the Qur'anic "inna al-sāʿata ātiyatun akādu": some held its meaning is "akādu an ātī bihā" (I almost bring it), then began: "wa-lakinnī ukhfīhā li-tujzā kullu nafsin bi-mā tasʿā." The line is by Dabi', not by his son as the author said.]

So he said "kidtu," and its meaning is "kidtu af'alu" (I almost did).

Others said: The meaning of "ukhfīhā" is "uzhirhā" (I make it manifest). They said: concealment and secrecy may be directed by the Arabs toward the meaning of manifestation, and some cited for their saying the line of al-Farazdaq:

*"Falammā ra'ā al-Ḥajjāja jarrada sayfahu ... asarra al-Ḥarūrī alladhī kāna aḍmarā"* [Footnote: I did not find this line in the Diwan of al-Farazdaq; it is among the witnesses of Abu ʿUbayda (al-Lisan, s-r-r). He said: "asrartu al-shayʾ" means I concealed it, and "asrartuhu" means I announced it; and from manifestation is His saying: "wa-asarrū al-nadāma lammā raʾaw al-ʿadhāb" (and they concealed the regret when they saw the punishment), meaning they made it manifest. He recited al-Farazdaq: "Falammā ra'ā al-Ḥajjāja..." The line. Shamir said: I did not find this line for al-Farazdaq, and no one but Abu ʿUbayda said that in "wa-asarrū al-nadāma" it means "uẓhirūhā." He said: I have not heard that from anyone else. Al-Azhari said: the lexicographers strongly denied Abu ʿUbayda. It was said: "asarrū al-nadāma" means: the leaders among the polytheists concealed the regret before their followers whom they misled, and they concealed it; so al-Zajjaj said, and this is the view of the exegetes. "Al-Ḥarūrī" is the Kharijite, a nisba to Harurā', which was their first gathering when they renounced Amir al-Mu'minin ʿAli and made manifest arbitration: "lā ḥukma illā lillāh." They were called the Muhakkima, the Harūriyya, and the Khawarij.]

He said: By his saying "asarra" he meant "aẓhara" (made manifest). He said: It may also be that the meaning of His saying "wa-asarrū al-nadāma" is "wa-aẓharūhā," because they said: "Yā laytanā nuraddu wa-lā nukadhdhiba bi-āyāti rabbinā" (Would that we were returned, and that we did not deny the signs of our Lord).

All these whose views we have related said: it is permissible that the saying of the one who said "the meaning is: I almost conceal it from myself" means: "I conceal it from my side and from my presence." All these views we have mentioned from those we have mentioned are interpretations by them that direct the speech to other than its well-known meaning, and it is not permissible to direct the meanings of Allah's speech to other than the predominant aspects known to those addressed by it. In that, together with their disagreement with the interpretation of the people of knowledge, there is a just witness against the error of what they went to.

* *

As for His saying ﴿so that every soul may be recompensed for what it strives for﴾

Al-Tabari, Jami' al-Bayan, on surah 20, verses 15–16 (part 2 of 2):

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: Indeed, the Hour is coming, so that every soul may be recompensed: that is, so that every soul which its Lord has tested through worship in this world may be rewarded for what it strives at, that is, for what it does of good and evil, of obedience and disobedience. As for His words, ﴿So let not one who does not believe in it turn you away from it﴾, He, may His remembrance be exalted, means: so let not one who does not believe in it, O Musa, turn you away from preparing for the Hour. By "one who does not believe in it" is meant one who does not acknowledge the rising of the Hour, does not affirm the resurrection after death, does not hope for reward, and does not fear punishment.

* *

As for His words, ﴿and follows his desire﴾, that is: follows the desire of his own self and opposes the command and prohibition of God, ﴿and so you will perish﴾, that is: you will be ruined if you are turned away from preparing for the Hour and from belief in it, and from the belief that God will raise the creation for its rising from their graves after their annihilation, by the turning away of one who disbelieves in it.

Some of them claimed that the pronoun (al-ha' wa'l-alif, "the ha and the alif") in His words, ﴿So let not one who does not believe in it turn you away from it﴾, refers back to belief (al-iman), saying: "It is said 'from it' (anha), while it refers back to belief, just as ﴿Indeed your Lord, after it [i.e., after that deed], is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ is said, referring to the deed." But there has been no mention of belief in this passage, so that this pronoun should be taken as referring to it. Rather, the mention has been of the Hour, so it is more appropriate that the pronoun refers to it.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 20, verses 17–18:

The interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And what is that in your right hand, O Musa?﴾ (17)

Exalted is He, He says: "And what is this that is in your right hand, O Musa?" The letter bāʾ in His saying ﴿bi-yamīnika﴾ (in your right hand) is connected to "tilka" (that). The Arabs connect "tilka" and "hādhihi" (this) just as they connect "alladhī" (the one who), and from this is the verse of Yazid ibn Mufarrigh:

ʿAdas, mā li-ʿabbādin ʿalayki imāra ... amintī, wa-hādhā tahmilīna ṭalīq
[The verse is by Zayd ibn Mufarrigh al-Himyari, addressing his mule when he fled from ʿUbayd Allah ibn Ziyad and his brother ʿAbbad. Ibn Mufarrigh used to satirise them whenever his stipend was delayed, and he has a well-known story. ʿAdas is a command to the mule, or the name of the mule. It is also narrated as "najawti fi makān" (you escaped to a place) instead of "amintī" (Lisan: ʿds). Hādhā: a demonstrative pronoun, which has been connected to the clause "tahmilīn," and so it has become one of the relative pronouns according to the view of some grammarians. Hādhā: a subject (mubtadaʾ), and the clause "tahmilīn" is its relative clause (ṣila); and ṭalīq is the predicate of the subject. That is, "and that which you carry is free, no one has authority over it."]

It is as if he said: "And that which you carry is free."

Perhaps someone will say: What is the purpose of God asking Musa about what is in his hand? Did He not know that what was in his hand was a staff? It is said to him: That is not as you have understood. Rather, Exalted is He said this to him when He wished to turn it into a serpent gliding, while it was a piece of wood. So He drew his attention to it and confirmed that it was a piece of wood on which he leans and with which he drives his sheep, in order to make him know His power over what He wills, the greatness of His authority, and the effectiveness of His command in what He loves, by transforming it into a serpent gliding, when He wished that for him, so that it would be a sign for Musa along with his other signs to Pharaoh and his people.

* *

The interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He said: It is my staff; I lean upon it, and I beat down [leaves] with it for my sheep, and for me in it are other uses﴾ (18)

Exalted is He, He says, reporting about Musa: Musa said, answering his Lord: ﴿It is my staff; I lean upon it, and I beat down [leaves] with it for my sheep﴾. He says: I strike the dry tree with it so that its leaves fall, and my sheep graze on them. It is said from this: "hashsha fulan al-shajara yahushshu hashshan," when he beats the branches of it so that its leaves fall, as the rajaz poet said:

Uhushshu bi-l-ʿaṣā ʿalā aghnāmī ... min nāʿimi l-arāki wa-l-bashām
[In Lisan (h-sh): al-hashsh is to shake the leaves off a tree with a staff. "Hashsha al-ghuṣn yahushshuhu hashshan" means he beat it and dropped its leaves for his sheep. From it is His saying: ﴿wa-ahushshu bihā ʿalā ghanamī﴾. Al-Farraʾ said: that is, I strike the dry tree with it so that its leaves fall and his sheep graze on them. Al-Arak and al-Bashām are two kinds of trees which livestock graze on, and their branches are soft; livestock eat them when they are green.]

The exegetes have said something similar to what we have said regarding this.

* Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Saʿid narrated to us, from Qatadah ﴿wa-ahushshu bihā ʿalā ghanamī﴾: He said: I beat.

* Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Saʿid narrated to us, from Qatadah ﴿wa-ahushshu bihā ʿalā ghanamī﴾: He said: The Prophet of God Musa (ﷺ) used to beat the leaves of the tree for his sheep.

* Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His saying ﴿It is my staff; I lean upon it, and I beat down [leaves] with it for my sheep﴾: He said: He leans on it when he walks with the sheep, and beats with it, shaking the tree until the leaves fall, the ḥabala and others.

* Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Yahya ibn Wadih narrated to us, saying: al-Hasan narrated to us, from ʿIkrimah ﴿wa-ahushshu bihā ʿalā ghanamī﴾: He said: I strike the tree with it, so its leaves fall upon me.

And His saying ﴿and for me in it are other uses﴾

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 20, verse 19–21:

The interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿He said, "Throw it down, O Musa!" (19) So he threw it down, and suddenly it was a snake, moving swiftly. (20) He said, "Seize it and do not fear; We will return it to its original condition." (21)﴾

Her Exalted Mention says: Allah said to Musa: "Throw down your staff that is in your right hand, O Musa." Allah, majestic is His majesty, says: So Musa threw it down, and Allah made it a snake moving swiftly. It had previously been a dry piece of wood, a staff that he leaned upon and with which he drove his sheep, and by the command of Allah it became a snake.

As related:

* Ahmad ibn ʿAbdah al-Dabbi narrated to us, he said: Hafs ibn Jumayʿ narrated to us, he said: Simak ibn Harb narrated to us, from ʿIkrimah, from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: When it was said to Musa, "Throw it down, O Musa," he threw it down, and ﴿suddenly it was a snake, moving swiftly﴾, and it had not been a snake before that. He said: It passed by a tree and ate it, and passed by a rock and swallowed it. He said: Musa began to hear the sound of the rock within its belly. He said: So he turned and fled, and he was called: "O Musa, seize it," but he did not take it. Then he was called a second time: "Seize it and do not fear," but he did not take it. Then in the third call he was told, ﴿"Indeed you are of the secure ones,"﴾ and he took it.

* Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, he said: ʿAmr narrated to us, he said: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, who said: His Lord said to him, that is, to Musa, ﴿"Throw it down, O Musa,"﴾ meaning ﴿so he threw it down, and suddenly it was a snake, moving swiftly﴾ ﴿so when he saw it moving like a jann, he turned and fled without looking back﴾, and he was called: ﴿"O Musa, do not fear. Indeed, those sent by Me do not fear in My presence."﴾

* Ibn Humayd narrated to us, he said: Salamah narrated to us, from Ibn Ishaq, from Wahb ibn Munabbih: ﴿He said, "Throw it down, O Musa." So he threw it down, and suddenly it was a snake, moving swiftly﴾, shaking, having fangs and a form as Allah willed it to be. He saw a dreadful thing, ﴿so he turned and fled without looking back﴾, and his Lord called to him: ﴿"O Musa, come forward and do not fear."﴾ ﴿"We will return it to its original condition."﴾

And His words ﴿He said, "Seize it and do not fear"﴾

Her Exalted Mention says: Allah said to Musa: "Seize the snake." The pronoun "ha" and "alif" refer to the snake. ﴿"And do not fear"﴾ means: do not fear this snake. ﴿"We will return it to its original condition"﴾ means: We will return it to its former form, which it had before We made it a snake, and We will restore it to being a staff as it was.

It is said of anyone who was in a state, then left it, turned away from it, and then returned to it: "So-and-so returned to his former conduct," "returned to his former conduct," "returned to his former conduct" (with the various prepositions).

The people of interpretation have said things similar to what we have said. Those who said so:

* ʿAli narrated to me, he said: ʿAbd Allah narrated to us, he said: Muʿawiyah narrated to me, from ʿAli, from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His words ﴿its original condition (siratuha al-ula)﴾: it means its first state.

* al-Qasim narrated to us, he said: al-Husayn narrated to us, he said: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Juraij, from Mujahid, the same.

* Ibn Humayd narrated to us, he said: Salamah narrated to us, from Ibn Ishaq, from Wahb ibn Munabbih, ﴿"We will return it to its original condition"﴾, that is, We will return it to being a staff as it was.

* Bishr narrated to us, he said: Yazid narrated to us, he said: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, ﴿"We will return it to its original condition"﴾, he said: to its original form.

The interpretation of His saying, ﴿Go to Pharaoh, for he has transgressed (24). [Moses] said, "My Lord, expand for me my breast (25) and ease for me my task (26) and untie the knot from my tongue (27) that they may understand my speech (28) and appoint for me a minister from my family (29), Aaron, my brother (30)."﴾

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says to His Prophet Moses, may the blessings of God be upon him: ﴿Go﴾, O Moses, ﴿to Pharaoh, for he has transgressed﴾. That is: he has exceeded his station and rebelled against his Lord. We have already explained the meaning of tughyan (transgression) in what has preceded, sufficiently so that it need not be repeated here.

In the speech there is an omission, which is dispensed with because the listener understands it from what has been mentioned, namely His saying ﴿Go to Pharaoh, for he has transgressed﴾: so call him to the Oneness of God and obedience to Him, and to sending the Children of Israel with you. ﴿He said, "My Lord, expand for me my breast"﴾: that is, "My Lord, expand my breast, so that I may retain from You what You entrust to me of Your revelation, and be emboldened thereby to address Pharaoh."

Those who interpret the Qur'an have said something similar to what we have said on this matter.

Mention of those who said that:

Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, concerning the words of God, ﴿My Lord, expand for me my breast﴾: "Boldness for me."

* *

As for His saying ﴿and untie the knot from my tongue﴾:

That is: "Loosen my tongue for speech." It is said that there was in it a non-Arabic quality (ʿujmah) in speech, which resulted from his putting the ember into his mouth on the day Pharaoh intended to kill him.

Report transmitted from those who said this: Muhammad ibn ʿAmr narrated to me, saying: Abu ʿAsim narrated to us, saying: ʿIsa narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Saʿid ibn Jubayr, concerning His saying ﴿a knot from my tongue﴾: "A non-Arabic quality (ʿujmah) from a live ember which he put into his mouth at the command of Pharaoh's wife, to ward off from him the punishment of Pharaoh, when he seized Moses by his beard while he did not understand, and said, 'This is my enemy.' She said to him, 'He does not understand.'"

Al-Harith narrated to me, saying: al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Warqa narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, concerning ﴿and untie the knot from my tongue﴾: "[It was due to] a live ember which he put into his mouth at the command of Pharaoh's wife, to ward off from him the punishment of Pharaoh, when he seized Moses by his beard, and Moses said, 'This is my enemy,' and she said to him, 'He does not understand.' This is the statement of Saʿid ibn Jubayr."

Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, concerning His saying ﴿and untie the knot from my tongue﴾: "The non-Arabic quality is from an ember of fire which he put into his mouth, at the command of Pharaoh's wife, to ward off from him the punishment of Pharaoh when he seized him by the beard."

Musa narrated to us, saying: ʿAmr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, who said: When the boy, meaning Moses, grew up, his mother Asiya suckled him as a child. While she was bouncing him and playing with him, she handed him to Pharaoh and said, "Take him." When he took him to himself, Moses seized his beard and plucked it. Pharaoh said, "Bring me the slaughterers!" Asiya said, ﴿Do not kill him; perhaps he will benefit us, or we may adopt him as a son﴾, [and said], "He is only a child who does not understand, and he did this only out of his childishness. I know that there is no one in the people of Egypt more discerning than I am. I will place before him ornaments of rubies and place before him an ember. If he takes the rubies, he understands, so slay him; but if he takes the ember, he is a child." She brought out her rubies and placed before him a basin of embers. Then Gabriel, peace be upon him, came and cast an ember into his hand, and Moses put it into his mouth, and it burned his tongue. This is what God, mighty and majestic, refers to in His saying ﴿and untie the knot from my tongue, that they may understand my speech﴾. The knot was thus removed from Moses on account of that.

The interpretation of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿He said: "You have been granted your request, O Moses. (36) And We had already bestowed favor upon you another time, (37) when We inspired to your mother that which is inspired. (38)"﴾

His statement, may His remembrance be exalted, means: God said to Moses (ﷺ): "You have been given what you asked of your Lord, O Moses: the expansion of your breast, the making easy of your task for you, the untying of the knot of your tongue, the making of your brother Harun (Aaron) a minister for you, the strengthening of your back through him, and his being made a partner with you in the prophethood."

﴿And We had already bestowed favor upon you another time﴾: His statement, may His remembrance be exalted, means: "We had already shown kindness to you, O Moses, another time before this time, and that was when We inspired to your mother, when she gave birth to you in the year in which Pharaoh was killing every male child of your people, what We inspired to her." Then He, may His remembrance be exalted, explained what He inspired to his mother, saying: it was, "Cast him into the chest," where "an" (that) is in the accusative position as a replacement for "ma" (what) in His saying ﴿that which is inspired﴾ and as a translation of it.
