* Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatada, ﴿"lest He destroy you with a punishment"﴾: he says, "lest He uproot you with a punishment."

* Al-Hasan related to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatada, regarding His saying, ﴿"lest He destroy you with a punishment"﴾, he said: "lest He uproot you with a punishment, destroying you."

* Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His saying, ﴿"lest He destroy you with a punishment"﴾, he said: "He destroys you with a destruction in which there is no remnant." He said: "And the one who is uprooted has no remnant."

* Musa related to us, saying: Amr related to us, saying: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi, ﴿"lest He destroy you with a punishment"﴾, he says: "He destroys you with a punishment."

The readers differed concerning the recitation of this. The majority of the readers of Madina and Basra, and some of the people of Kufa, recited ﴿fa-yasahtakum﴾ with a fatha on the ya, from sahata yashat. The majority of the readers of Kufa recited ﴿fa-yusihtakum﴾ with a damma on the ya, from asaha yusihu.

Abu Ja'far said: Our view regarding this is that they are two well-known recitations and two known dialects with one meaning. Whichever of them the reader recites is correct, though the fatha is more pleasing to me, because it is the dialect of the people of al-Aliya, and it is more eloquent, while the other, the damma, is the dialect of Najd.

His saying, ﴿"and indeed he fails who fabricates"﴾.

He says: whoever invents a lie does not attain success, and by his lie he does not attain the need he sought through it, nor the goal he hoped to reach by it.

**Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on Surah 20, verses 62–63:**

On the interpretation of His words, ﴿So they disputed their affair among themselves, and secretly conferred﴾ (62) ﴿They said: "Indeed, these two are certainly sorcerers who intend to drive you out of your land with their sorcery and to do away with your ideal way of life."﴾ (63)

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: The sorcerers disputed their affair among themselves.

Their dispute over their affair among themselves, as it is related, was that some of them said to others:

* Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His words ﴿So they disputed their affair among themselves, and secretly conferred﴾: "The sorcerers said among themselves: 'If this is a sorcerer, we will surely overcome him; and if it is from heaven, then it has a matter (of its own).'"

Others said: Rather, it was that some of them said to others: "This is not the speech of a sorcerer."

Mention of those who said this: Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salamah narrated to us, from Ibn Ishaq, who said: I was told, from Wahb ibn Munabbih, who said: Every sorcerer gathered his ropes and staffs, and Musa went out with his brother, leaning on his staff, until he came to the assembly place, while Pharaoh was in his council, with the nobles of his kingdom, and the people had been made to gather in rows for him. Musa said to the sorcerers when he came to them: ﴿Woe to you! Do not invent a lie against God, lest He destroy you with a punishment; and he who invents has indeed failed.﴾ So the sorcerers argued among themselves, and some of them said to others: "This is not the speech of a sorcerer."

* * *

As for His words ﴿and secretly conferred﴾:

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: The sorcerers privately conferred among themselves.

Then the scholars differed concerning the secret conference they held. Some of them said: It was the saying of some of them to others: "If this is a sorcerer, we will surely overcome him; and if it is a matter from heaven, then it will surely overcome us."

Others said, regarding this:

* Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salamah narrated to us, from Ibn Ishaq, who said: I was told, from Wahb ibn Munabbih, who said: Some of them signalled to others with a private consultation: ﴿Indeed, these two are certainly sorcerers who intend to drive you out of your land with their sorcery.﴾

* Musa narrated to me, saying: 'Amr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, regarding ﴿So they disputed their affair among themselves, and secretly conferred﴾, "apart from Musa and Harun." They said in their private conference: ﴿Indeed, these two are certainly sorcerers who intend to drive you out of your land with their sorcery, and to do away with your ideal way of life.﴾ They said: "Indeed these two are sorcerers," meaning by their saying "these two": Musa and Harun, "are sorcerers who intend to drive you out of your land with their sorcery."

As also:

* Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His words ﴿Indeed, these two are certainly sorcerers who intend to drive you out of your land with their sorcery﴾: "Musa and Harun, peace be upon them both."

The readers differed concerning the recitation of His words ﴿Inna hadhani la-sahirani (Indeed, these two are certainly sorcerers)﴾. The majority of the readers of the major cities recited ﴿Inna hadhani﴾ with the *inna* (indeed) doubled (in pronunciation, i.e., *inna* with a shaddah) and with an *alif* in *hadhani*, and they said: "We recite it thus, and it is so." Some of the grammarians (*ahl al-'arabiyyah*, the scholars of Arabic grammar) of Basra said: "*Inna* is light (*khafifah*) in meaning heavy (*thaqilah*), and it is the dialect of a people who put it in the nominative case, and they add the *lam* to distinguish it from the one which means *ma* (not)." Some grammarians of Kufa said: "That is on two bases. One of them is according to the dialect of the Banu al-Harith ibn Ka'b and those adjacent to them, who make the dual, in its nominative, accusative and genitive cases, with an *alif*." A man of the Asad tribe recited to me, from some of the Banu al-Harith ibn Ka'b:

*So he lowered his gaze as the viper lowers its gaze, and if it had found a way in, the viper would have struck his two fangs and made them dumb.* [[The verse is by al-Mutalammis, Jarir ibn 'Abd al-'Uzza, or, it is said, Jarir ibn 'Abd al-Masih, from an ode he composed, transmitted by Ibn al-Shajari (see the book of al-Ashmuni on grammar with the commentary of the scholar Muhyi al-Din 'Abd al-Hamid, the Halabi edition, 1:47). He says: "Atraqa" means he was silent and did not speak, and he let his eyes fall to the ground. "Al-shuja'" is a type of snake that is slender and fine, and it is the boldest of them; or it is the large snake that leaps at the horseman and the pedestrian and rears on its tail, and it may reach the horseman's head, and it is found in the deserts. "Musaghan" is a place noun from *saagha yasuughu*, meaning to enter and penetrate. "Sammama" means arm and... (sic) [the text here reads "'adad wa naib", i.e., a grip and a fang]. The verse follows the dialect of the Banu al-Harith ibn Ka'b and those who speak like them, and the evidence in it is that his saying *linabahu* (to his two fangs) is a dual in the genitive preceded by the *lam*, yet it came with an *alif*. This is the dialect of the Banu al-Harith ibn Ka'b, Banu al-'Anbar, Banu al-Hujaym, clans of Rabi'ah, Bakr ibn Wa'il, Zubayd, Khath'am, Hamdan and 'Udhrah. Some grammarians take His words ﴿Indeed these two are certainly sorcerers﴾ and the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "There are no two witr prayers in one night" as based on this dialect.] Al-Farra' said in *Ma'ani al-Qur'an* (folio 198 of the University photocopy, no. 24059): "Our recitation with the doubled *inna* and the *alif* is on two grounds. One of them is the dialect of the Banu al-Harith ibn Ka'b, who make the dual in its nominative and genitive with the *alif*. A man of the Asad recited to me from them: 'So he lowered his gaze...' the verse. And that man related from them: 'This is the handwriting of the two hands of my brother, I recognise it by its appearance.' And that, though rare, is more regular."

[The author carried on with al-Farra's words to their end.]

He said: He also related from him: "This is the handwriting of the two hands of my brother, I recognise it." He said: "And that, though rare, is more regular, because the Arabs said *muslimun* (Muslims), so they made the *waw* follow the *damma* because it is not inflected; then they said *ra'aytu al-muslimin* (I saw the Muslims), so they made the *ya'* follow the *kasra* of the *mim*. They said: 'When they saw that the *ya'* of the dual could not take on a *kasra* on what precedes it, and it remained open, they left the *alif* to follow it, and they said *rajulan* (two men) in every case.'" He said: "The Arabs have agreed on affirming the *alif* in *kilta* (both) and *kilaa* in the two men, whether in the nominative, accusative or genitive, and they are two. Except the Banu Kinanah, who say: *ra'aytu kili al-rajulayn* (I saw both of the two men), and *marartu bi kili al-rajulayn* (I passed by both of the two men), and that is ugly and rare; they went according to analogy." He said: "The other way is that you say: 'I found the *alif* of this is a support, and it is not a radical of the verb. When I formed it, I added to it a *nun*, then I left the *alif* fixed in its state and not removed in any case, as the Arabs said *alladhi* (who/which), then they added a *nun* indicating the plural and said *alladhina* in its nominative, accusative and genitive, just as they left *hadhani* in its nominative, accusative and genitive.' He said: 'The analogy would have been that they say *alladhun*.' Another of them said: 'That is from the loose *jazm* (apocopation), and if it were in the accusative, it would have become *insiyat* (extension).'"

* And I was told, from Abu 'Ubaydah Ma'mar ibn al-Muthanna, who said: Abu 'Amr, 'Isa ibn 'Umar and Yunus said: "*Inna hadhayni la-sahirani*" in pronunciation, and it is written as they intend in the script, and the pronunciation is correct. He said: Abu al-Khattab claimed that he heard some people of the Banu Kinanah and others raise the dual in the position of the genitive and accusative. He said: Bishr ibn Hilal said: "*Inna* is for the beginning and affirmation. Do you not see that it governs what follows it, and does not govern what comes after the one that follows it, so it raises the predicate and does not put it in the accusative, as it put the noun in the accusative? So the meaning of '*inna hadhani la-sahirani*' is the meaning of two sentences; its origin is: 'Indeed, yes (*inna*), then I said: *hadhani sahirani*'. Do you not see that they raise the coordinated noun, as in the saying of Dabi'":

*Whoever has his camp in Medina at dusk, indeed I and Qayyar are strangers there.* [[The verse is by Dabi' ibn al-Harith al-Burjumi, the first of the verses he composed while imprisoned in Medina during the time of 'Uthman ibn 'Affan. After it are three verses recited by Abu al-'Abbas al-Mubarrad in *al-Kamil* (Khizanat al-Adab by al-Baghdadi, 4:323–328), and the grammarians cited it as evidence that *Qayyar* is a subject whose predicate is omitted, and the sentence is parenthetical between the subject of *inna* and its predicate. The meaning is: 'Indeed I and Qayyar are, likewise, strangers.' He did not make the predicate belong to Qayyar, and the predicate of *inna* be omitted, because the *lam* does not enter the predicate of a subject until it is placed first, as in *la-qa'imun Zayd* (indeed Zayd is standing). This explanation goes against the school of Sibawayh, for the sentence in his view is intended to be delayed, so it is coordinated, not parenthetical. Al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' claimed that the accusative of *inna* is weak, because it changes only the noun and not the predicate. Al-Zajjaj said: 'This is a mistake, because *inna* has operated in two ways, raising and putting in the accusative, and there is no governing accusative in Arabic that is not accompanied by a raised noun, because every accusative is compared to the object, and the object cannot exist without an agent, except in the passive. How could the accusative of *inna* be weak when it passes over adverbs and governs what follows it, as in *inna fiha qawman jabbarin* (indeed in it are tyrannical people)? The accusative after *inna* is among the strongest of the accusatives.' End.]]

And His saying:

*Indeed the swords, in their morning and evening, have left Hawazin like the horn of the broken-horned (ibex).* [[The verse is by al-Akhtal (Khizanat al-Adab by al-Baghdadi, 2:372), from an ode of sixteen verses he composed in praise of al-'Abbas ibn Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah ibn al-'Abbas. The verse is cited by grammarians as evidence that the first word may be considered in form while the second is not, i.e., the replaced noun is considered in form and not the substitute. For his saying "*ghadwuha*" is a substitute for "*al-suyuf*". Al-Mubarrad said in *al-Kamil*: "It is a substitution of inclusion (*badal al-ishtimal*), and the replaced noun has been observed in form by returning a pronoun to it from the predicate, and the substitute was not observed. If it had been observed, it would have said *taraka* in the dual." Hawazin: the father of a tribe, Hawazin ibn Mansur ibn 'Ikrimah ibn Khasafah ibn Qays 'Aylan ibn Mudar. "Al-A'adab" is one whose one horn is broken. The author cited the verse as evidence that they may raise the coordinated word after the noun of *inna*; but there is no coordination after the noun of *inna* in the verse; it is rather a substitution of the accusative, as established by al-Mubarrad and Abu 'Ali al-Farisi in *Idah al-Shi'r*.]]

He said: Some of them say: "*Inna Allaha wa mala'ikatahu yusalluna 'ala al-Nabi*" (Indeed God and His angels send blessings upon the Prophet), and they raise it by the partnership of the beginning, and *inna* does not govern it. He said: I have heard eloquent people of the pilgrims say: "*Inna al-hamda wa al-ni'mata laka wa al-mulka, la sharika lak*" (Indeed praise and blessing are yours, and sovereignty, you have no partner). He said: Some people recited it with the *nun* of *inna* lightened and unvoweled. He said: This is permissible, because they have put the *lam* in the beginning, and it is a separator. He said:

*Umm al-Hulays is an old woman, a crone.* [[This is a line of half-rajaz metre attributed by al-Saghani in *al-'Ubab* to 'Antarah ibn 'Arus, with the *shin* at its end, and it is said with the *sin*, a client of Thaqif. (Khizanat al-Adab al-Kubra by al-Baghdadi, 4:328–330). It is evidence that the *lam* entering the predicate of a postponed subject, without *inna*, is an anomaly. Some explained it as: "*la-hiya 'ajuzun*" (indeed she is an old woman), so that it is in the estimate entering the subject. Ibn al-Sarraj said in *al-Usul*: Abu 'Uthman said: Sa'id ibn Jubayr recited (*illa annahum la ya'kuluna al-ta'am*) with the *alif* of *anna* opened, and he made the *lam* superfluous as it is superfluous in the saying: *Umm al-Hulays la-'ajuzun shahrabah / tarda min al-lahm bi-'azm al-raqabah*. End. Ibn Jinni held that it is not superfluous, but in the verse it is a necessity of poetry. He said in *Sirr al-Sina'ah*: As for the necessity by which the *lam* enters the predicate of *inna*, it is one of the necessities of poetry, and it is not to be made an analogy; the correct form is to say: '*la-Umm al-Hulays 'ajuzun shahrabah*', as one says *la-Zayd qa'im* (indeed Zayd is standing). The author cited the verse as evidence that the *lam* in "*wa Qayyar biha la-gharib*" is the *lam* of the beginning which was moved to the predicate, as in the saying of the rajiz: *Umm al-Hulays la-'ajuz*, and its origin is: *la-Umm al-Hulays 'ajuz*.]]

He said: Some people claimed that it is not permissible, because when the *nun* of *inna* is lightened, it must be followed by *illa* (except), so he says: "*Inna hadha illa sahiran*" (This is none but sorcerers).

Abu Ja'far said: The correct recitation in our view is *Inna* with its *nun* doubled, and *hadhani* with the *alif*, because the authoritative consensus (*ijma' al-hujjah*) of the readers is upon it, and that it is so in the script of the Mushaf. Its basis when recited thus is its resemblance to *alladhina*, when they added a *nun* to *alladhi*, and kept the case-marking in all states on one form. Likewise *Inna hadhani* had a *nun* added to it, and the case-marking in all states is kept on one form. And it is the dialect of al-Harith ibn Ka'b, Khath'am, Zubayd and those who neighbour them from the tribes of Yemen.

* * *

As for His words ﴿and do away with your ideal way of life﴾:

He says: "They will overpower your leaders and nobles." It is said: "He is the way and the example of his people," and "the reference and the focus of his people," when he is their leader, their noble, and the one looked to. This is said of the singular and the plural, and they sometimes pluralise it, saying: "These are the ways (*tara'iq*) of their people." And from it is the saying of God, blessed and exalted: ﴿We were in various ways (*tara'iqa qiddan*)﴾. And "These are the peers of their people" (*naza'ir qawmihim*).

As for His words ﴿al-muthla (the ideal)﴾: it is the feminine of *al-amthal*. It is said of the feminine: "Take the *muthla* of them both," and of the masculine: "Take the *amthal* of them both." He used the singular *muthla*, though it is an adjective and epithet for the plural, as it is said ﴿To Him belong the most beautiful names (al-asma' al-husna)﴾. It is also possible that *al-muthla* is feminine because of the feminine of "way" (*tariqa*).

The people of interpretation (*ahl al-ta'wil*) have said the same as what we have said concerning the meaning of His words ﴿your ideal way of life﴾.

Mention of those who said this:

* 'Ali narrated to me, saying: Abu Salih narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiyah narrated to me, from 'Ali, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words ﴿and do away with your ideal way of life﴾: he says: "your best ones, who are the Children of Israel."

* Muhammad ibn 'Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, saying: 'Isa narrated to us, and al-Harith narrated to me, saying: al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Warqa' narrated to us, all from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His words ﴿and do away with your ideal way of life﴾: he said: "those possessing intellect, nobility and lineage."

* al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, regarding His words ﴿and do away with your ideal way of life﴾, he said: "those possessing intellects, nobility and lineages."

* Abu Kurayb and Abu al-Sa'ib narrated to us, both saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His words: ﴿and do away with your ideal way of life﴾: "Their ideal way of life that day was the Children of Israel, and they were the most numerous of the people in number, wealth and children. The enemy of God said: 'They only want to take them away for themselves.'"

* al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah, regarding His words ﴿your ideal way of life﴾: "the Children of Israel."

* Musa narrated to me, saying: 'Amr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, regarding ﴿and do away with your ideal way of life﴾: he says: "they would take away your noble people."

Others said: The meaning of that is: "They will change your sunnah (custom) and your religion which you follow," from their saying: "So-and-so has a good way (*husn al-tariqah*)."

Mention of those who said this:

* Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, who said: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His words ﴿and do away with your ideal way of life﴾: "They will take away what you follow, changing what you are upon." And he recited: ﴿Leave me to kill Musa, and let him call upon his Lord. Indeed I fear that he will change your religion, or that he will cause corruption to appear in the land﴾ (40:26). He said: "This is His saying: ﴿and do away with your ideal way of life﴾." And he said: "It means: your way today is a good way, and if it is changed, this way will be gone."

It is related from 'Ali concerning the meaning of His words ﴿and do away with your ideal way of life﴾:

* al-Qasim narrated this to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hushaym narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Ishaq informed us, from al-Qasim, from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, who said: "They will turn people's faces toward them."

Abu Ja'far said: This saying which Ibn Zayd said regarding His words ﴿and do away with your ideal way of life﴾, though it is an opinion which the wording may bear, the interpretation of the people of interpretation is contrary to it, so I do not consider it permissible to hold that view.

When I formed it, I added to it a *nun*, then I left the *alif* fixed in its state and not removed in any case, as the Arabs said *alladhi* (who/which), then they added a *nun* indicating the plural and said *alladhina* in its nominative, accusative and genitive, just as they left *hadhani* in its nominative, accusative and genitive.' He said: 'The analogy would have been that they say *alladhun*.' Another of them said: 'That is from the loose *jazm* (apocopation), and if it were in the accusative, it would have become *insiyat* (extension).'"

* And I was told, from Abu 'Ubaydah Ma'mar ibn al-Muthanna, who said: Abu 'Amr, 'Isa ibn 'Umar and Yunus said: "*Inna hadhayni la-sahirani*" in pronunciation, and it is written as they intend in the script, and the pronunciation is correct. He said: Abu al-Khattab claimed that he heard some people of the Banu Kinanah and others raise the dual in the position of the genitive and accusative. He said: Bishr ibn Hilal said: "*Inna* is for the beginning and affirmation. Do you not see that it governs what follows it, and does not govern what comes after the one that follows it, so it raises the predicate and does not put it in the accusative, as it put the noun in the accusative? So the meaning of '*inna hadhani la-sahirani*' is the meaning of two sentences; its origin is: 'Indeed, yes (*inna*), then I said: *hadhani sahirani*'. Do you not see that they raise the coordinated noun, as in the saying of Dabi'":

*Whoever has his camp in Medina at dusk, indeed I and Qayyar are strangers there.* [[The verse is by Dabi' ibn al-Harith al-Burjumi, the first of the verses he composed while imprisoned in Medina during the time of 'Uthman ibn 'Affan. After it are three verses recited by Abu al-'Abbas al-Mubarrad in *al-Kamil* (Khizanat al-Adab by al-Baghdadi, 4:323–328), and the grammarians cited it as evidence that *Qayyar* is a subject whose predicate is omitted, and the sentence is parenthetical between the subject of *inna* and its predicate. The meaning is: 'Indeed I and Qayyar are, likewise, strangers.' He did not make the predicate belong to Qayyar, and the predicate of *inna* be omitted, because the *lam* does not enter the predicate of a subject until it is placed first, as in *la-qa'imun Zayd* (indeed Zayd is standing). This explanation goes against the school of Sibawayh, for the sentence in his view is intended to be delayed, so it is coordinated, not parenthetical. Al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' claimed that the accusative of *inna* is weak, because it changes only the noun and not the predicate. Al-Zajjaj said: 'This is a mistake, because *inna* has operated in two ways, raising and putting in the accusative, and there is no governing accusative in Arabic that is not accompanied by a raised noun, because every accusative is compared to the object, and the object cannot exist without an agent, except in the passive. How could the accusative of *inna* be weak when it passes over adverbs and governs what follows it, as in *inna fiha qawman jabbarin* (indeed in it are tyrannical people)? The accusative after *inna* is among the strongest of the accusatives.' End.]]

And His saying:

*Indeed the swords, in their morning and evening, have left Hawazin like the horn of the broken-horned (ibex).* [[The verse is by al-Akhtal (Khizanat al-Adab by al-Baghdadi, 2:372), from an ode of sixteen verses he composed in praise of al-'Abbas ibn Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah ibn al-'Abbas. The verse is cited by grammarians as evidence that the first word may be considered in form while the second is not, i.e., the replaced noun is considered in form and not the substitute. For his saying "*ghadwuha*" is a substitute for "*al-suyuf*". Al-Mubarrad said in *al-Kamil*: "It is a substitution of inclusion (*badal al-ishtimal*), and the replaced noun has been observed in form by returning a pronoun to it from the predicate, and the substitute was not observed. If it had been observed, it would have said *taraka* in the dual." Hawazin: the father of a tribe, Hawazin ibn Mansur ibn 'Ikrimah ibn Khasafah ibn Qays 'Aylan ibn Mudar. "Al-A'adab" is one whose one horn is broken. The author cited the verse as evidence that they may raise the coordinated word after the noun of *inna*; but there is no coordination after the noun of *inna* in the verse; it is rather a substitution of the accusative, as established by al-Mubarrad and Abu 'Ali al-Farisi in *Idah al-Shi'r*.]]

He said: Some of them say: "*Inna Allaha wa mala'ikatahu yusalluna 'ala al-Nabi*" (Indeed God and His angels send blessings upon the Prophet), and they raise it by the partnership of the beginning, and *inna* does not govern it. He said: I have heard eloquent people of the pilgrims say: "*Inna al-hamda wa al-ni'mata laka wa al-mulka, la sharika lak*" (Indeed praise and blessing are yours, and sovereignty, you have no partner). He said: Some people recited it with the *nun* of *inna* lightened and unvoweled. He said: This is permissible, because they have put the *lam* in the beginning, and it is a separator. He said:

*Umm al-Hulays is an old woman, a crone.* [[This is a line of half-rajaz metre attributed by al-Saghani in *al-'Ubab* to 'Antarah ibn 'Arus, with the *shin* at its end, and it is said with the *sin*, a client of Thaqif. (Khizanat al-Adab al-Kubra by al-Baghdadi, 4:328–330). It is evidence that the *lam* entering the predicate of a postponed subject, without *inna*, is an anomaly. Some explained it as: "*la-hiya 'ajuzun*" (indeed she is an old woman), so that it is in the estimate entering the subject. Ibn al-Sarraj said in *al-Usul*: Abu 'Uthman said: Sa'id ibn Jubayr recited (*illa annahum la ya'kuluna al-ta'am*) with the *alif* of *anna* opened, and he made the *lam* superfluous as it is superfluous in the saying: *Umm al-Hulays la-'ajuzun shahrabah / tarda min al-lahm bi-'azm al-raqabah*. End. Ibn Jinni held that it is not superfluous, but in the verse it is a necessity of poetry. He said in *Sirr al-Sina'ah*: As for the necessity by which the *lam* enters the predicate of *inna*, it is one of the necessities of poetry, and it is not to be made an analogy; the correct form is to say: '*la-Umm al-Hulays 'ajuzun shahrabah*', as one says *la-Zayd qa'im* (indeed Zayd is standing). The author cited the verse as evidence that the *lam* in "*wa Qayyar biha la-gharib*" is the *lam* of the beginning which was moved to the predicate, as in the saying of the rajiz: *Umm al-Hulays la-'ajuz*, and its origin is: *la-Umm al-Hulays 'ajuz*.]]

He said: Some people claimed that it is not permissible, because when the *nun* of *inna* is lightened, it must be followed by *illa* (except), so he says: "*Inna hadha illa sahiran*" (This is none but sorcerers).

Abu Ja'far said: The correct recitation in our view is *Inna* with its *nun* doubled, and *hadhani* with the *alif*, because the authoritative consensus (*ijma' al-hujjah*) of the readers is upon it, and that it is so in the script of the Mushaf. Its basis when recited thus is its resemblance to *alladhina*, when they added a *nun* to *alladhi*, and kept the case-marking in all states on one form. Likewise *Inna hadhani* had a *nun* added to it, and the case-marking in all states is kept on one form. And it is the dialect of al-Harith ibn Ka'b, Khath'am, Zubayd and those who neighbour them from the tribes of Yemen.

* * *

As for His words ﴿and do away with your ideal way of life﴾:

He says: "They will overpower your leaders and nobles." It is said: "He is the way and the example of his people," and "the reference and the focus of his people," when he is their leader, their noble, and the one looked to. This is said of the singular and the plural, and they sometimes pluralise it, saying: "These are the ways (*tara'iq*) of their people." And from it is the saying of God, blessed and exalted: ﴿We were in various ways (*tara'iqa qiddan*)﴾. And "These are the peers of their people" (*naza'ir qawmihim*).

As for His words ﴿al-muthla (the ideal)﴾: it is the feminine of *al-amthal*. It is said of the feminine: "Take the *muthla* of them both," and of the masculine: "Take the *amthal* of them both." He used the singular *muthla*, though it is an adjective and epithet for the plural, as it is said ﴿To Him belong the most beautiful names (al-asma' al-husna)﴾. It is also possible that *al-muthla* is feminine because of the feminine of "way" (*tariqa*).

The people of interpretation (*ahl al-ta'wil*) have said the same as what we have said concerning the meaning of His words ﴿your ideal way of life﴾.

Mention of those who said this:

* 'Ali narrated to me, saying: Abu Salih narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiyah narrated to me, from 'Ali, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words ﴿and do away with your ideal way of life﴾: he says: "your best ones, who are the Children of Israel."

* Muhammad ibn 'Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, saying: 'Isa narrated to us, and al-Harith narrated to me, saying: al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Warqa' narrated to us, all from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His words ﴿and do away with your ideal way of life﴾: he said: "those possessing intellect, nobility and lineage."

* al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, regarding His words ﴿and do away with your ideal way of life﴾, he said: "those possessing intellects, nobility and lineages."

* Abu Kurayb and Abu al-Sa'ib narrated to us, both saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His words: ﴿and do away with your ideal way of life﴾: "Their ideal way of life that day was the Children of Israel, and they were the most numerous of the people in number, wealth and children. The enemy of God said: 'They only want to take them away for themselves.'"

* al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah, regarding His words ﴿your ideal way of life﴾: "the Children of Israel."

* Musa narrated to me, saying: 'Amr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, regarding ﴿and do away with your ideal way of life﴾: he says: "they would take away your noble people."

Others said: The meaning of that is: "They will change your sunnah (custom) and your religion which you follow," from their saying: "So-and-so has a good way (*husn al-tariqah*)."

Mention of those who said this:

* Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, who said: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His words ﴿and do away with your ideal way of life﴾: "They will take away what you follow, changing what you are upon." And he recited: ﴿Leave me to kill Musa, and let him call upon his Lord. Indeed I fear that he will change your religion, or that he will cause corruption to appear in the land﴾ (40:26). He said: "This is His saying: ﴿and do away with your ideal way of life﴾." And he said: "It means: your way today is a good way, and if it is changed, this way will be gone."

It is related from 'Ali concerning the meaning of His words ﴿and do away with your ideal way of life﴾:

* al-Qasim narrated this to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hushaym narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Ishaq informed us, from al-Qasim, from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, who said: "They will turn people's faces toward them."

Abu Ja'far said: This saying which Ibn Zayd said regarding His words ﴿and do away with your ideal way of life﴾, though it is an opinion which the wording may bear, the interpretation of the people of interpretation is contrary to it, so I do not consider it permissible to hold that view.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 20, verse 64:

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So settle your plan, then come in a row. And he has succeeded today who prevails.﴾

The reciters differed over the recitation of His saying ﴿fa-ajmi'u kaydakum﴾. The majority of the reciters of Medina and Kufa recited it ﴿fa-ajmi'ū kaydakum﴾ with a hamza on the alif of ﴿fa-ajmi'ū﴾, and they understood its meaning to be: firmly establish your plot and resolve upon it, from the saying of people, "Ajma'a fulan al-khurūj" and "Ajma'a 'alā al-khurūj" (so-and-so resolved upon going out), just as one says "azmaa 'alayhi" (he resolved upon it). Among this is the verse of the poet:

Would that I knew, though hopes do not avail, whether I shall go out one day while my affair is resolved (mujmi').[[The line is cited in (Lisan al-'Arab: j-m-') without attribution. It says: jama'a amrahu and ajma'a 'alayhi meant "he resolved upon it," as if he gathered himself for it, and the matter is mujma'. It is also said: ajma'a amraka wa-la tada'hu muntashiran (resolve your matter and do not leave it scattered). Another poet said: "Would that I knew... the line." And His saying, exalted is He: "So resolve your affair and your partners" means "and call your partners." He said: so it is in the recitation of 'Abdullah, because one does not say "ajma'tu shurakā'ī" (I resolved my partners); one says "jama'tu" (I gathered). Al-Farra' said: al-ijma' is preparing and firm resolve upon a matter. He said: the accusative of "shurakā'ī" is by a hidden verb, as if you said, "So resolve your affair and call your partners." Abu Ishaq said: what al-Farra' said is an error in its supposed hidden verb, "and call your partners," because the speech then has no benefit, since they used to call their partners to gather their affair. He said: the meaning is "so resolve your affair together with your partners," and if the calling is for nothing then there is no benefit in it. They said: the waw has the meaning of "with," as in your saying, "If he rides the she-camel with her young, he will suckle it," meaning "if he rides the she-camel together with her young." He said: whoever recites "fa-ajmi'ū amrakum wa-shurakā'akum" with a connected alif makes "shurakā'akum" a conjunction to "amrakum." He said: it is permissible to say "fa-ajmi'ū amrakum ma'a shurakā'ikum" (resolve your affair together with your partners).]]

The meaning of "mujmi'" here is: he has firmly established it and resolved upon it. Among this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever has not resolved upon fasting from the night, there is no fast for him."

Some of the reciters of Basra recited it ﴿fa-jma'ū kaydakum﴾ with a connected alif and without the hamza, from "jama'tu al-shay'" (I gathered the thing), as if they directed its meaning to: do not leave any of your plot except that you bring it. Some who recited this way were said, as it was reported to me, to justify their recitation by His saying ﴿Then Pharaoh turned away and gathered his plot﴾.

Abu Ja'far said: the correct recitation in our view is the hamza on the alif of "ajma'a," because the reciters of the proof (al-hujjah) are unanimous upon it, and because the sorcerers were the ones known for it. There is no sense in saying to them, "Gather what you have been called to, of which you are knowledgeable," because a person only gathers what is not with him to what is with him. That was not the day on which their knowledge of the sorcery they practised increased; rather it was the day of its display, or it was scattered among what they had, some of it to other parts. The sorcery was not scattered among them so that they would gather it. As for His saying ﴿fa-jama'a kaydahu﴾, its meaning is not similar to His saying ﴿fa-ajmi'ū kaydakum﴾, because Pharaoh was the one who gathered and made ready, with what would overcome Moses, what was not gathered and present with him. Thus it was said: "Then Pharaoh turned away and gathered his plot."

* *

And His saying ﴿Then come in a row (ṣaffan)﴾

He says: come forward and approach in a row. Here "ṣaff" (row) is a verbal noun, which is why it is singular, and its meaning is: then come in rows. The word "ṣaff" has another usage in the speech of the Arabs: the Arabs say, "I came to the ṣaff today," meaning the place of prayer in which one prays.

* *

And His saying ﴿And he has succeeded today who prevails﴾

He says: he has attained his need today who rises above his companion and overpowers him.

As:

⁕ Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salamah narrated to us, from Ibn Ishaq, who said: I was told, from Wahb ibn Munabbih, who said: Pharaoh gathered the people for that gathering, then he commanded the sorcerers, saying ﴿come in a row, and he has succeeded today who prevails﴾, meaning: he has succeeded today who has prevailed over his companion.

**Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on Surah 20, verses 65–66:**

Concerning the interpretation of His words, ﴿They said, "O Musa, either you throw, or we will be the first to throw."﴾ (65) ﴿He said, "Rather, you throw." And suddenly their ropes and their staffs, because of their magic, appeared to him as though they were moving.﴾ (66)

His saying, exalted is His remembrance: "So the magicians gathered their stratagem, then they came in a row (saff) and said to Musa, ﴿O Musa, either you throw, or we will be the first to throw.﴾" The omission of mention of that part of the speech is because the meaning of the speech indicates it.

Scholars differed about the number of magicians who came in a row that day. Some said they were seventy thousand magicians, with each magician having a rope and a staff.

Those who said this:

Ya'qub ibn Ibrahim told me, he said: Ibn 'Ulayyah related to us, from Hisham al-Dastuwa'i, he said: al-Qasim ibn Abi Bazzah related to us, he said: Fir'awn gathered seventy thousand magicians, and they threw seventy thousand ropes and seventy thousand staffs. Musa threw his staff, and behold, it was a clearly visible serpent, its mouth wide open, and it swallowed their ropes and their staffs. ﴿So the magicians were cast down prostrate﴾ at that moment, and they did not raise their heads until they saw Paradise and Hell and the reward of their people. At that point ﴿they said, "We will never prefer you over the clear proofs that have come to us."﴾

Others said: Rather, they were more than thirty thousand men.

Those who said this:

Musa related to us, he said: 'Amr related to us, he said: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi, he said: ﴿They said, "O Musa, either you throw, or we will be the first to throw." He said, "Rather"﴾ [you throw], so they threw their ropes and their staffs. They were a few dozen thousand men, and there was not a man among them except that he had a rope and a staff.

Others said: Rather, they were fifteen thousand.

Those who said this:

Ibn Humayd related to us, he said: Salamah related to us, from Ibn Ishaq, he said: It was related to me from Wahb ibn Munabbih, he said: Fifteen thousand magicians lined up, each magician with his ropes and his staffs.

Others said: They were nine hundred.

Those who said this:

al-Qasim related to us, he said: al-Husayn related to us, he said: Hajjaj told me, from Ibn Jurayj, he said: The magicians were three hundred from al-'Arish, three hundred from Fayyum, and three hundred from Iskandariyyah, and they said to Musa: "Either you throw what you have before us, or we will throw what we have before you." That is His saying, ﴿and we will be the first to throw.﴾ The *an* in His saying ﴿either "an"﴾ is in the accusative position. The meaning of the speech is: "Choose, O Musa, one of these two matters: either you throw before us, or we will be the first to throw." Had someone said that it is in the nominative position, it would have been a valid view, as though he directed it toward being a statement, like the saying of the poet:

*So travel, for either there is a need you two will fulfill,*
*or a good resting place and a friend.* [[This verse is among the evidences cited by al-Farra' in Ma'ani al-Qur'an (the University photocopy, folio 198). He said: His saying "either you throw, or we will be the first to throw": *an* and *an* are in the accusative position, and the meaning is: choose one of these two. If it were nominative, since the verb does not appear, it would be correct, as though it were a statement, like the saying of the poet: "So travel..." (the verse). If one reads "either We show favor after, or ransom" it would also be correct. His view is like his saying "either retention in kindness or release with good." The accusative in His saying "either you throw" and in His saying "either We show favor after, or ransom" is better than the nominative, because it is not a general matter, as you see in the meaning of His saying "either retention" and "then fasting three days." Since the meaning encompasses people in retention with kindness, and in fasting three days in the expiation for an oath, it is a conditional, so it is nominative for that reason. The choice here is only a single act.]]

* *

As for His saying, ﴿He said, "Rather, you throw."﴾

His saying, exalted is His remembrance: Musa said to the magicians, "Rather, you throw what you have before me."

* *

As for His saying, ﴿And suddenly their ropes and their staffs appeared to him, because of their magic, as though they were moving.﴾

In this speech there is something omitted, which is: "So they threw what they had of ropes and staffs, and suddenly their ropes..." Its mention was omitted because the speech that was mentioned indicates it. It is also reported that the magicians bewitched the eyes of Musa and the eyes of the people before they threw their ropes and staffs, so it then appeared to Musa that they were moving.

As related:

Ibn Humayd told me, he said: Salamah related to us, from Ibn Ishaq, he said: It was related to me from Wahb ibn Munabbih, he said: They said, "O Musa, ﴿either you throw, or we will be the first to throw.﴾ He said, 'Rather, you throw.'" So the first thing they snatched by their magic was the sight of Musa and the sight of Fir'awn, then the sights of the people after that. Then each man among them threw what was in his hand of staffs and ropes, and suddenly they were snakes like the shapes of ropes, filling the valley, some riding over others.

The readers differed concerning the recitation of His saying ﴿yukhayyalu ilayhi﴾ ("it appeared to him"). The majority of the readers of the regional cities recited ﴿yukhayyalu ilayhi﴾ with the *ya'* (masculine prefix), meaning: "their running appeared to him." When it is recited this way, *an* is in the nominative position. It is related from al-Hasan al-Basri that he recited it as ﴿tukhayyalu﴾ with the *ta'* (feminine prefix), meaning: "their ropes and their staffs appeared, by [their] running." When recited this way, *an* is in the accusative position, because the verb *takhayyala* governs it. It is also reported from some that he recited it as ﴿tukhayyalu ilayhi﴾, meaning: "it appears to him," and when recited this way too, *an* is in the accusative position, meaning: "it appears to him by their running."

The recitation that, in my view, is not permissible other than this is ﴿yukhayyalu﴾ with the *ya'*, because of the consensus of the authoritative readers upon it.

As for His saying, ﴿He said, "Rather, you throw."﴾

His saying, exalted is His remembrance: Musa said to the magicians, "Rather, you throw what you have before me."

* *

As for His saying, ﴿And suddenly their ropes and their staffs appeared to him, because of their magic, as though they were moving.﴾

In this speech there is something omitted, which is: "So they threw what they had of ropes and staffs, and suddenly their ropes..." Its mention was omitted because the speech that was mentioned indicates it. It is also reported that the magicians bewitched the eyes of Musa and the eyes of the people before they threw their ropes and staffs, so it then appeared to Musa that they were moving.

As related:

Ibn Humayd told me, he said: Salamah related to us, from Ibn Ishaq, he said: It was related to me from Wahb ibn Munabbih, he said: They said, "O Musa, ﴿either you throw, or we will be the first to throw.﴾ He said, 'Rather, you throw.'" So the first thing they snatched by their magic was the sight of Musa and the sight of Fir'awn, then the sights of the people after that. Then each man among them threw what was in his hand of staffs and ropes, and suddenly they were snakes like the shapes of ropes, filling the valley, some riding over others.

The readers differed concerning the recitation of His saying ﴿yukhayyalu ilayhi﴾ ("it appeared to him"). The majority of the readers of the regional cities recited ﴿yukhayyalu ilayhi﴾ with the *ya'* (masculine prefix), meaning: "their running appeared to him." When it is recited this way, *an* is in the nominative position. It is related from al-Hasan al-Basri that he recited it as ﴿tukhayyalu﴾ with the *ta'* (feminine prefix), meaning: "their ropes and their staffs appeared, by [their] running." When recited this way, *an* is in the accusative position, because the verb *takhayyala* governs it. It is also reported from some that he recited it as ﴿tukhayyalu ilayhi﴾, meaning: "it appears to him," and when recited this way too, *an* is in the accusative position, meaning: "it appears to him by their running."

The recitation that, in my view, is not permissible other than this is ﴿yukhayyalu﴾ with the *ya'*, because of the consensus of the authoritative readers upon it.

The commentary of al-Tabari (Jami' al-Bayan) on Surah 20, verses 67–69:

The explanation of His, may He be exalted, words: ﴿So Musa sensed fear within himself﴾

He, may He be exalted and remembered, means by His words: "So Musa sensed fear within himself" — he felt fear.

* *

As for His words ﴿We said, "Fear not; indeed, you are the superior ones"﴾

He, may He be exalted and remembered, says: We said to Musa, when he sensed fear within himself: ﴿Fear not; indeed, you are the superior ones﴾ over these sorcerers, over Pharaoh and his army, and the one who overpowers them. ﴿And throw what is in your right hand; it will swallow up what they have made﴾ — meaning: throw your staff, and it will swallow up their ropes and staffs, which they had enchanted, until it appeared to you that they were moving.

* *

As for His words ﴿What they have made is only the plot of a sorcerer﴾

The reciters differed in their reading of this. The majority of the reciters of Madina and Basra, and some of the reciters of Kufa, read ﴿innama sana'u kaydu sahir﴾ with kayd in the nominative case and with an alif in sahir, meaning: what these sorcerers made is a plot of a sorcerer. The majority of the reciters of Kufa read ﴿innama sana'u kaydu sihr﴾ with kayd in the nominative case and without the alif in sihr, meaning: what they made is a plot of sorcery.

My view on this is that they are two well-known readings, close in meaning. Kayd is scheming and deception, so the sorcerer's scheming and deception come from sorcery (sihr), which deceives, and the scheming of sorcery is its imagining to the one bewitched, contrary to what it actually is. Thus the sorcerer schemes through sorcery, and sorcery schemes through illusion. Whichever of the two you attribute the kayd to, it is correct. It has been reported from some people that they read ﴿kayda sihr﴾ with kayd in the accusative. Whoever reads it that way makes innama a single particle and governs kayd by sana'u.

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: I do not permit reciting it that way, because the consensus of the authoritative reciters is against it.

* *

As for His words ﴿And the sorcerer does not succeed, wherever he comes﴾

He means: the sorcerer does not attain his aim from his sorcery, wherever he is. It has been reported from some people that they said: the meaning of this is that the sorcerer is killed wherever he is found. Some grammarians of Basra mentioned that in the reading of Ibn Mas'ud it is ﴿wa la yufliḥu as-sāḥiru ayna atā﴾, and said: the Arabs say, "I came to you from where you do not know" and "from whence you do not know." Another of the early Arabic scholars said: it is a recompense: the sorcerer is killed wherever he comes and wherever he goes. He said: as for the Arabs' saying, "I came to you from where you do not know," it is an answer to one who did not understand, so he asks, as they say, "Where is the water and the grass?"

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 20, verses 70–71:

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So the magicians were thrown down prostrate. They said, "We have believed in the Lord of Aaron and Moses."﴾ (70) ﴿[Pharaoh] said, "Have you believed in him before I gave you permission? Indeed, he is your chief who taught you magic. So I will surely cut off your hands and your feet on opposite sides, and I will crucify you on the trunks of palm trees, and you will surely know whose punishment is more severe and more lasting."﴾ (71)

In this statement there is an omitted part, which is understood from what is mentioned after it, and it is: "Then Moses threw his staff, and it swallowed up what they had made," ﴿So the magicians were thrown down prostrate. They said, "We have believed in the Lord of Aaron and Moses."﴾. It is mentioned that when Moses threw what was in his hand, it turned into a serpent, and it swallowed up everything the magicians had thrown of ropes and staves.

Mention of the narration from those who said that: Ibn Humayd related to us, he said: Ya'qub related to us, from Ja'far, from Sa'id, who said: When they gathered and threw what was in their hands of magic, ﴿It was imagined to him, because of their magic, that they were moving,﴾ ﴿so Moses felt a fear within himself. We said, "Do not fear; indeed, you are the superior one. And throw what is in your right hand; it will swallow what they have made."﴾ So he threw his staff, and behold, it was a clearly visible serpent. He said: It opened its mouth, and there was nothing like a pit, then it placed its lower jaw on the ground and raised the upper one, then it engulfed everything they had thrown of magic. Then it came to them and seized them, and behold, it was a staff. So the magicians fell down prostrate ﴿and said, "We have believed in the Lord of Aaron and Moses."﴾ He said: The first to cut off the hands and feet on opposite sides was Pharaoh's doing, ﴿and I will crucify you on the trunks of palm trees.﴾ He said: The first to be crucified on the trunks of palm trees was Pharaoh.

Ibn Humayd related to us, he said: Ya'qub related to us, from Ja'far, from Sa'id: ... (narration as above).

Musa ibn Harun related to us, he said: 'Amr related to us, he said: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi, ﴿so Moses felt a fear within himself﴾ — then God revealed to him, ﴿"Do not fear, and throw what is in your right hand; it will swallow what they have fabricated."﴾ So he threw his staff, and it devoured every serpent they had. When they saw that, they prostrated and ﴿said, "We have believed in the Lord of Aaron and Moses."﴾

Ibn Humayd related to us, he said: Salamah related to us, from Ibn Ishaq, he said: I was told by Wahb ibn Munabbih, ﴿so Moses felt a fear within himself﴾ when he saw what they had thrown of ropes and staves, and it was imagined to him that they were moving. He said: "By God, if these were staves in their hands, they have turned into serpents, and my staff does not overcome them," or as he spoke to himself. Then God revealed to him that ﴿"throw what is in your right hand; it will swallow what they have made. What they have made is only the trick of a magician, and a magician does not prosper wherever he comes."﴾ Moses rejoiced, and threw his staff from his hand, and it sped through what they had thrown of their ropes and staves, and they were serpents in the eye of Pharaoh and in the eyes of the people, moving. So it began to swallow them, serpent after serpent, until in the valley not a little nor a lot of what they had thrown remained. Then Moses took it, and behold, it was a staff in his hand as it had been. The magicians fell down prostrate, saying, "We have believed in the Lord of Aaron and Moses. Had this been magic, it would not have overcome us."

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 20, verses 72–73:

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They said, "We will never prefer you over the clear proofs that have come to us and over He who created us. So decide what you are going to decide. You can only decide concerning this worldly life. Indeed, we have believed in our Lord that He may forgive us our sins and that which you compelled us to do of magic. And Allah is better and more enduring."﴾

His saying, may His remembrance be exalted: The magicians said to Pharaoh when he threatened them with what he threatened them with, ﴿We will never prefer you﴾, i.e., we will follow you and deny Musa for your sake, ﴿over the clear proofs that have come to us﴾, meaning over the proofs and evidences of the truth of what Musa called them to. ﴿And over He who created us﴾: they said, "We will never prefer you over what has come to us of clear proofs, and over He who created us." By His saying ﴿He who created us﴾ he means He created us. The "alladhi" in His saying ﴿and He who created us﴾ is in the genitive, governed by the preposition implied in ﴿what has come to us﴾. It is also possible that His saying ﴿and He who created us﴾ is in the genitive by way of an oath, so the meaning of the speech would be: "We will never prefer you over what has come to us of clear proofs, by Allah." His saying ﴿So decide what you are going to decide﴾ means: do what you are going to do, and act toward us as you wish. ﴿You can only decide concerning this worldly life﴾ means: you are only able to punish us in this worldly life, which passes away. The phrase "this worldly life" is in the accusative as a time expression, and "innama" is treated as a single particle.

In accordance with what we have said concerning this, the people of interpretation have said.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 20, verses 72–73:

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They said, "We will never prefer you over the clear proofs that have come to us and over He who created us. So decide what you are going to decide. His saying, may His remembrance be exalted: The magicians said to Pharaoh when he threatened them with what he threatened them with, ﴿We will never prefer you﴾, i.e., we will follow you and deny Musa for your sake, ﴿over the clear proofs that have come to us﴾, meaning over the proofs and evidences of the truth of what Musa called them to. ﴿And over He who created us﴾: they said, "We will never prefer you over what has come to us of clear proofs, and over He who created us." By His saying ﴿He who created us﴾ he means He created us. The "alladhi" in His saying ﴿and He who created us﴾ is in the genitive, governed by the preposition implied in ﴿what has come to us﴾. It is also possible that His saying ﴿and He who created us﴾ is in the genitive by way of an oath, so the meaning of the speech would be: "We will never prefer you over what has come to us of clear proofs, by Allah." His saying ﴿So decide what you are going to decide﴾ means: do what you are going to do, and act toward us as you wish. ﴿You can only decide concerning this worldly life﴾ means: you are only able to punish us in this worldly life, which passes away. The phrase "this worldly life" is in the accusative as a time expression, and "innama" is treated as a single particle.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 20, verses 74–76:

The interpretation of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, whoever comes to his Lord as a criminal, for him is Hell; he will neither die therein nor live.﴾ (74) ﴿But whoever comes to Him as a believer who has done righteous deeds, for them are the high ranks.﴾ (75)

He, the Exalted, says, reporting the words of the magicians to Pharaoh: ﴿Indeed, whoever comes to his Lord﴾ from among His creation ﴿as a criminal﴾, meaning: one who has earned disbelief in Him, ﴿for him is Hell﴾, meaning: indeed, for him Hell is a dwelling and a residence, as recompense for his disbelief. ﴿He will neither die therein﴾, so that his soul would depart, ﴿nor live﴾, so that his soul would settle in its place and be at rest; rather, their souls cling to their throats. ﴿But whoever comes to Him as a believer﴾, one who affirms His oneness and does not associate anything with Him, ﴿who has done righteous deeds﴾, meaning: has done what his Lord commanded him and refrained from what He forbade him, ﴿for them are the high ranks﴾, meaning: those are the ones who have the high ranks of Paradise.

* *

The interpretation of His saying: ﴿Gardens of Eden, beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. That is the reward of one who purifies himself.﴾ (76)

He, the Exalted, says: And whoever comes to Him as a believer who has done righteous deeds, for them are the high ranks. Then He explains what those high ranks are, saying: they are ﴿Gardens of Eden﴾, meaning: gardens of lasting abode, from which there is no departure, no exhaustion and no extinction. ﴿Beneath which rivers flow﴾, meaning: rivers flow beneath their trees. ﴿Abiding therein﴾, meaning: remaining therein without any determined end. The word "gardens" in His saying ﴿Gardens of Eden﴾ is in the nominative case as a substitution for "the ranks."

As narrated:

⁕ Al-Qasim narrated to us, he said: al-Husayn narrated to us, he said: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, concerning His saying ﴿But whoever comes to Him as a believer who has done righteous deeds, for them are the high ranks﴾, he said: "Eden."

* *

As for His saying ﴿That is the reward of one who purifies himself﴾:

He says: and these high ranks, which are the Gardens of Eden as described by Him, the Majestic, are the reward of one who purifies himself, meaning: who cleanses himself from sins, obeys God in what He commanded him, and does not defile his soul with disobedience to what He forbade him.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 20, verse 77:

On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿And We had already revealed to Moses: "Travel by night with My servants, and strike for them a dry path through the sea; you will have no fear of being overtaken, nor will you be afraid."﴾

He, exalted is His remembrance, says: ﴿And We revealed to﴾ our Prophet ﴿Moses﴾ when We had continued to present him with proofs against Pharaoh, and he refused to heed the command of his Lord, persisted in his rebellion, and went on in his transgression: ﴿"Travel by night"﴾ ﴿"with My servants"﴾, meaning with My servants from the Children of Israel.

﴿"And strike for them a dry path through the sea"﴾ means: make for them a dry path in the sea. Al-yabas and al-yabs (both meaning "dry") have the plural ayba's (طرق الأيباس is the form used). You say: "They stood on ayba's of the land," and al-yabs (with the light vowelling) has the plural yubus.

Interpreters of the Qur'an have said the same as what we have said about this.

Those who said this:

- Muhammad ibn Amr told me, saying: Abu Asim told us, saying: Isa told us; and al-Harith told me, saying: al-Hasan told us, saying: Warqa' told us, all of them from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His words ﴿yabasan﴾, he said: "dry."

- Al-Qasim told us, saying: al-Husayn told us, saying: Hajjaj told me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, the like of it.

As for His words ﴿"you will have no fear of being overtaken, nor will you be afraid"﴾, it means: do not fear Pharaoh and his soldiers overtaking you from behind, and do not fear drowning from before you and sinking in mud.

Interpreters of the Qur'an have said the same as what we have said in interpreting this.

Those who said this:

- Ali told me, saying: Abu Salih told us, saying: Mu'awiya told me, from Ali, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿"you will have no fear of being overtaken, nor will you be afraid"﴾, he said: ﴿"you will not fear"﴾ the family of Pharaoh ﴿"being overtaken, nor will you be afraid"﴾ of drowning in the sea.

- Bishr told us, saying: Yazid told us, saying: Sa'id told us, from Qatada, regarding ﴿"you will have no fear of being overtaken, nor will you be afraid"﴾, he said: you will not fear that Pharaoh will overtake you after you, nor will you fear drowning before you.

- Al-Qasim told us, saying: al-Husayn told us, saying: Hajjaj told me, saying: Ibn Jurayj said: The companions of Moses said: "This is Pharaoh, he has overtaken us, and this sea has surrounded us." So God revealed ﴿"you will have no fear of being overtaken"﴾ by the companions of Pharaoh ﴿"nor will you be afraid"﴾ of the sea's mud.

- Ahmad ibn al-Walid al-Ramli told me, saying: Amr ibn Awn told us, saying: Hushaym told us, from some of his companions, regarding ﴿"nor will you be afraid"﴾, he said: it is the mire (al-wahal).

The reciters differed over the reading of His words ﴿"you will have no fear of being overtaken"﴾. The majority of the reciters of the regional centres, other than al-A'mash and Hamza, recited ﴿lā takhāfu darakan﴾ as a new sentence with the negation lā, like His words ﴿"And persevere in it; We do not ask you for provision"﴾, which is in the nominative; and most of what comes in this kind of construction, as an answer, is with lā. Al-A'mash and Hamza recited ﴿lā takhaf darakan﴾ with the jussive on "takhaf" as a conditional answer, and the nominative on ﴿"nor will you be afraid"﴾ as a new sentence, like His words, majestic is His praise, ﴿"They will turn their backs to you, then they will not be helped"﴾, where He begins anew with "then" (thumma). Had one intended the jussive for His words ﴿"nor will you be afraid"﴾, with the ya' in it, it would have been permissible, as the rajaz poet said:

"Shake the trunk toward you; it will drop the ripe dates upon you."

The reading I prefer of the two is to recite ﴿lā takhāfu﴾ in the nominative, because it is the more eloquent of the two dialects, although the other is also permissible. Some grammarians of Basra used to say: the meaning of His words ﴿lā takhāfu darakan﴾ is: strike for them a path in which you will not fear being overtaken; he said: the pronoun "fīhi" (in it) has been omitted, as you say: "Zayd, you honoured" while meaning "you honoured him," and as you say ﴿"And guard yourselves against a day when no soul will avail another soul at all"﴾, meaning, on which no soul will avail. As for the grammarians of Kufa, they reject omitting "fīhi" except with times, because it is acceptable with them to say "I stood today" and "I stood on today," and they do not permit this with nouns.

**Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on Surah 20, verses 78–80**

On the interpretation of His words, the Exalted: ﴿Then Pharaoh pursued them with his armies, and the sea covered them with what covered them (78). And Pharaoh led his people astray, and did not guide them (79).﴾

His Exalted Remembrance says: Moses set out by night with the Children of Israel after We had revealed to him that he should travel with them by night. Pharaoh pursued them with his armies when they had crossed the sea, and the sea covered Pharaoh and his army with what covered them, so they all drowned. ﴿And Pharaoh led his people astray and did not guide them.﴾ His Majestic Praise says: Pharaoh led his people beyond the even path and took them in a crooked direction. This is because he led them on the road of the people of the Fire, by commanding them to disbelieve in God and to deny His messengers. ﴿And did not guide them﴾ means: he did not lead them on the straight path. He forbade them to follow the messenger of God, Moses, and to believe in him, and they obeyed him. So he did not guide them by his command to them to do this, and they were not guided by following him.

* *

On the interpretation of His words, the Exalted: ﴿O Children of Israel, We had delivered you from your enemy, and We made a appointment with you on the right side of Mount Sinai, and We sent down upon you the manna and the quails (80). Eat of the good things with which We have provided you, and do not transgress therein, lest My wrath descend upon you (81).﴾

His Exalted Remembrance says: When Moses had brought his people safely out of the sea, and Pharaoh's people had been overtaken by what overtook them from the sea, We said to the people of Moses: ﴿O Children of Israel, We had delivered you from your enemy, Pharaoh, and We made an appointment with you on the right side of Mount Sinai, and We sent down upon you the manna and the quails.﴾ We have already mentioned how God's appointment with Moses and his people on the right side of the Mount came about. We have also explained the manna and the quails, with the differing views of those who differ about them, and we have cited the evidence for the correct view on this matter earlier, so there is no need to repeat it here.

The readers (qurra', sing. qari') differed in their recitation (qira'a) of His words ﴿We had delivered you﴾ (anjaynakum). The majority of the readers of Medina and Basra recite it as ﴿anjaynakum﴾ with a nun and an alif, and they recite all the other similar verbs in the same way. The majority of the readers of Kufa recite it as ﴿anjaytukum﴾ with a ta', and likewise all the other verbs, up to His words ﴿and We sent down upon you the manna and the quails﴾, where they agree with the others and recite it with a nun and an alif.

In my view, these are two well-known recitations with the same meaning, so whichever of them the reader recites is correct.

* *

On His words: ﴿Eat of the good things with which We have provided you﴾.

His Exalted Remembrance says to them: Eat, O Children of Israel, of the desirable provision that We have given you, and of its lawful things that We have made good for you. ﴿And do not transgress therein﴾ means: do not exceed the limits in it, and do not let some of you wrong others in it.

As follows:-

◊ Ali related to us, he said: Abu Salih related to us, he said: Mu'awiya told me, from Ali, from Ibn Abbas, concerning His words: ﴿And do not transgress therein﴾, he said: "Do not wrong [one another]."

* *

On His words: ﴿lest My wrath descend upon you﴾.

He says: lest My punishment come down upon you.

As follows:-

◊ Bishr related to us, he said: Yazid related to us, he said: Sa'id related to us from Qatada, concerning His words: ﴿lest My wrath descend upon you﴾, he said: "lest My wrath come down upon you."

The readers differed in their recitation of this. The majority of the readers of Hijaz, Medina, Basra and Kufa recite it as ﴿fayahilla ʿalaykum﴾ with a kasra on the ha', and ﴿wa-man yahlil﴾ with a kasra on the lam, and they interpreted its meaning as: "then My wrath will be due upon you." A group of the people of Kufa recite it as ﴿fayahulla ʿalaykum﴾ with a damma on the ha', and they interpreted its meaning in line with what we have mentioned from Qatada, that it means: "then it will fall and descend upon you, My wrath."

Abu Ja'far said: The correct view on this matter is that both are well-known recitations, and scholars among the readers have recited each of them. God has warned those to whom this statement was addressed among the Children of Israel of the coming of His might upon them and its descent upon them for their disobedience to Him, if they disobeyed Him, and He frightened them that it would be due upon them. So whether it is recited as "falling" or as "being due," it makes no difference, because they had been warned of both meanings together.

**Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on Surah 20, verses 78–80**

On the interpretation of His words, the Exalted: ﴿Then Pharaoh pursued them with his armies, and the sea covered them with what covered them (78). And Pharaoh led his people astray, and did not guide them (79).﴾

His Exalted Remembrance says: Moses set out by night with the Children of Israel after We had revealed to him that he should travel with them by night. Pharaoh pursued them with his armies when they had crossed the sea, and the sea covered Pharaoh and his army with what covered them, so they all drowned. ﴿And Pharaoh led his people astray and did not guide them.﴾ His Majestic Praise says: Pharaoh led his people beyond the even path and took them in a crooked direction. This is because he led them on the road of the people of the Fire, by commanding them to disbelieve in God and to deny His messengers. ﴿And did not guide them﴾ means: he did not lead them on the straight path. He forbade them to follow the messenger of God, Moses, and to believe in him, and they obeyed him. So he did not guide them by his command to them to do this, and they were not guided by following him.

* *

On the interpretation of His words, the Exalted: ﴿O Children of Israel, We had delivered you from your enemy, and We made a appointment with you on the right side of Mount Sinai, and We sent down upon you the manna and the quails (80). Eat of the good things with which We have provided you, and do not transgress therein, lest My wrath descend upon you (81).﴾

His Exalted Remembrance says: When Moses had brought his people safely out of the sea, and Pharaoh's people had been overtaken by what overtook them from the sea, We said to the people of Moses: ﴿O Children of Israel, We had delivered you from your enemy, Pharaoh, and We made an appointment with you on the right side of Mount Sinai, and We sent down upon you the manna and the quails.﴾ We have already mentioned how God's appointment with Moses and his people on the right side of the Mount came about. We have also explained the manna and the quails, with the differing views of those who differ about them, and we have cited the evidence for the correct view on this matter earlier, so there is no need to repeat it here.

The readers (qurra', sing. qari') differed in their recitation (qira'a) of His words ﴿We had delivered you﴾ (anjaynakum). The majority of the readers of Medina and Basra recite it as ﴿anjaynakum﴾ with a nun and an alif, and they recite all the other similar verbs in the same way. The majority of the readers of Kufa recite it as ﴿anjaytukum﴾ with a ta', and likewise all the other verbs, up to His words ﴿and We sent down upon you the manna and the quails﴾, where they agree with the others and recite it with a nun and an alif.

In my view, these are two well-known recitations with the same meaning, so whichever of them the reader recites is correct.

* *

On His words: ﴿Eat of the good things with which We have provided you﴾.

His Exalted Remembrance says to them: Eat, O Children of Israel, of the desirable provision that We have given you, and of its lawful things that We have made good for you. ﴿And do not transgress therein﴾ means: do not exceed the limits in it, and do not let some of you wrong others in it.

81

Commentary on the words of God Most High: ﴿And whoever is subject to My wrath, he has indeed fallen﴾ (81) ﴿And indeed I am Forgiving to those who repent, believe, and do righteous deeds, and then remain guided﴾ (82).

God, may His remembrance be exalted, says: "Whoever has My wrath descend upon him, so that it befalls him, has indeed fallen," meaning he has perished and become wretched.

As related:

Ali narrated to me, saying: Abu Salih narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiyah narrated to me, from Ali, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿he has indeed fallen﴾: he means he has become wretched.

* *

As for His words ﴿And indeed I am Forgiving to those who repent﴾:

He means: And indeed I am Possessor of forgiveness for those who repent of their polytheism and turn from it to faith in Me. ﴿And believe﴾ means: and devote worship to Me alone as God, not associating anyone else with Me in their worship. ﴿And do righteous deeds﴾ means: and perform the obligations I have made incumbent upon them and avoid My disobedience. ﴿Then remain guided﴾ means: then they persist in that and remain upright, without neglecting any part of it.

The exegetes have said the same as what we have said regarding the interpretation of His words ﴿And indeed I am Forgiving to those who repent, believe, and do righteous deeds, then remain guided﴾.

Those who said so:

Ali narrated to me, saying: Abu Salih narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiyah narrated to me, from Ali, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿to those who repent﴾ from polytheism ﴿and believe﴾ means: he affirms the Oneness of God ﴿and do righteous deeds﴾ means: he performs My obligations.

Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His words ﴿to those who repent﴾ of their sin ﴿and believe﴾ in Him ﴿and do righteous deeds﴾ in what lies between him and God.

Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Abu Ja'far al-Razi, from al-Rabi' regarding His words ﴿to those who repent﴾ from polytheism ﴿and believe﴾ means: he devotes himself sincerely to God and acts in that sincerity.

The exegetes differed regarding the meaning of His words ﴿then remain guided﴾. Some of them said: its meaning is: he did not doubt his faith.

Those who said so:

Ali narrated to me, saying: Abdullah narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiyah narrated to me, from Ali, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿then remain guided﴾ means: he did not doubt.

Others said: its meaning is: then he persisted in faith and righteous deeds.

Those who said so: Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding ﴿then remain guided﴾: he persisted in Islam until he died upon it.

Others said: rather, its meaning is: then he remained upright.

Those who said so:

Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Abu Ja'far al-Razi, from al-Rabi' ibn Anas regarding ﴿then remain guided﴾: he said: he adhered to the sunnah of His Prophet (ﷺ).

Others said: rather, its meaning is: he hit upon the right action.

Those who said so:

Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said regarding His words ﴿and do righteous deeds, then remain guided﴾: he said: he hit upon the right action.

Others said: its meaning is: he recognized the one who rewards him.

Those who said so:

Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Hakkam narrated to us, from Anbasa, from al-Kalbi regarding ﴿And indeed I am Forgiving to those who repent﴾ from sin ﴿and believe﴾ from polytheism ﴿and do righteous deeds﴾ he performed what I obligated upon him ﴿then remain guided﴾: he recognized the one who rewards him, that if it is good then good, and if it is evil then evil.

Others said, citing:

Isma'il ibn Musa al-Fazari narrated to us, saying: Umar ibn Shakir informed us, saying: I heard Thabit al-Bunani say regarding His words ﴿And indeed I am Forgiving to those who repent, believe, and do righteous deeds, then remain guided﴾: he said: [this refers] to loyalty to the family of the Prophet (ﷺ).

Abu Ja'far said: We have chosen the view we have chosen in this matter because guidance is steadfastness upon the right path, and there is no meaning to steadfastness upon it unless it encompasses faith, righteous deeds, and repentance. Whoever does that and remains firm in it, there is no doubt of his being guided.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 20, verses 83–84:

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And what has made you hasten from your people, O Moses? (83) He said, "They are close upon my footsteps, and I hastened to You, my Lord, that You may be pleased."﴾

His saying, exalted is His remembrance: ﴿And what has made you hasten﴾ — and what thing has made you hasten ﴿from your people, O Moses?﴾ So that you went ahead of them and left them behind you, and you were not with them.

﴿He said, "They are close upon my footsteps"﴾ — meaning: my people are upon my footsteps, following after me. ﴿"And I hastened to You, my Lord, that You may be pleased"﴾ — meaning: I hastened, so I outpaced them, my Lord, so that You would be pleased with me.

Allah, exalted is His remembrance, said to Moses, "What has made you hasten from your people?" because He, majestic is His praise, as has reached us, when He had delivered him and the Children of Israel from Pharaoh and his people, and had led them across the sea, and had appointed them the side of the blessed mount on the right, Moses hastened to his Lord, and Harun remained among the Children of Israel, leading them on the trail of Moses.

As related:

Ibn Humayd narrated to us, he said: Salamah narrated to us, from Ibn Ishaq, he said: Allah promised Moses, when He destroyed Pharaoh and his people and delivered him and his people, thirty nights, then completed it with ten, so the appointed time of his Lord was forty nights, during which He spoke with him as He willed. Moses appointed Harun over the Children of Israel, and with him was the Samiri, leading them on the trail of Moses so as to catch up with him. So when Allah spoke to Moses, He said to him, ﴿And what has made you hasten from your people, O Moses?﴾ He said, ﴿"They are close upon my footsteps, and I hastened to You, my Lord, that You may be pleased."﴾

As related:

Yunus narrated to me, he said: Ibn Wahb informed us, he said: Ibn Zayd said regarding His saying, ﴿"And I hastened to You, my Lord, that You may be pleased"﴾: "[It means] so that I may please You."

**The discussion on the ta'wil (interpretation) of His saying, the Exalted:** ﴿He said, "Indeed, We have tested your people after you, and the Samiri has led them astray." By His saying ﴿after you﴾ He means after your departure from them. God, blessed and exalted, says ﴿and the Samiri led them astray﴾, and the Samiri's leading them astray was his calling them to worship the calf.

And His saying ﴿So Musa returned to his people﴾

He says: Musa went back to his people from among the Children of Israel after the forty nights had ended, ﴿angry and grieved﴾, enraged at his people and sorrowful over what they had done after him of disbelief in God.

As follows:
