As for His words ﴿by our power [bi-mulkina]﴾:

He, may His remembrance be exalted, informs about them that they acknowledged against themselves their error, and said: "We were not able to bring ourselves to what is right, and we did not have control over our affair, until we fell into what we fell into of trial."

The reciters differed in the recitation of this word. The majority of the reciters of Madina read ﴿bi-malkina﴾ with a fatha on the mim. The majority of the reciters of Kufa read ﴿bi-mulkina﴾ with a damma on the mim. Some of the people of Basra read ﴿bi-milkina﴾ with a kasra. As for the fatha and the damma, they have one meaning, namely "by our capacity and our ability," except that one of them is a verbal noun (masdar) and the other is a noun (ism). As for the kasra, it means "the ownership of a thing and its being in the possession of its owner."

The exegetes (ahl al-ta'wil, those who interpret the Qur'an) also differed about its interpretation. Some of them said: its meaning is, "We did not break our promise to you by our command."

Those who said that:

* Ali related to me, saying: Abd Allah narrated to us, saying: Muawiya related to me, from Ali, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿We did not break our promise to you by our power﴾: he said, "By our command."

* Muhammad ibn Amr related to me, saying: Abu Asim narrated to us, saying: Isa narrated to us, and al-Harith related to me, saying: al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Warqa narrated to us, all of them from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His words ﴿by our power﴾: he said, "By our command."

* al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Juraij, from Mujahid, the like of it.

Others said: its meaning is "by our strength."

Those who said that:

* Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatada, regarding ﴿They said: "We did not break our promise to you by our power"﴾: i.e., "by our strength."

* Musa narrated to us, saying: Amr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from as-Suddi, regarding ﴿They said: "We did not break our promise to you by our power"﴾: he says, "by our strength."

Others said: its meaning is, "We did not break our promise to you by our desire (hawa), but we did not have control over ourselves."

Those who said that:

* Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His words ﴿We did not break our promise to you by our power﴾: he said: "He says, 'by our desire.'" He said: "But three [parties] came, and with them were ornaments which they had borrowed from the family of Pharaoh, and garments."

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: All these three sayings concerning this are close in meaning, because whoever does not have control over himself, because his desire overcomes what he is commanded, is not excluded in the Arabic language from saying: "So-and-so did this affair, while he does not control himself and his action; he does not restrain it and his action; he is not able to abandon it." If that is the case, then whichever of the three recitations the reader recites, it is the same, because whoever reads it with a kasra from "malk" (ownership) directs the meaning of the sentence to: "We did not break our promise to you, and we had the power to fulfill it, because our selves overcame us in opposing it," and takes it from the saying of the speaker: "This is the ownership (milk) of so-and-so," for what he owns of possessions. And whoever reads it with a fatha directs the meaning of the sentence to something similar to that, except that he makes it a verbal noun from the saying of the speaker: "I possessed (malaktu) the thing, I possess it, possession (malkan) and capacity (malkatan)," just as it is said: "I overcame so-and-so, I overcome him, overcoming (ghalban) and dominance (ghalabatan)." And whoever reads it with a damma directs its meaning to: "We did not break our promise to you by our authority and our power," i.e., "and we are able to refrain from it, because whoever subdues something has authority over it." Some people have denied the recitation of whoever read it with a damma, and said: "What kind of sovereignty did the children of Israel have on that day? They were only oppressed in Egypt." He thereby neglected the meaning of the people and went far from what they intended. Those who read it with a damma did not intend the meaning that this one who denied it supposed about them; they only intended that its meaning is: "We did not break our promise to you by an authority that we had over ourselves, by which we were able to restrain them from what they did, because their desire overcame us, so that we opposed your promise."

* * *

As for His words ﴿but we were loaded with burdens of the people's adornments﴾:

He says: "But we were loaded with weights and loads of the people's adornments," meaning the ornaments of the family of Pharaoh. That was because when Musa wanted to lead the children of Israel by night out of Egypt, by Allah's command to him to do so, he ordered them to borrow from the goods and ornaments of the family of Pharaoh, and said: "Allah will make it spoil for you." They did so, and they borrowed from the ornaments of their women and their goods. That is their saying to Musa when he said to them: ﴿Has the promise seemed long to you, or do you desire that anger from your Lord should descend upon you, so that you broke your promise to me?﴾ (20:86) They said: ﴿We did not break our promise to you by our power, but we were loaded with burdens of the people's adornments﴾.

Exegetes spoke in agreement with what we have said about this.

Those who said that:

* Muhammad ibn Sa'd related to me, saying: my father related to me, saying: my uncle related to me, saying: my father related to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿but we were loaded with burdens of the people's adornments﴾: it is what the children of Israel had of the ornaments of the family of Pharaoh; he says: "They made us sinful by what we took of the ornaments of our enemy."

* Muhammad ibn Amr related to me, saying: Abu Asim narrated to us, saying: Isa narrated to us, and al-Harith related to me, saying: al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Warqa narrated to us, all of them from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His words ﴿burdens [awzaran]﴾: he said, "loads," and regarding His words ﴿of the people's adornments﴾: he said: "They are the ornaments which they borrowed from the family of Pharaoh, so they are loads."

* al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Juraij, from Mujahid, regarding ﴿but we were loaded with burdens﴾: he said, "loads," ﴿of the people's adornments﴾: he said, "their ornaments."

* Musa narrated to us, saying: Amr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from as-Suddi, regarding ﴿but we were loaded with burdens of the people's adornments﴾: he says, "from the ornaments of the Copts."

* Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His words ﴿but we were loaded with burdens of the people's adornments﴾: he said: "The ornaments that they borrowed and the garments are not at all sins. If they were sins, we would have been loaded with them and would carry them. They are not at all from sins."

The reciters differed in the recitation of this. The majority of the reciters of Madina and some of the Meccans read ﴿hummilna﴾ with a damma on the ha and a shadda on the mim, meaning that Musa was loading them with that. The majority of the reciters of Kufa and Basra and some of the Meccans read ﴿hamalna﴾ with the ha and mim unvocalized (without shadda), meaning that they carried that without anyone imposing its carrying on them.

Abu Ja'far said: The view I hold regarding the interpretation of this is that they are two well-known recitations, close in meaning, because the people carried it, and Musa had indeed commanded them to carry it. So whichever of the two a reader recites, he is correct.

* * *

As for His words ﴿so we threw them﴾:

He says: "So we cast those burdens of the people's adornments into the pit," ﴿thus as-Samiri cast﴾ means: "Just as we ourselves cast those loads, so as-Samiri cast what he had of the dust of the hoof of Jibril's horse."

Exegetes spoke in agreement with what we have said about this.

Those who said that:

* Muhammad ibn Amr related to me, saying: Abu Asim narrated to us, saying: Isa narrated to us, and al-Harith related to me, saying: al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Warqa narrated to us, all of them from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His words ﴿so we threw them﴾: he said, "so we cast them," ﴿thus as-Samiri cast﴾: "thus he did."

* al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Juraij, from Mujahid, regarding ﴿so we threw them﴾: he said, "so we cast them," ﴿thus as-Samiri cast﴾: "so he did."

* Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatada, regarding ﴿so we threw them﴾: i.e., "so we discarded them."

* * *

As for His words ﴿Then he brought out for them a calf, a body with a lowing sound﴾:

He says: "Then as-Samiri brought out for them, from what they had cast and what he had cast, a calf, a body with a lowing sound." By "lowing" he means the sound, which is the sound of cattle.

Then the people of knowledge differed about the manner in which as-Samiri brought out the calf. Some of them said: he fashioned it by shaping, then he cast some of the dust of the hoof of Jibril's horse into its mouth, and it lowed.

Those who said that:

* Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatada, regarding ﴿thus as-Samiri cast﴾, he said: Allah had appointed for Musa thirty nights, then completed them with ten. When the thirty passed, the enemy of Allah, as-Samiri, said: "What has befallen you has only befallen you as a punishment for the ornaments that were with you. So come on, and they were ornaments which they had borrowed [[Possibly "taʿawwarūhā" (they borrowed them), as cited in Lisan regarding the story of the calf from a hadith of Ibn Abbas.]] from the family of Pharaoh. They travelled with them, and they threw them to him, so he fashioned them into the form of a cow. He had tied up in his turban or in his garment a handful of the trace of Jibril's horse, and he threw it with the ornaments and the image: ﴿Then he brought out for them a calf, a body with a lowing sound﴾, so it began to low the lowing of cattle, and they said: ﴿This is your god and the god of Musa﴾.

* al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatada, who said: When Musa was slow in returning to his people, as-Samiri said to them: "He has only been detained from you because of the ornaments you have." They had borrowed ornaments from the family of Pharaoh, and they gathered them, and gave them to as-Samiri, who fashioned from them a calf. Then he took the handful he had taken from the trace of the horse, the horse of the king, and threw it into its inside, and behold, it was a calf, a body with a lowing sound. They said: "This is your god and the god of Musa, but Musa forgot his Lord with you."

Others said regarding this, as follows:

* Musa related to me, saying: Amr narrated to us, saying: he said: Asbat narrated to us, from as-Suddi, who said: As-Samiri took some dust from the hoof, the hoof of Jibril's horse. Musa departed, and he appointed Harun as successor over the children of Israel, and promised them thirty nights, but Allah completed them with ten. Harun said to them: "O children of Israel, the spoils of war are not lawful for you, and the ornaments of the Copts are only spoils. So gather them all together, dig a pit for them, and bury them. If Musa comes and makes them lawful, you may take them, and if not, they will be something you did not eat." They gathered those ornaments into that pit. As-Samiri came with that handful and threw it, and Allah brought forth from the ornaments a calf, a body with a lowing sound. The children of Israel counted the appointment of Musa, so they counted the night as a day and the day as a day, and when it reached the twentieth, the calf came out for them. When they saw it, as-Samiri said to them: ﴿This is your god and the god of Musa, but he forgot﴾, so they bowed down before it, worshipping it, and it would low and walk. ﴿Thus as-Samiri cast﴾: that was when Harun said to them: "Dig a pit for these ornaments and throw them into it," so they threw them, and as-Samiri cast his dust. And His words ﴿so they said: "This is your god and the god of Musa"﴾ mean: the people of Musa who worshipped the calf said: "This is your object of worship and the object of worship of Musa." And His words ﴿but he forgot﴾ mean: he went astray and abandoned.

Then the exegetes differed regarding His words ﴿but he forgot﴾: who is its speaker, to whom is it attributed, and what is its meaning? Some of them said: this is from Allah, a report about as-Samiri, and as-Samiri is the one described by it. They said its meaning is: he abandoned the religion with which Allah sent Musa, which is Islam.

Those who said that:

* Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salama narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ishaq related to me, from Hakim ibn Jubayr, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas, who said: Allah says ﴿but he forgot﴾: i.e., he abandoned what he had been upon of Islam, meaning as-Samiri.

Others said: rather, this is a report from Allah about as-Samiri, that he said to the children of Israel, and that he described Musa as having gone seeking his Lord, and so he lost his way, and this is the calf.

Those who said that:

* Muhammad ibn Sa'd related to me, saying: my father related to me, saying: my uncle related to me, saying: my father related to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas, regarding ﴿so we threw them﴾: he means the adornments of the people, when as-Samiri commanded us, after he had taken a handful of the trace of Jibril, peace be upon him, and threw the handful upon their ornaments, and it became a calf, a body with a lowing sound. ﴿They said: "This is your god and the god of Musa"﴾, whom he went seeking. ﴿But he forgot﴾: he means Musa forgot; he went astray from it and did not find the way to it.

* Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatada, regarding ﴿but he forgot﴾: he says: "Musa sought this, but the way went astray for him."

* al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatada, regarding ﴿but he forgot﴾: he says: As-Samiri said: "Musa forgot his Lord with you."

* Muhammad ibn Amr related to me, saying: Abu Asim narrated to us, saying: Isa narrated to us, and al-Harith related to me, saying: al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Warqa narrated to us, all of them from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His words ﴿but he forgot﴾, Musa: he said: They say it: "Musa erred; the Lord erred about the calf."

* al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Juraij, from Mujahid, regarding ﴿but he forgot﴾: he said: "Musa forgot; the Lord erred about the calf. The people of Musa say it."

* Musa related to me, saying: Amr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from as-Suddi, regarding ﴿but he forgot﴾: he says: "Musa left his god here and went seeking it."

* Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His words ﴿This is your god and the god of Musa, but he forgot﴾: he said: "He says: he forgot where his Lord promised him, here, but he forgot."

* I was told by al-Husayn, who said: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: Ubayd informed us, saying: I heard ad-Dahhak say, regarding His words ﴿This is your god and the god of Musa, but he forgot﴾: he says: "Musa forgot his Lord and missed Him, and this calf is the god of Musa."

Abu Ja'far said: The view that is closer to the interpretation of this is the saying we have mentioned from these, namely that it is a report from Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, about as-Samiri, that he described Musa as having forgotten his Lord, and that his Lord whom he went seeking is the calf which as-Samiri brought out. This is due to the consensus of the authoritative exegetes upon it, and because it follows the mention of Musa, so that it being a report from as-Samiri about him is more fitting than anything else.

And al-Harith related to us, saying: al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Warqa narrated to us, all of them from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His words ﴿my promise﴾, he said: "My covenant." That covenant and promise is what we explained earlier.

He had tied up in his turban or in his garment a handful of the trace of Jibril's horse, and he threw it with the ornaments and the image: ﴿Then he brought out for them a calf, a body with a lowing sound﴾, so it began to low the lowing of cattle, and they said: ﴿This is your god and the god of Musa﴾.

* al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatada, who said: When Musa was slow in returning to his people, as-Samiri said to them: "He has only been detained from you because of the ornaments you have." They had borrowed ornaments from the family of Pharaoh, and they gathered them, and gave them to as-Samiri, who fashioned from them a calf. Then he took the handful he had taken from the trace of the horse, the horse of the king, and threw it into its inside, and behold, it was a calf, a body with a lowing sound. They said: "This is your god and the god of Musa, but Musa forgot his Lord with you."

Others said regarding this, as follows:

* Musa related to me, saying: Amr narrated to us, saying: he said: Asbat narrated to us, from as-Suddi, who said: As-Samiri took some dust from the hoof, the hoof of Jibril's horse. Musa departed, and he appointed Harun as successor over the children of Israel, and promised them thirty nights, but Allah completed them with ten. Harun said to them: "O children of Israel, the spoils of war are not lawful for you, and the ornaments of the Copts are only spoils. So gather them all together, dig a pit for them, and bury them. If Musa comes and makes them lawful, you may take them, and if not, they will be something you did not eat." They gathered those ornaments into that pit. As-Samiri came with that handful and threw it, and Allah brought forth from the ornaments a calf, a body with a lowing sound. The children of Israel counted the appointment of Musa, so they counted the night as a day and the day as a day, and when it reached the twentieth, the calf came out for them. When they saw it, as-Samiri said to them: ﴿This is your god and the god of Musa, but he forgot﴾, so they bowed down before it, worshipping it, and it would low and walk. ﴿Thus as-Samiri cast﴾: that was when Harun said to them: "Dig a pit for these ornaments and throw them into it," so they threw them, and as-Samiri cast his dust. And His words ﴿so they said: "This is your god and the god of Musa"﴾ mean: the people of Musa who worshipped the calf said: "This is your object of worship and the object of worship of Musa." And His words ﴿but he forgot﴾ mean: he went astray and abandoned.

Then the exegetes differed regarding His words ﴿but he forgot﴾: who is its speaker, to whom is it attributed, and what is its meaning? Some of them said: this is from Allah, a report about as-Samiri, and as-Samiri is the one described by it. They said its meaning is: he abandoned the religion with which Allah sent Musa, which is Islam.

Those who said that:

* Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salama narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ishaq related to me, from Hakim ibn Jubayr, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas, who said: Allah says ﴿but he forgot﴾: i.e., he abandoned what he had been upon of Islam, meaning as-Samiri.

Others said: rather, this is a report from Allah about as-Samiri, that he said to the children of Israel, and that he described Musa as having gone seeking his Lord, and so he lost his way, and this is the calf.

Those who said that:

* Muhammad ibn Sa'd related to me, saying: my father related to me, saying: my uncle related to me, saying: my father related to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas, regarding ﴿so we threw them﴾: he means the adornments of the people, when as-Samiri commanded us, after he had taken a handful of the trace of Jibril, peace be upon him, and threw the handful upon their ornaments, and it became a calf, a body with a lowing sound. ﴿They said: "This is your god and the god of Musa"﴾, whom he went seeking. ﴿But he forgot﴾: he means Musa forgot; he went astray from it and did not find the way to it.

* Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatada, regarding ﴿but he forgot﴾: he says: "Musa sought this, but the way went astray for him."

* al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatada, regarding ﴿but he forgot﴾: he says: As-Samiri said: "Musa forgot his Lord with you."

* Muhammad ibn Amr related to me, saying: Abu Asim narrated to us, saying: Isa narrated to us, and al-Harith related to me, saying: al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Warqa narrated to us, all of them from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His words ﴿but he forgot﴾, Musa: he said: They say it: "Musa erred; the Lord erred about the calf."

* al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Juraij, from Mujahid, regarding ﴿but he forgot﴾: he said: "Musa forgot; the Lord erred about the calf. The people of Musa say it."

* Musa related to me, saying: Amr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from as-Suddi, regarding ﴿but he forgot﴾: he says: "Musa left his god here and went seeking it."

* Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His words ﴿This is your god and the god of Musa, but he forgot﴾: he said: "He says: he forgot where his Lord promised him, here, but he forgot."

* I was told by al-Husayn, who said: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: Ubayd informed us, saying: I heard ad-Dahhak say, regarding His words ﴿This is your god and the god of Musa, but he forgot﴾: he says: "Musa forgot his Lord and missed Him, and this calf is the god of Musa."

Abu Ja'far said: The view that is closer to the interpretation of this is the saying we have mentioned from these, namely that it is a report from Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, about as-Samiri, that he described Musa as having forgotten his Lord, and that his Lord whom he went seeking is the calf which as-Samiri brought out. This is due to the consensus of the authoritative exegetes upon it, and because it follows the mention of Musa, so that it being a report from as-Samiri about him is more fitting than anything else.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 20, verse 89–91:

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do they not see that it returns no word to them and that it controls for them neither harm nor benefit?﴾ (89) ﴿And Aaron had already said to them before: "O my people, you are only being tested by it, and indeed your Lord is the Most Merciful, so follow me and obey my command."﴾ (90) ﴿They said, "We will not cease to be devoted to it until Moses returns to us."﴾ (91)

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says, rebuking the worshippers of the calf and those who said of it, ﴿This is your god and the god of Moses, but he has forgotten﴾, and reproaching them for that and mocking their reasoning by what they did and what they brought upon themselves: Do they not see that the calf, which they claimed to be their god and the god of Moses, does not speak to them, and if they spoke to it, it would not return them an answer, and it has no power to bring harm or benefit? So how could something with this description be a god?

As:

* Muhammad ibn Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu Asim told us, saying: Isa told us. (Also) al-Harith narrated to me, saying: al-Hasan told us, saying: Warqa' told us, all of them from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, ﴿that it returns no word to them﴾: the calf.

* al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn told us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, ﴿Do they not see that it returns no word to them﴾, he said: the calf.

* Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid told us, saying: Sa'id told us, from Qatadah, who said: God (says) ﴿Do they not see that it does not return to them﴾, that is the calf which they had taken ﴿a word, and it controls for them neither harm nor benefit﴾.

He says: Aaron had already said to the worshippers of the calf among the Children of Israel, before Moses returned to them, and what he said to them is what God related: ﴿You are only being tested by it﴾, meaning: God only tested your faith and your steadfastness in your religion through this calf, into which He caused the lowing to enter, so that by it He might know the sound of faith among you from the one whose heart is diseased, the one who doubts his religion.

As:

* Musa narrated to me, saying: Amr told us, saying: Asbat told us, from al-Suddi, who said: Aaron said to them, ﴿You are only being tested by it﴾, meaning: you are only being tried by it, that is, by the calf.

And His saying, ﴿They said, "We will not cease to be devoted to it"﴾, means: the worshippers of the calf from the people of Moses said: We will not cease to remain upon the calf, worshipping it, until Moses returns to us.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 20, verses 92–94:

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Moses said, "O Aaron, what prevented you, when you saw them going astray, from following me? Then have you disobeyed my order?" [Aaron] said, "O son of my mother, do not seize [me] by my beard or by my head. Indeed, I feared that you would say, 'You have caused division among the Children of Israel and did not observe my word.'"﴾

He, exalted is He, says: Moses said to his brother Aaron, when he had finished addressing his people and disputing with them over the error of their actions: "O Aaron, what prevented you, when you saw them going astray from their religion, disbelieving in God and worshipping the calf, from following me?"

The people of interpretation differed concerning the meaning for which Moses rebuked his brother for not following him. Some of them said: he rebuked him for leaving off travelling with those who obeyed him in his footsteps, as he had been commanded.

Those who said this:

Ibn Humayd narrated to us, he said: Salamah narrated to us, from Ibn Ishaq, from Hakim ibn Jubayr, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas, who said: When the people said, ﴿We will not cease to be devoted to it until Moses returns to us﴾, Aaron remained with those among the Muslims who had followed him and had not been seduced, and he kept those who worshipped the calf at their worship of the calf. Aaron feared that if he set out with those Muslims who were with him, Moses would say to him, ﴿You have caused division among the Children of Israel and did not observe my word﴾; and he was in awe of him and obedient to him.

Yunus narrated to me, he said: Ibn Wahb informed us, he said: Ibn Zayd said, concerning His saying, ﴿What prevented you, when you saw them going astray, from following me?﴾ He said: "[It means] you left them."

Others said: Rather, he rebuked him for leaving off setting right the corruption of the people.

Those who said this:

Al-Qasim narrated to us, he said: al-Husayn narrated to us, he said: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Juraij, concerning His saying, ﴿What prevented you, when you saw them going astray, from following me?﴾ He said: Moses commanded Aaron to reform, and not to follow the way of the corrupters; and that is His saying, ﴿from following me. It is: Then Moses seized his brother Aaron by the beard and head, dragging him towards himself, and Aaron said, ﴿O son of my mother, do not seize [me] by my beard or by my head.﴾

And His saying, ﴿Indeed, I feared that you would say, "You have caused division among the Children of Israel and did not observe my word."﴾

The people of knowledge differed concerning the nature of the division among them which Aaron feared. Some of them said: Aaron feared that he would travel with those who obeyed him and remain upon his religion following Moses, leaving behind the calf-worshippers, when they had said to him, ﴿We will not cease to be devoted to it until Moses returns to us﴾; so Moses would say to him, ﴿You have caused division among the Children of Israel and did not observe my word﴾, by your going with one group and leaving another group behind you.

Those who said this:

Yunus narrated to me, he said: Ibn Wahb informed us, Ibn Zayd said, concerning the saying of God, exalted is He, ﴿What prevented you, when you saw them going astray, from following me? Then have you disobeyed my order?" [Aaron] said, "I feared that you would say, 'You have caused division among the Children of Israel and did not observe my word.'﴾ He said: "I feared that some of them would follow me and some would remain behind."

Others said: Rather, the meaning of that is: I feared that we would fight and some of us would kill others.

Those who said this:

Al-Qasim narrated to us, he said: al-Husayn narrated to us, he said: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Juraij, concerning ﴿Indeed, I feared that you would say, "You have caused division among the Children of Israel and did not observe my word."﴾ He said: "We would become two factions, and some of us would kill others until we annihilated one another."

Abu Ja'far said: The most correct of these two opinions in interpretation is the statement related from Ibn Abbas, that Moses rebuked his brother Aaron for leaving off following his command with those who followed him from among the people of faith. So Aaron said to him: "Indeed, I feared that you would say, 'You have caused division among their community, leaving some of them behind you and bringing others'"; and this is evident in Aaron's words to the people, ﴿O my people, you are only being tested by it, and indeed your Lord is the Most Merciful, so follow me and obey my order﴾, and in the people's reply to him and their saying, ﴿We will not cease to be devoted to it until Moses returns to us﴾.

He says: "and did not wait for my word and preserve it," from the verb "raqaba al-shay'" (to observe a thing), which means to watch over it and keep it safe.

As related:

Al-Qasim narrated to us, he said: al-Husayn narrated to us, he said: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Juraij, who said: Ibn Abbas said, ﴿and did not observe my word﴾: "He did not preserve my word."

Others said: Rather, he rebuked him for leaving off setting right the corruption of the people.

Those who said this:

Al-Qasim narrated to us, he said: al-Husayn narrated to us, he said: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Juraij, concerning His saying, ﴿What prevented you, when you saw them going astray, from following me?﴾ He said: Moses commanded Aaron to reform, and not to follow the way of the corrupters; and that is His saying, ﴿from following me. Then have you disobeyed my order?﴾ And His saying, ﴿[Aaron] said, "O son of my mother, do not seize [me] by my beard or by my head."﴾ In this speech something has been omitted, its mention left out being sufficient because the context indicates it. It is: Then Moses seized his brother Aaron by the beard and head, dragging him towards himself, and Aaron said, ﴿O son of my mother, do not seize [me] by my beard or by my head.﴾

And His saying, ﴿Indeed, I feared that you would say, "You have caused division among the Children of Israel and did not observe my word."﴾

The people of knowledge differed concerning the nature of the division among them which Aaron feared. Some of them said: Aaron feared that he would travel with those who obeyed him and remain upon his religion following Moses, leaving behind the calf-worshippers, when they had said to him, ﴿We will not cease to be devoted to it until Moses returns to us﴾; so Moses would say to him, ﴿You have caused division among the Children of Israel and did not observe my word﴾, by your going with one group and leaving another group behind you.

Those who said this:

Yunus narrated to me, he said: Ibn Wahb informed us, Ibn Zayd said, concerning the saying of God, exalted is He, ﴿What prevented you, when you saw them going astray, from following me? Then have you disobeyed my order?" [Aaron] said, "I feared that you would say, 'You have caused division among the Children of Israel and did not observe my word.'﴾ He said: "I feared that some of them would follow me and some would remain behind."

Others said: Rather, the meaning of that is: I feared that we would fight and some of us would kill others.

Those who said this:

Al-Qasim narrated to us, he said: al-Husayn narrated to us, he said: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Juraij, concerning ﴿Indeed, I feared that you would say, "You have caused division among the Children of Israel and did not observe my word."﴾ He said: "We would become two factions, and some of us would kill others until we annihilated one another."

Abu Ja'far said: The most correct of these two opinions in interpretation is the statement related from Ibn Abbas, that Moses rebuked his brother Aaron for leaving off following his command with those who followed him from among the people of faith. So Aaron said to him: "Indeed, I feared that you would say, 'You have caused division among their community, leaving some of them behind you and bringing others'"; and this is evident in Aaron's words to the people, ﴿O my people, you are only being tested by it, and indeed your Lord is the Most Merciful, so follow me and obey my order﴾, and in the people's reply to him and their saying, ﴿We will not cease to be devoted to it until Moses returns to us﴾.

And His saying, ﴿and did not observe my word﴾

He says: "and did not wait for my word and preserve it," from the verb "raqaba al-shay'" (to observe a thing), which means to watch over it and keep it safe.

As related:

Al-Qasim narrated to us, he said: al-Husayn narrated to us, he said: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Juraij, who said: Ibn Abbas said, ﴿and did not observe my word﴾: "He did not preserve my word."

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 20, verses 95–96:

The interpretation of His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿He said, "What is your situation, O Samiri?" (95) He said, "I perceived what they did not perceive, so I took a handful from the trace of the messenger and threw it. Thus my soul enticed me."﴾ (96)

He, the Exalted, means by His words ﴿What is your situation, O Samiri?﴾ that Moses said to the Samiri: "What is your matter, O Samiri, and what prompted you to what you did?"

As related:

* Yunus told me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, concerning His words ﴿What is your situation, O Samiri?﴾: "What is your affair? What is your matter? What is this that brought you into what you entered into?"

* Musa told us, saying: Amr told us, saying: Asbat told us, from al-Suddi, ﴿He said, "What is your situation, O Samiri?"﴾ He said: "What is wrong with you, O Samiri?"

* * *

As for His words ﴿I perceived what they did not perceive﴾:

It means: the Samiri said, "I knew what they did not know." The verb is from *basar* (perception, insight), meaning: I became one who perceives and knows through what I did.

Those who said this:

* al-Qasim told us, saying: al-Husayn told us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Juraij, who said: When Pharaoh killed the boys, the mother of the Samiri said: "I wish I had removed him from me so that I would not see him and not know that he was killed." So she placed him in a cave. Then Gabriel came, and he put his own palm in his mouth, and he began to nurse him with honey and milk. He continued to visit him until he recognized him. Hence his recognition of him when he said: ﴿So I took a handful from the trace of the messenger﴾.

Others said: it means "I saw what they did not see," and they said: one says "basartu bi-l-shay'" and "absartuhu," just as one says "asra'tu" and "sara'tu" as you wish.

Those who said it means "absartu": Bishr told us, saying: Yazid told us, saying: Sa'id told us, from Qatada, ﴿He said, "I perceived what they did not perceive"﴾, meaning the horse of Gabriel, peace be upon him.

* * *

As for His words ﴿So I took a handful from the trace of the messenger﴾:

It means: I took a handful from the trace of the hoof of Gabriel's horse.

The people of interpretation have said things similar to what we have said.

Those who said that:

* Ibn Humayd told us, saying: Salama told us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ishaq related to me, from Hakim ibn Jubayr, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas, who said: When the Children of Israel threw what they had of the adornments of the family of Pharaoh into the fire, and it melted, and the Samiri saw the trace of the horse of Gabriel, peace be upon him, he took some dust from the trace of its hoof, then came to the fire and threw it in, and said: "Be a calf, a body with a lowing sound." So it became a source of trial and temptation.

* Muhammad ibn Sa'd told me, saying: My father told me, saying: My paternal uncle told me, saying: My father told me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas, who said: He took a handful from the trace of Gabriel, and threw the handful upon their ornaments, and it became a calf, a body with a lowing sound, and he said: "This is your god and the god of Musa."

* Muhammad ibn Amr told me, saying: Abu Asim told us, saying: Isa told us; and al-Harith told me, saying: al-Hasan told us, saying: Warqa told us, all of them from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, concerning the word of God: ﴿So I took a handful from the trace of the messenger, and threw it﴾, he said: "From beneath the hoof of Gabriel's horse. The Samiri threw it onto the ornaments of the Children of Israel, and it was melted into a calf, a body with a lowing sound; the sound of the wind in it is its lowing." And the calf is the young of a cow.

The reciters differed in the reading of these two words. The majority of the reciters of Medina and Basra read ﴿I perceived what they did not perceive﴾ with the *ya'* (third person), meaning: the Samiri said, "I perceived what the Children of Israel did not perceive." The majority of the reciters of Kufa read ﴿I perceived what you did not perceive﴾ with the *ta'* (second person), addressing Moses ﷺ and his companions, meaning: the Samiri said to Moses, "I perceived what you and your companions did not perceive."

My view on this is that both are well-known readings, each recited by scholars among the reciters, and the meaning of each is sound. It is possible that the Samiri saw Gabriel, and that what was in his mind—whether his soul suggested it to him or by other means—was that the dust of his horse's hoof on which he stood was suitable for what he said when he threw it into the inside of the calf, and this knowledge was not with Moses, nor with his companions among the Children of Israel. Therefore he said to Moses ﴿I perceived what you did not perceive﴾, i.e., "I knew what you did not know." As for the reading ﴿I perceived what they did not perceive﴾ with the *ya'*, there is no difficulty in it, since it is known that the Children of Israel did not know what that dust was suitable for.

As for His words ﴿So I took a handful from the trace of the messenger﴾, the readers of the regional centers read it with the *dad* (ق ب ض, *qabda*), meaning: "I took with my hand dust from the dust of the trace of the horse of the messenger."

It has been related from al-Hasan al-Basri and Qatada that:

* Ahmad ibn Yusuf told me, saying: al-Qasim told us, saying: Hushaym told us, from Abbad ibn Awf, from al-Hasan, that he read it ﴿fa-qabasstu qabsah﴾ with the *sad* (ص).

* And Ahmad ibn Yusuf told me, saying: al-Qasim told us, saying: Hushaym told us, from Abbad, from Qatada, the same, with the *sad*, meaning: "I took with my fingers dust from the trace of the horse of the messenger." The *qabdah* in the speech of the Arabs is taking with the whole palm, while the *qabsah* is taking with the tips of the fingers.

* * *

As for His words ﴿and threw it﴾:

It means: "I cast it away." ﴿Thus my soul enticed me﴾ means: "Just as I did, casting the handful I had taken from the trace of the horse onto the ornaments that I kindled upon until they melted and became a calf, a body with a lowing sound, ﴿my soul enticed me﴾," meaning: "my soul made it attractive to me that it should be so."

As related:

* Yunus told me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, concerning ﴿Thus my soul enticed me﴾: "Thus my soul spoke to me."

I'll translate this passage as it stands.

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Said [Moses], "Then go, for indeed, [in] your life is [the penalty] that you should say, 'No contact [mis\u0101s].' And indeed, for you is an appointment you will not fail to meet. And look at your god to which you remained devoted; we will surely burn it and then we will blow it away into the sea with a [thorough] blowing away."﴾ [20:97]. "Indeed, your god is only Allah, other than whom there is no deity, He has encompassed all things in knowledge."﴾ [20:98]

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: Moses said to the Samiri, "Go, for indeed, during the days of your life you shall say, 'No contact' (lā misās), meaning: 'Do not touch me, and I will not touch you.'" It is mentioned that Moses commanded the Children of Israel not to eat with him, not to mix with him, and not to trade with him. Therefore he said to him, "Indeed, in your life you will say, 'No contact,'" and this remained among his tribe, as is mentioned.

As related:

* Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah, who said: By God, the Samiri was a great man among the great men of the Children of Israel, from a tribe called Samirah. But the enemy of God became a hypocrite after the Children of Israel crossed the sea. His saying, "Go, for indeed, in your life you shall say, 'No contact,'" so their descendants today say, "No contact."

* *

His saying, ﴿And indeed, for you is an appointment you will not fail to meet﴾

The reciters differed in its recitation. The majority of the reciters of Medina and Kufa recited ﴿lan tukhlafahu﴾ with a damma on the tā' and a fatha on the lām, meaning: "And indeed, for you is an appointment for your punishment and retribution for what you did of misguiding my people until they worshipped the calf besides God; God will not fail it for you, rather He will make you taste it." Al-Hasan, Qatadah, and Abu Nuhayk recited it ﴿wa inna laka maw'idan lan tukhlifahu﴾ with a damma on the tā' and a kasra on the lām, meaning: "And indeed, for you is an appointment that you will not fail, you, O Samiri," and they interpreted it as: "you will not be absent from it."

Mention of those who said that:

* Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Yahya ibn Wadih related to us, saying: Abd al-Mu'min related to us, saying: I heard Abu Nuhayk recite ﴿lan tukhlifahu anta﴾, saying: "You will not be absent from it."

* Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah ﴿wa inna laka maw'idan lan tukhlafahu﴾, saying: "You will not be absent from it."

Abu Ja'far said: My view on this is that they are two well-known readings, close in meaning, for there is no doubt that God fulfills His promise to His creation of gathering them for the standing of reckoning, and that all creatures will meet that day. So God does not fail them in that, nor do they fail Him by being absent from it. Thus whichever of the two readings the reciter uses, he is correct.

* *

His saying, ﴿And look at your god to which you remained devoted﴾

He says: And look at your deity which you remained persistently worshipping.

As related:

* Ali related to me, saying: Abu Salih related to us, saying: Mu'awiyah related to me, from Ali, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying, ﴿zalta alayhi ākifan﴾: "to which you kept devotion."

* Muhammad ibn Sa'd related to me, saying: My father related to me, saying: My paternal uncle related to me, saying: My father related to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas, who said: Moses said to him, ﴿And look at your god to which you remained devoted﴾, meaning: "to which you kept devotion." Among the Arabs there are two dialects regarding ﴿ẓalta﴾: opening the ẓā' (fatha), which is the reading of the reciters of the major cities, and kasra on it. Those who used the kasra seem to have transferred the vowel of the lām, which is the middle radical of the verb, from ẓalaltu to it, while those who used the fatha kept the vowel it had before anything was deleted from it. The Arabs do this with doubled letters, saying in massista: mast and mist, and in hammta bidhalika: hamt bihi, and hal ahasta fulānan wa ahsastahu, as the poet said:

"Except that the swift camels among the mounts... ahsanna bihi, fahunna ilayhi shus" [a line of Abu Zubayd al-Ta'i (Lisan: h-s-s), the second hemistich of which is reported as "hasinna bihi fahunna ilayhi shus"]. It is said: "hassa bi al-shay'" (a verb with vowel patterns), "ahassa bihi" and "ahassahu" meaning he perceived it. The verb "ahassa bi" is elided to avoid the meeting of two identical letters. Sibawayh said: the same is done with any form whose final radical is pronounced with sukun, which cannot take a vowel, since they treat it like aqamta. Al-Azhari: "hal ahasta" means "ahsasta". It is also said: "hasta bi al-shay'" when one knows and recognizes it. He said: it is said: "ahsastu al-khabar" and "ahastuhu" and "hasaytu" and "hasta" when one knows a part of it; one says "ma ahsastu bi al-khabar" and "ma ahasta" and "ma hasaytu" and "ma hasta," meaning I did not know anything of it... Sometimes they say "hasaytu bi al-khabar" and "ahsaytu bihi," replacing the sin with a ya'. Abu Zubayd said: "khala anna..." [the line]. Al-Jawhari and Abu Ubayda narrate Abu Zubayd's line as "ahassa bihi fahuwa ilayhi shus," and its origin is ahassa. Ends. It is said of ẓalla and similar doubled verbs with a kasra on the middle radical in the past: "ẓalaltu af'alu kadhā" with two lams, "ẓaltu af'alu kadhā" with the first lam deleted and the fa' fatha, and "ẓalta af'alu kadhā" with the lam deleted and its vowel moved to the ẓā'.

* *

His saying, ﴿Surely we will burn it﴾

The reciters differed in its recitation. The majority of the reciters of the Hijaz and Iraq recited ﴿lanuḥarriqannahu﴾ with a damma on the nūn and tashdid on the rā', meaning: "we will burn it with fire piece by piece." It is related from al-Hasan al-Basri that he recited it ﴿lanuḥriqannahu﴾ with a damma on the nūn and a light rā', meaning: "we will burn it with fire in a single burning." Abu Ja'far the reciter recited ﴿lanaḥruqannahu﴾ with a fatha on the nūn and a damma on the rā', meaning: "we will file it down with files," from haraqtuhu uhriquhu and uharriquhu, as the poet said:

"At Dhi Firqayn, on the day the sons of Habib [...] their fangs grinding against us" [a line recited by al-Mufaddal al-Dabbi and attributed to Amir ibn Shaqiq (Lisan: h-r-q; Mu'jam ma Asta'jam of al-Bakri, 210). Dhu Firqayn is a hill in the lands of Banu Tamim between the Basra and Kufa roads]. [Further commentary on the poem follows in the source.]

The correct reading in our view is ﴿lanuḥarriqannahu﴾ with a damma on the nūn and tashdid on the rā', from burning with fire.

As related:

* Ali related to me, saying: Abu Salih related to us, saying: Mu'awiyah related to me, from Ali, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿lanuḥarriqannahu﴾: "with fire."

* Muhammad ibn Sa'd related to me, saying: My father related to me, saying: My paternal uncle related to me, saying: My father related to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas ﴿lanuḥarriqannahu﴾: "then he burned it and scattered it into the sea." I chose this reading because the authoritative reciters agree upon it.

As for Abu Ja'far, I think he followed what:

* Musa ibn Harun related to us, saying: Amr related to us, saying: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi, regarding ﴿And look at your god to which you remained devoted; we will surely burn it, then we will blow it away into the sea with a [thorough] blowing away﴾: "Then he seized it and slaughtered it, then burned it with a file, then scattered it into the sea, so that no sea that day remained without some of it falling into it."

* Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah regarding ﴿And look at your god... we will surely burn it, then we will blow it away into the sea with a [thorough] blowing away﴾, he said: In some readings: "we will surely slaughter it, then we will burn it, then we will blow it away into the sea with a [thorough] blowing away."

* Al-Hasan related to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah, regarding the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: ﴿wa-nẓur ilā ilāhika alladhī ẓaltā ʿalayhi ʿākifan la-nadhbaḥannahu thumma la-nuḥarriqannahu thumma la-nansifannahu fī al-yammi nasfan﴾.

* *

His saying, ﴿Then we will blow it away into the sea with a [thorough] blowing away﴾

He says: then we will scatter it in the sea by scattering, from which one says: "fulan nasafa al-ta'ām bi al-minsaf," when he winnows food, so that its husks and dust are blown away by hand or by wind.

The people of interpretation said things similar to what we have said.

Mention of those who said that:

* Ali related to me, saying: Abdullah related to us, saying: Mu'awiyah related to me, from Ali, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿thumma la-nansifannahu fī al-yammi nasfan﴾: "we will scatter it in the sea."

* Muhammad ibn Sa'd related to me, saying: My father related to me... from Ibn Abbas, who said: "He scattered it into the yamm, and yamm means the sea."

* Musa related to us, saying: Amr related to us, saying: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi, who said: "He scattered it into the yamm."

* Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah regarding "al-yamm," who said: "the sea."

* *

His saying, ﴿Indeed, your god is only Allah, other than whom there is no deity﴾

He says: You people have no deity except the One to whom all creatures owe worship; worship is not fitting for anyone other than Him, and it is not proper for it to be directed to anyone but Him. ﴿He has encompassed all things in knowledge﴾: He has encompassed everything in knowledge, so He knows it, and nothing is hidden from Him, nor is His knowledge of all of that constrained. From this one says: "fulan yasa'u li hadha al-amr" when he is able for it and strong enough for it, and "la yasa'u lahu" when he is unable to do it and is not strong enough for it.

Qatadah used to say about this what:

* Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying ﴿He has encompassed all things in knowledge﴾: "He filled everything with knowledge, blessed and exalted is He."

I'll translate this passage as it stands.

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Said [Moses], "Then go, for indeed, [in] your life is [the penalty] that you should say, 'No contact [mis\u0101s].' And indeed, for you is an appointment you will not fail to meet. And look at your god to which you remained devoted; we will surely burn it and then we will blow it away into the sea with a [thorough] blowing away."﴾ [20:97]. "Indeed, your god is only Allah, other than whom there is no deity, He has encompassed all things in knowledge."﴾ [20:98]

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: Moses said to the Samiri, "Go, for indeed, during the days of your life you shall say, 'No contact' (lā misās), meaning: 'Do not touch me, and I will not touch you.'" It is mentioned that Moses commanded the Children of Israel not to eat with him, not to mix with him, and not to trade with him. Therefore he said to him, "Indeed, in your life you will say, 'No contact,'" and this remained among his tribe, as is mentioned.

As related:

* Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah, who said: By God, the Samiri was a great man among the great men of the Children of Israel, from a tribe called Samirah. But the enemy of God became a hypocrite after the Children of Israel crossed the sea. His saying, "Go, for indeed, in your life you shall say, 'No contact,'" so their descendants today say, "No contact."

* *

His saying, ﴿And indeed, for you is an appointment you will not fail to meet﴾

The reciters differed in its recitation. The majority of the reciters of Medina and Kufa recited ﴿lan tukhlafahu﴾ with a damma on the tā' and a fatha on the lām, meaning: "And indeed, for you is an appointment for your punishment and retribution for what you did of misguiding my people until they worshipped the calf besides God; God will not fail it for you, rather He will make you taste it." Al-Hasan, Qatadah, and Abu Nuhayk recited it ﴿wa inna laka maw'idan lan tukhlifahu﴾ with a damma on the tā' and a kasra on the lām, meaning: "And indeed, for you is an appointment that you will not fail, you, O Samiri," and they interpreted it as: "you will not be absent from it."

Mention of those who said that:

* Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Yahya ibn Wadih related to us, saying: Abd al-Mu'min related to us, saying: I heard Abu Nuhayk recite ﴿lan tukhlifahu anta﴾, saying: "You will not be absent from it."

* Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah ﴿wa inna laka maw'idan lan tukhlafahu﴾, saying: "You will not be absent from it."

Abu Ja'far said: My view on this is that they are two well-known readings, close in meaning, for there is no doubt that God fulfills His promise to His creation of gathering them for the standing of reckoning, and that all creatures will meet that day. So God does not fail them in that, nor do they fail Him by being absent from it. Thus whichever of the two readings the reciter uses, he is correct.

* *

His saying, ﴿And look at your god to which you remained devoted﴾

He says: And look at your deity which you remained persistently worshipping.

As related:

* Ali related to me, saying: Abu Salih related to us, saying: Mu'awiyah related to me, from Ali, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying, ﴿zalta alayhi ākifan﴾: "to which you kept devotion."

* Muhammad ibn Sa'd related to me, saying: My father related to me, saying: My paternal uncle related to me, saying: My father related to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas, who said: Moses said to him, ﴿And look at your god to which you remained devoted﴾, meaning: "to which you kept devotion." Among the Arabs there are two dialects regarding ﴿ẓalta﴾: opening the ẓā' (fatha), which is the reading of the reciters of the major cities, and kasra on it. Those who used the kasra seem to have transferred the vowel of the lām, which is the middle radical of the verb, from ẓalaltu to it, while those who used the fatha kept the vowel it had before anything was deleted from it. The Arabs do this with doubled letters, saying in massista: mast and mist, and in hammta bidhalika: hamt bihi, and hal ahasta fulānan wa ahsastahu, as the poet said:

"Except that the swift camels among the mounts... ahsanna bihi, fahunna ilayhi shus" [a line of Abu Zubayd al-Ta'i (Lisan: h-s-s), the second hemistich of which is reported as "hasinna bihi fahunna ilayhi shus"]. It is said: "hassa bi al-shay'" (a verb with vowel patterns), "ahassa bihi" and "ahassahu" meaning he perceived it. The verb "ahassa bi" is elided to avoid the meeting of two identical letters. Sibawayh said: the same is done with any form whose final radical is pronounced with sukun, which cannot take a vowel, since they treat it like aqamta. Al-Azhari: "hal ahasta" means "ahsasta". It is also said: "hasta bi al-shay'" when one knows and recognizes it. He said: it is said: "ahsastu al-khabar" and "ahastuhu" and "hasaytu" and "hasta" when one knows a part of it; one says "ma ahsastu bi al-khabar" and "ma ahasta" and "ma hasaytu" and "ma hasta," meaning I did not know anything of it... Sometimes they say "hasaytu bi al-khabar" and "ahsaytu bihi," replacing the sin with a ya'. Abu Zubayd said: "khala anna..." [the line]. Al-Jawhari and Abu Ubayda narrate Abu Zubayd's line as "ahassa bihi fahuwa ilayhi shus," and its origin is ahassa. Ends. It is said of ẓalla and similar doubled verbs with a kasra on the middle radical in the past: "ẓalaltu af'alu kadhā" with two lams, "ẓaltu af'alu kadhā" with the first lam deleted and the fa' fatha, and "ẓalta af'alu kadhā" with the lam deleted and its vowel moved to the ẓā'.

* *

His saying, ﴿Surely we will burn it﴾

The reciters differed in its recitation. The majority of the reciters of the Hijaz and Iraq recited ﴿lanuḥarriqannahu﴾ with a damma on the nūn and tashdid on the rā', meaning: "we will burn it with fire piece by piece." It is related from al-Hasan al-Basri that he recited it ﴿lanuḥriqannahu﴾ with a damma on the nūn and a light rā', meaning: "we will burn it with fire in a single burning." Abu Ja'far the reciter recited ﴿lanaḥruqannahu﴾ with a fatha on the nūn and a damma on the rā', meaning: "we will file it down with files," from haraqtuhu uhriquhu and uharriquhu, as the poet said:

"At Dhi Firqayn, on the day the sons of Habib [...] their fangs grinding against us" [a line recited by al-Mufaddal al-Dabbi and attributed to Amir ibn Shaqiq (Lisan: h-r-q; Mu'jam ma Asta'jam of al-Bakri, 210). Dhu Firqayn is a hill in the lands of Banu Tamim between the Basra and Kufa roads]. [Further commentary on the poem follows in the source.]

The correct reading in our view is ﴿lanuḥarriqannahu﴾ with a damma on the nūn and tashdid on the rā', from burning with fire.

As related:

* Ali related to me, saying: Abu Salih related to us, saying: Mu'awiyah related to me, from Ali, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿lanuḥarriqannahu﴾: "with fire."

* Muhammad ibn Sa'd related to me, saying: My father related to me, saying: My paternal uncle related to me, saying: My father related to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas ﴿lanuḥarriqannahu﴾: "then he burned it and scattered it into the sea." I chose this reading because the authoritative reciters agree upon it.

As for Abu Ja'far, I think he followed what:

* Musa ibn Harun related to us, saying: Amr related to us, saying: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi, regarding ﴿And look at your god to which you remained devoted; we will surely burn it, then we will blow it away into the sea with a [thorough] blowing away﴾: "Then he seized it and slaughtered it, then burned it with a file, then scattered it into the sea, so that no sea that day remained without some of it falling into it."

* Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah regarding ﴿And look at your god... we will surely burn it, then we will blow it away into the sea with a [thorough] blowing away﴾, he said: In some readings: "we will surely slaughter it, then we will burn it, then we will blow it away into the sea with a [thorough] blowing away."

* Al-Hasan related to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah, regarding the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: ﴿wa-nẓur ilā ilāhika alladhī ẓaltā ʿalayhi ʿākifan la-nadhbaḥannahu thumma la-nuḥarriqannahu thumma la-nansifannahu fī al-yammi nasfan﴾.

* *

His saying, ﴿Then we will blow it away into the sea with a [thorough] blowing away﴾

He says: then we will scatter it in the sea by scattering, from which one says: "fulan nasafa al-ta'ām bi al-minsaf," when he winnows food, so that its husks and dust are blown away by hand or by wind.

The people of interpretation said things similar to what we have said.

Mention of those who said that:

* Ali related to me, saying: Abdullah related to us, saying: Mu'awiyah related to me, from Ali, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿thumma la-nansifannahu fī al-yammi nasfan﴾: "we will scatter it in the sea."

* Muhammad ibn Sa'd related to me, saying: My father related to me... from Ibn Abbas, who said: "He scattered it into the yamm, and yamm means the sea."

* Musa related to us, saying: Amr related to us, saying: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi, who said: "He scattered it into the yamm."

* Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah regarding "al-yamm," who said: "the sea."

* *

His saying, ﴿Indeed, your god is only Allah, other than whom there is no deity﴾

He says: You people have no deity except the One to whom all creatures owe worship; worship is not fitting for anyone other than Him, and it is not proper for it to be directed to anyone but Him. ﴿He has encompassed all things in knowledge﴾: He has encompassed everything in knowledge, so He knows it, and nothing is hidden from Him, nor is His knowledge of all of that constrained. From this one says: "fulan yasa'u li hadha al-amr" when he is able for it and strong enough for it, and "la yasa'u lahu" when he is unable to do it and is not strong enough for it.

Qatadah used to say about this what:

* Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying ﴿He has encompassed all things in knowledge﴾: "He filled everything with knowledge, blessed and exalted is He."

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 20, verses 99–100:

The interpretation of His saying: ﴿Thus do We relate to you (O Muhammad) some news of what has passed before. And We have certainly given you from Us a reminder (dhikr)﴾ [20:99] ﴿Whoever turns away from it, he will bear on the Day of Resurrection a burden (wizr)﴾ [20:100]

His exalted mention says to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ): Just as We have related to you, O Muhammad, the account of Musa and Fir'awn and his people, and the reports of the Children of Israel with Musa, (﴿Thus do We relate to you some news of what has passed before﴾) means: Thus do We inform you of the accounts of things that occurred before you, which you did not witness and did not observe. And His saying ﴿And We have certainly given you from Us a reminder﴾ means, His exalted mention says to Muhammad (ﷺ): And We have certainly given you, O Muhammad, from Our presence a reminder by which those of intellect and understanding are reminded and admonished, and it is this Qur'an which Allah sent down to him, and He made it a reminder for the worlds. And His saying ﴿Whoever turns away from it﴾ means, His exalted mention says: whoever turns his back on it, withdraws, does not affirm it and does not acknowledge it. ﴿He will bear on the Day of Resurrection a burden﴾ means: he will come to his Lord on the Day of Resurrection carrying a heavy load, and that is the great sin.

As related:

• Muhammad ibn Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu Asim narrated to us, saying: Isa narrated to us; and al-Harith narrated to me, saying: al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Warqa narrated to us, all of them from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His saying ﴿on the Day of Resurrection a burden (wizr)﴾, he said: "a sin (ithm)."

• al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, the like of it.

The interpretation of His saying, ﴿Abiding therein; and evil will it be for them on the Day of Resurrection, a burden.﴾

He, exalted is His remembrance, says: "Abiding in their burden." Thus He informs about those who turned away from His remembrance in the world, that they abide in their burdens. The meaning is: they abide in the Fire because of their burdens. But since the intended meaning of the speech was known, what was mentioned sufficed for what was not mentioned.

* *

As for His saying, ﴿And evil will it be for them on the Day of Resurrection, a burden﴾

He, exalted is His remembrance, says: "And that burden and load of sin will be evil on the Day of Resurrection, a burden." It is right that this should distress them, for He has brought them to a destruction from which there is no escape.

The people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) said things in agreement with what we have said.

Mention of those who said that:

Ali related to me, saying: Abdullah told us, saying: Mu'awiyah related to me, from Ali, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿And evil will it be for them on the Day of Resurrection, a burden﴾: he says, "Wretched is what they have carried."

Muhammad ibn Sa'd related to me, saying: my father related to me, saying: my paternal uncle related to me, saying: my father related to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿And evil will it be for them on the Day of Resurrection, a burden﴾: he means by that their sins.

* *

As for His saying ﴿The Day when the Horn is blown﴾

He, exalted is His remembrance, says: "And evil will it be for them on the Day of Resurrection, the day when the Horn is blown." His saying ﴿The Day when the Horn is blown﴾ is an explanation (radd) of "the Day of Resurrection." We have already explained the meaning of the blowing into the Horn and mentioned the disagreement of those who differ about the meaning of the Horn (al-sur); the sound position on this in my view, with its proofs, makes it unnecessary to repeat it here.

The readers differed in reading this. The general body of readers of the cities (qurra' al-amsar) read ﴿The Day when the Horn is blown﴾ with the yā' and with a ḍammah on it, in the passive form (ma lam yusamma fa'iluh), meaning: the Day when Allah commands Israfil and he blows into the Horn. Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' used to read it ﴿The Day when We blow into the Horn﴾ with the nūn, meaning: the Day when We blow into the Horn. It seems that what prompted him to read it thus was his seeking harmony between it and His saying ﴿And We gather the criminals﴾, since there is no disagreement among the readers that "nahshuru" is with the nūn.

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) says: The reading I choose in this is "yunfakhu" with the yā' in the passive form, because that is the reading upon which the readers of the cities agree, although the reading of Abu 'Amr has a valid aspect.

* *

As for His saying ﴿And We gather the criminals that Day, blue-eyed﴾

He, exalted is His remembrance, says: "And We drive the people of disbelief in Allah that Day to the place of standing on the Day of Resurrection, blue-eyed." It has been said: what is meant by "zurqan" (blue-eyed) in this place is what appears in their eyes from the intense thirst they experience at the gathering, visibly, as blueness. And it has been said: what is intended is that they are gathered blind, as in what Allah said: ﴿And We gather them on the Day of Resurrection upon their faces, blind﴾.

* *

As for His saying ﴿They will whisper among themselves, "You stayed not but ten."﴾

He, exalted is His remembrance, says: "They will murmur among themselves, and some of them will confide secretly to others: 'You stayed in the world only ten [days]'," meaning that some of them will say to others: "You stayed in the world only ten."

The people of interpretation said things in agreement with what we have said.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 20, verses 104–107:

The interpretation of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿We know best what they will say when their most intelligent in path says, "You remained not but a day."﴾ (20:104)

He, the Exalted, says: We know better than they do when they confide and whisper among themselves, saying, ﴿You remained not except ten﴾, and nothing that they confide among themselves is hidden from Us. ﴿When their most intelligent in path says, "You remained not but a day"﴾: He, the Exalted, says, when the one most sound of mind among them and the most knowledgeable of them says: You remained in the world only a day.

And the people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) have said what is similar to what we have said regarding this.

Those who said so:

Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Ya'qub related to us, from Ja'far, from Shu'bah, regarding His saying, ﴿When their most intelligent in path says﴾: "the most sound of mind among them."

The Exalted only meant, by the report of their saying this statement on that day, to inform His servants that the people of disbelief will forget, because of the immensity of what they witness of the terror of the Day of Resurrection and the severity of their anguish from the great thing they face, the bliss and pleasures they had in the world and the extent of the periods they lived there, until it appears to their most intelligent, most mindful and most understanding among them that they did not live there except a day.

* *

The interpretation of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And they ask you concerning the mountains. Say, "My Lord will blow them away with blowing [and scatter them]." Then He will leave them as a level plain, in which you will not see any crookedness or unevenness﴾ (20:105–107)

He, the Exalted, says: And they ask you, O Muhammad, your people, concerning the mountains. Say to them: My Lord will scatter them with scattering, and will make them fly by uprooting them from their bases, and by crushing some of them upon others, and by making them into scattered dust.

﴿Then He will leave them as a level plain﴾: He, the Exalted, says: Then He will leave their places on the earth when He blows them away with blowing. Qa'an: meaning a smooth ground. Safsaf: meaning level, with no vegetation in it, no rise, and no elevation.

And the people of interpretation have said what is similar to what we have said regarding this.

Those who said so:

Ali related to me, saying: Abu Salih related to us, saying: Mu'awiyah related to me, from Ali, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿qa'an safsafa﴾: he said: level, with no vegetation in it.

Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His saying ﴿So He will leave it a level plain﴾: He said: level; al-safsaf: the level.

Yunus related to me, saying: Abdullah ibn Yusuf informed us, saying: Abdullah ibn Lahi'ah related to us, saying: Abu al-Aswad related to us, from Urwah, who said: We were sitting with Abd al-Malik when Ka'b said: The rock is the place of the foot of the Merciful on the Day of Resurrection. He said: Ka'b has lied; the rock is only one of the mountains. Indeed God says, ﴿And they ask you concerning the mountains. Say, "My Lord will blow them away with blowing."﴾ Then Abd al-Malik fell silent.

Muhammad ibn Amr related to me, saying: Abu Asim related to us, saying: Isa related to us; and al-Harith related to me, saying: al-Hasan related to us, saying: Warqa' related to us, all together, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His saying ﴿safsafa﴾: he said: level.

Al-Qasim related to us, saying: al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Juraij, from Mujahid, the like of it.

Abu Ja'far said: Some of the scholars of the Arabic language from the people of Kufa used to say: al-qa': the bed where water collects, and al-safsaf: that in which there is no vegetation.

* *

And His saying: ﴿You will not see in it any crookedness or unevenness﴾

That is: you will not see in the earth any crookedness or unevenness.

The people of interpretation differed regarding the meaning of al-awaj and al-amt. Some of them said: by al-awaj in this place is meant the valleys, and by al-amt the hills and elevations.

Those who said so:

Ali related to me, saying: Abu Salih related to us, saying: Mu'awiyah related to me, from Ali, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿You will not see in it crookedness or unevenness﴾: he said: a valley; and al-amt: he said: a hill.

Muhammad ibn Abd Allah al-Makhrami related to me, saying: Abu Amir al-Aqadi related to us, from Abd al-Wahid ibn Safwan, client of Uthman, who said: I heard Ikrimah say: Ibn Abbas was asked about His saying ﴿You will not see in it crookedness or unevenness﴾, and he said: It is the white land, or he said: the smooth land in which there is no raised brick.

Muhammad ibn Amr related to me, saying: Abu Asim related to us, saying: Isa related to us; and al-Harith related to me, saying: al-Hasan related to us, saying: Warqa' related to us, all together, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding ﴿You will not see in it crookedness or unevenness﴾: he said: elevation nor depression.

Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His saying ﴿You will not see in it crookedness or unevenness﴾: He said: no enmity; al-amt is al-ta'adi (enmity).

Others said: by al-awaj in this place is meant the cracks, and by al-amt the rise of hills and the like.

Those who said so:

Al-Hasan ibn Yahya related to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying: ﴿You will not see in it crookedness﴾: he said: a crack; ﴿nor unevenness﴾: he said: nor a mound.

Others said: by al-awaj is meant the slope, and by al-amt the trace.

Those who said so:

Muhammad ibn Sa'd related to me, saying: my father related to me, saying: my uncle related to me, saying: my father related to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿You will not see in it crookedness﴾: he said: you will not see in it a slope; and al-amt: the trace like a sandal strap.

Others said: al-amt: the bends and the humps.

Those who said so:

Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah, who said: al-amt: the hump.

Abu Ja'far said: The most correct of the sayings concerning this is the saying of the one who said: by al-awaj is meant the slope, because that is what is known in the speech of the Arabs.

If someone says: Is there any crookedness on the earth today, so that it is said: you will not see in it on that day any crookedness? It is said: The meaning of that is: there are no valleys and obstacles in it that prevent the one who looks or travels in it from taking a straight course, as one who takes some of its paths today needs at times to go right and at times left, because of the mountains, valleys and seas in it. As for al-amt, among the Arabs it means bending and weakness, as heard from them: He stretched his rope until he left no amt in it, that is, no bend; and he filled his waterskin until he left no amt in it. From this is the saying of the rajiz (rajaz poet):

"There is no amt in the drawing of his journey"[[The verse is from mashtur rajaz, and it is by al-Ajjaj as in (Lisan al-Arab: amt), and the transmission in it is: * ma fi intiqal rakbihi min amt *

He said: In the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri: "The Prophet ﷺ prohibited wine, so there is no amt in it, and I forbid intoxication and what intoxicates." Abu Mansur said: The meaning of Abu Sa'id's saying from the Prophet is that he intended that he forbade it with a prohibition in which there is no leniency and no softness, but he made its prohibition severe; and it is from your saying: I travelled a journey with no amt in it, that is, no weakness and no feebleness. It is also possible that the meaning is that he forbade it with a prohibition in which there is no doubt. Its origin is from amt in the sense of estimation and assessment, because doubt enters it. Al-Ajjaj said: * ma fi intiqal rakbihi min amt *

That is, from slackness and limpness. End.]]

That is: from weakness and feebleness. So, if that is the meaning of amt among them, the most correct interpretation of it is: no elevation and no depression, because depression occurs only after elevation. If that is so, the meaning of the speech is: you will not see in it any deviation from evenness, nor elevation, nor depression, but it will be level and smooth, as His saying, the Exalted, states: ﴿a level plain, safsafa﴾.
